q.orig: eighteen distinct attributes of a buddha
the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas
the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas

div.p: And the benefit of directly witnessing is the passage teaching that they

q.p:
“obtain the dhāraṇi gateways and meditative stabilizations.” This should possibly be emended to “obtain the meditative stabilization gateways,” or, alternatively, it should be taken as a summary paraphrase of the whole section; cf. khri brgyad
, ’bum –, nyi khri –.
q.orig: obtain all the dhāraṇī gateways and meditative stabilization gateways
attain all the dhāraṇī gateways and all the gateways of meditative stability
who wish to attain these and other gateways of meditative stability

div.p: Then it teaches two more benefits: K, N. it teaches the benefit that they

q.p: “fulfill all the intentions of beings”
q.orig: fulfill the aspirations of all beings
bodhisattva great beings who wish to fulfill the aspirations of all beings

div.p: and that they

q.p: “complete all the wholesome roots.”
q.orig: fulfill the roots of virtue
who wish to fulfill such roots of virtue

div.p: These two are also just those characteristic of the perfecting spoken about earlier. This means they are included in the third of the four benefits listed just above, but for stylistic purposes explained later. They are taught last because they set the scene for the big flaw.

q.p: “The big flaw” “Big flaw” renders skyon chen po attested at ’bum ka 319b5, nyi khri ka 120a7. khri brgyad ka 71a1 skyon gyi spyi gtsug, and le’u brgyad ma ga 124b1 rtse mo’i skyon (“hardheadedness”), render Ghoṣa 486 bodhi­sattvasyāmaḥ or PSP 1-1: 150 bodhi­sattva­mūrdhāmaḥ more exactly; cf. Edg, s.v. mūdhāma, who comments on Ghoṣa’s reading, and Conze’s notes to LSPW pp. 119–21.—
q.orig: hardheadedness
great immaturity
great immaturity

div.p: this is called “the big flaw” because it is the head or main fault, or because it is the flaw during the peaked This renders spyi bor gyur pa (mūrdhagata; usually rendered rtse mor gyur pa). Our author likely intends the second of the four divisions of the aids to knowledge that penetrates reality. period characterized by special insight.

q.p: “A conforming love for dharmas” khri brgyad, ’bum, and nyi khri omit mthun. mthun pa’i chos renders anudharma, a word specific to this context that means something is a proper practice, but it is not so from a bodhisattva’s perspective if it is polluted by a persistent negative attachment to it. Edg, s.v. undharma, cites Childers’ Pāli Dictionary, s.v. anudhammam, as an adverb meaning “in accordance with the dhamma.”—
q.orig: a[15] love for dharmas.
craving for the Dharma
is craving for the Dharma

div.p: this is “conforming” because it is in the form of the cause that eliminates error. It is “love for dharmas” because it is together with the mental construction of them as dharmas. This relates āma = skyon (“rawness,” “hardheadedness”) with āmana (“affection for something”) and hence with vikalpa (“mental construction”).

q.p: “Form a persistent negative attachment to the notion”—
q.orig: form the notion
attached and adhere to the notion
become attached to, fixate on, and form the notion

div.p: wrong view together with mental construction is “negative attachment” when it is big; the mind is “persistent” when it is middling; and discrimination causes “the notion” when it is small. These three dharmas are in conformity with error: with erroneous discrimination, erroneous mind, and erroneous view. It also teaches that there is love for two sorts of dharma: the true dharmic nature of the perfect view of reality, and the true dharmic nature of practice.
The locution

q.p: “flawlessness”
q.orig: maturity
maturity

div.p: connotes an absence, because the thing that is the flaw does not exist, hence “flawlessness.” This explains nyāma (skyon med pa) as niyā and āma; MDPL, s.v. nyāma, “way of salvation.”

q.p: “Do not see in inner emptiness outer emptiness”—
q.orig: do not observe the emptiness of external phenomena in the emptiness of internal phenomena
they do not observe the emptiness of external phenomena in the emptiness of internal phenomena

div.p: inner emptiness is empty of the intrinsic nature of inner emptiness; it has not been made empty of the other emptinesses, outer emptiness and so on. So this means that an outer emptiness is not to be sought for in inner emptiness in order to make it empty.
Similarly,

q.p: “And… in outer emptiness inner emptiness”—
q.orig: and do not see in outer emptiness inner emptiness
do not observe the emptiness of internal phenomena in the emptiness of external phenomena
they do not observe the emptiness of external phenomena in the emptiness of internal phenomena

div.p: this means it is not sought for in order to make it empty, because it is an emptiness of its own intrinsic nature.

q.p:
“Train so that they know form but do not falsely project anything because of it” khri brgyad
.—
q.orig: train so that…they know form but do not falsely project anything because of it
While they are training, they should by all means be aware of physical forms, but they should not give rise to conceits on account of those physical forms
While they are training, they should by all means cognize physical forms, but they should not give rise to conceit on account of those physical forms

div.p: this means that they know that all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic natures and are merely just names, and with the knowledge that they are merely just names they do not falsely project anything. It explains like that up to

q.p: “the eighteen distinct attributes of a buddha,”
q.orig: eighteen distinct attributes of a buddha
the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas
should not give rise to conceit on account of those eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas

div.p: and then teaches the thought of awakening together with its good qualities, with bodhisattvas

q.p: “do not falsely project anything even because of the thought of awakening.”
q.orig: they should not give rise to conceits even on account of the mind of enlightenment
they should not give rise to conceit even on account of the mind of enlightenment

q.p: “Because that thought is no thought”—
q.orig: because that mind is not mind
because that mind is not mind

div.p: take the word “thought” as imaginary thought. It says it “is no thought” because the thoroughly established—the unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening thought in the form of the dharma body—transcends everything marked by mental construction and conceptualization, and hence does not have the mark of a thought. Therefore, it says

q.p: “the basic nature of thought is clear light,”
q.orig: The nature of the mind is…luminosity
The nature of the mind is luminosity

div.p: that is, the nature of the thought that is the dharma body is clear light. So, it “is no thought” means that it is no imaginary thought.

q.p: “A thought that is not conjoined with greed nor disjoined from greed”
q.orig: a thought that is neither conjoined with greed nor disjoined from greed
mind neither has…desire[2]
mind neither has desire, nor is it without desire

div.p: teaches just the basic nature, clear light. Even during the earlier period when greed and hatred and so on arise in an ordinary person, like space, because it is not sullied by any stains, it is “not conjoined.” Correct D bden to ldan. Later, even when a buddha, because that thought is separated from the afflictive emotions plucked out of thin air and abides in its natural purity, those stains have absolutely not arisen, and so, like space that is not conjoined with clouds and so on, it is clear light and hence “not disjoined” either. This is saying that it is not the case that it was conjoined earlier and later became disjoined, because, since it is naturally pure even during the earlier period when it is together with stains, it is not conjoined with them, and therefore later as well it is not disjoined from them either.

q.p: “Venerable Subhūti, the thought of which you say ‘it is no thought,’ does that thought exist?” khri brgyad . Śāriputra is asking Subhūti the question.
q.orig: “Venerable Subhūti, the thought of which you say ‘it is no thought,’ does it exist?”
Venerable Subhūti! Does this mind that is not the mind exist
Venerable Subhūti! Does this mind that is not the mind exist

div.p: What does he have in mind? He inquires thinking like this: When the elder Subhūti said “because that thought is no thought,” even then he gave expression to the word “thought,” so that thought would come to exist with the mark of thought. D; Golden 128b3 sems ma yin pa “with the mark of no thought.”

Then the elder Subhūti, having in mind, “I am not saying the mark of thought or the mark of no thought exists. It is not right to say, when talking about an absolute purity established as being inexpressible in its nature as being different, that it is something different, so I am saying ‘thought’ and ‘no thought’ through the force of prior usage,” inquires of him,

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, can you apprehend existence or nonexistence there, in that state of no thought?”
q.orig: “Venerable Śāriputra,” Subhūti asked in return, “can you apprehend existence or nonexistence there, in that state of no thought?”
Venerable Śāradvatīputra,” replied Subhūti, “does that which is not mind exist or not exist? Is it apprehensible
Venerable Śāradvatī­putra,” Subhūti asked in return, “if it is thus not mind, can existence or nonexistence be apprehended, or do they exist in that which is not mind?

div.p: He intends to say that when it is no thought you cannot say it either exists or does not exist, because that would be resorting to two extremes. Therefore it says,

q.p: “No, Venerable Subhūti.”

div.p: Then the elder Subhūti, because it is not suitable to express it at that time in either way because of the danger posed by the two extremes, again asks why he asks that:

q.p:
“Is then… this argumentative investigation of yours… appropriate?” This is the same at khri brgyad
. nyi khri “is then… your question… appropriate?” is better.
q.orig: how can you be correct in asking, ‘Does this mind that is not the mind exist
can you be correct in asking ‘Does this mind that is not the mind exist

div.p: After he has said that, Śāriputra, thinking that if he is saying it neither exists nor does not exist then even the mark of no thought does not exist, so why does he say it is no thought, counters,

q.p: “Venerable Subhūti, what is the state of no thought?”
q.orig: “Venerable Subhūti,” Śāriputra asked in return, “what is the state of no thought?”
Venerable Subhūti, what is that which is not the mind
what is that which is not the mind

div.p: Then the elder Subhūti thinks: I am not saying to him “no thought,” having in mind a mark of no thought in some other form. It has to be called “thought” during the earlier period when it is together with stains, because it has distortion and conceptualization, and, because something like that does not exist— “no thought” having asserted the mere nonexistence of the thing called “thought.” In order to teach that, he says,

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, the state of no thought is a state without distortion and without conceptualization,”
q.orig: “Venerable Śāriputra,” replied Subhūti, “the state of no thought is a state without distortion and without conceptualization
Venerable Śāradvatīputra,” replied Subhūti, “that which is not the mind is unchanging and without conceptual notions
Venerable Śāradvatī­putra,” replied Subhūti, “that which is not the mind is unchanging and without conceptual notions.

div.p: by which he means that the nonexistence of something that has distortion and conceptualization—like thought during the earlier period—is “no thought.”

When he says that, the elder Śāriputra, wondering if during that period it is only thought that is without distortion and without conceptualization, or whether all dharmas are without distortion and without conceptualization, asks

q.p: “Venerable Subhūti, just as thought is without distortion and without conceptualization, so too is form without distortion and without conceptualization?”
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti, just as the mind is unchanging and without conceptual notions, are physical forms also unchanging and without conceptual notions
Venerable Subhūti, just as the mind is unchanging and without conceptual notions, are physical forms also unchanging and without conceptual notions

div.p: Then the elder Subhūti explains that the buddhadharmas up to

q.p: “unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening are without distortion and without conceptualization as well.”
q.orig: unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening without distortion and without conceptualization as well
all-aspect omniscience, are also unchanging and without conceptual notions
And so too is all-aspect omniscience unchanging and without conceptual notions

q.p: “The Lord’s son, close to his bosom”—
q.orig: You are the son and heir of the Blessed Lord
You are the son and heir of the Blessed Lord

div.p: children born miraculously, in that they are born from their father’s heart, are called “children close to his bosom.” Alternatively, take this as the foremost child. So this elder, in that he is a son born from the heart-mind, is “close to his bosom,” because he has come about from attention to calm abiding and special insight. He is

q.p: “born from his mouth,”

div.p: because he has come about from explanations of the doctrine;

q.p: “born from his Dharma,”
q.orig: arisen from the Dharma
arisen from the Dharma

div.p: because he has come about from Dharma practice;

q.p: “magically produced from his Dharma,”
q.orig: emanated by the Dharma
emanated by the Dharma

div.p: because he is born from path, result, and realization Dharma;

q.p: “his Dharma heir,”
q.orig: inheritor of the Dharma
inheritor of the Dharma

div.p: because he takes ownership of nirvāṇa—the Dharma;

q.p: “not heir to material possessions,”
q.orig: not an inheritor of material things
not an inheritor of material things

div.p: because he has eliminated craving;

q.p: “a direct eyewitness to the dharmas,”
q.orig: one who sees the dharmas in plain sight
but an immediate physical eyewitness

div.p: because he is not captured by anything other than the true nature of dharmas; and

q.p: “who witnesses with your body,”
q.orig: witnesses them in the body
to the attributes of the buddhas

div.p: because he has attained the form and formless absorptions and has witnessed the dharma body.
He is

q.p: “foremost of those who are at the conflict-free stage.”
q.orig: foremost of śrāvakas who are at the conflict-free stage
foremost among śrāvakas who practice without afflicted mental states
to be supreme among śrāvakas who practice without afflicted mental states

div.p: In the śrāvaka system the meditative absorption that discourages harmful words is called the conflict-free meditative absorption. Because he is at that stage he is called “at the conflict-free stage.” Here, all conceptual thought construction is called “conflict.” Because all of that is absent, the nonconceptual meditative absorption is called without conflict. Because he is at that stage he is called “at the conflict-free stage.”
Then the elder Śāriputra causes delight by praising with

q.p: “excellent!”

div.p: and so on, teaches that a bodhisattva engaged in such an endeavor is irreversible from achieving awakening, and, having set forth all training at the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha level, and at the Bodhisattva level as benefiting this perfection of wisdom, rejoices in the fact that

q.p: “in this perfection of wisdom is detailed instruction for the three vehicles,”
q.orig: through this perfection of wisdom that the three vehicles in which bodhisattva great beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas should train at all times, without interruption, are extensively taught
it is because the three vehicles through which bodhisattva great beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas should train at all times, without interruption, are extensively taught therein

div.p: bringing the benefits of the endeavor to a conclusion.

div.head: Subdivisions of the endeavor This section begins the seventh of the eight subsections introduced earlier ( ).
div.p:
Having thus taught the benefits of the endeavor, there has to be an explanation of the subdivisions of the endeavor for those who wonder about the endeavor’s many aspects, so from here on there is an explanation of six practices that cause going forth. nges par ’byin pa, nairyāṇika, “cause going forth” (describing the true path) is derived from nges par ’byung ba, niryāṇa (describing the true cessation). Here nges par ’byung ba has the meaning of “going forth.” Below ( ) it has the additional meaning of a “definite emergence” or “escape,” and at
a yāna is understood as both a “going,” and a “vehicle,” and the great niryāṇa is equated with the Great Vehicle and has the meaning of “that from which going has gone.” The six practices that cause going forth are

item.p: practice free from the two extremes,
practice that does not stand,
practice that does not fully grasp,
practice that has made a full investigation,

practice of method, Alternatively, thabs la sgrub pa may be rendered “progress in the method.” Below ( ) our author calls this section brtson par sgrub pa, “practice as perseverance,” and ( ) brtson pa’i sgrub pa “practice of perseverance,” with the practice of method as a subset. and
practice for quickly fully awakening.

div.p: The Lord himself also teaches that these sorts of practices cause going forth when he sums up in conclusion with khri brgyad is closest but Subhūti, not the Lord, is speaking, and “will be near the knowledge of all aspects” is omitted.

q.p: “those bodhisattva great beings stand on the irreversible level by way of not taking their stand on it and will go forth to the knowledge of all aspects and will be near the knowledge of all aspects,”
q.orig: those bodhisattva great beings stand on the irreversible level by way of not taking their stand on it and will go forth to the knowledge of all aspects
they will certainly attain realization, abiding on the level of an irreversible bodhisattva. The expression…means in the manner of nondwelling.

div.p: and so on. It teaches each of the six in its own place below.

div.head: Practice free from the two extremes
div.p: Now, the elder Subhūti, in order to set the scene for these six practices, says, khri brgyad .

q.p: “Lord, given that I do not find, do not apprehend, and do not see a bodhisattva or the perfection of wisdom, to which bodhisattva will I give advice and instruction in what perfection of wisdom?”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, since I do not apprehend and do not find a bodhisattva great being or the perfection of wisdom, what bodhisattva great being should I teach and instruct, and in what perfection of wisdom

Blessed Lord, since I do not apprehend and do not find a bodhisattva great being or the perfection of wisdom, which bodhisattva great being should I teach and instruct, and in which perfection of wisdom?

div.p: and so on. This is a fourfold teaching of a bodhisattva and the perfection of wisdom, as well as of a person who is suitable to be given instruction in what cannot be apprehended by the three valid cognitions governed by direct perception, inference, or conclusive teaching, “Scripture that is authoritative about a specific instruction” (gtan la dbab pa’i bstan pa, upadeśa) is the twelfth of the twelve divisions of a buddha’s sacred speech (pravacana), an authoritative statement about a specific karmic result that has a specific karmic cause utterly hidden from any ordinary knowledge, usually a story in the Vinaya to explain particular occurrences that occasion instructions on a particular point of conduct; cf. Haribhadra (Wogihara, pp. 92–93) āgamapramāṇa (lung gi tshad ma), “valid cognition based on a scripture,” “authoritative scripture.” and a perfection of wisdom that is a suitable instruction. Thinking that he does not see them, so, as to what person K, N gang zag gang la. should they be construed, he poses the question in the passage ending with “give advice and instruction in what perfection of wisdom?”

Then, since no real thing suitable to be the instructions can be apprehended with the three valid cognitions either, “this”—the instruction in an unreal dharma by an unreal dharma—“really” makes him “uneasy,” which is to say, thinking he is unable to give instruction in a dharma that cannot be apprehended he thus teaches the passage from,

q.p: “Lord, given that I do not find, do not apprehend, and do not see any real basis…—Lord, while not finding, not apprehending, and not seeing any real basis, which dharma will advise and instruct which dharma?”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, I do not apprehend, do not find, and do not observe an entity, so, Blessed Lord, without apprehending, finding, and observing an entity, what phenomenon should I teach and instruct, and in which phenomenon

div.p: ending with

q.p: “this really is something I might be uneasy about.”

div.p: Here do not take “uneasy” as mental regret; “uneasy” is about a thing done badly. “Uneasy” renders ’gyod pa (kaukṛtya); “done badly” (nyes par byas pa) is explaining the word based on the root kṛ (“to do”) and the suffix ku (“deviating,” “bad”). He intends, “It would be a fault because I would not have understood.”

Again, persons and dharmas that are real things do not exist when presented Golden 131b1 bzhag. as in the explanation of the instruction above; therefore, having taken them as simply just names, how could the persons and the dharmas wax and wane? With that thought he makes this statement:

q.p: “Because, Lord, given that I do not find, do not apprehend, and do not see all dharmas, this really is something I might be uneasy about, how I might make just the name bodhisattva and just the name perfection of wisdom wax and wane.”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, for me, apprehending or finding thus neither an increase nor a decrease in any phenomena, to cause an increase or decrease in just the names…would be regrettable
Blessed Lord…to increase or decrease as mere names

div.p: “Wax” is the over-reification of what does not truly exist; “wane” is the over-negation of what does truly exist.
Then, in order to teach that even those very names are not real things, he says,

q.p: “Lord, furthermore, that name does not stand alone and does not meet up with anything. And why? It is because that name does not exist.”
q.orig: Lord, furthermore, that name does not stand alone and does not meet up with anything…And why? It is because that name does not exist
Blessed Lord, those names, too, have no location, no presence, and no influence…Why? It is because those names do not exist that those names have no location, no presence, and no influence
“Blessed Lord, even those names are unstable, intangible, and powerless… Why? Since those names do not exist, therefore those names are unstable, intangible, and powerless.

div.p: “Does not stand alone” means a compounded dharma thus does not stand; “does not meet up with anything” means that an uncompounded dharma like space and so on does not stand.

After teaching like that, Subhūti, in order to further teach that, having seen every other dharma freed from the extremes of over-reification and over-negation, he does not see anything that could be labeled with the names bodhisattva or perfection of wisdom, says,

q.p: “Lord, given that I do not apprehend and do not see the waxing and waning of form,”
q.orig: Lord, given that I do not apprehend and do not see the waxing and waning of form
Blessed Lord, I do not apprehend and do not consider whether physical forms increase or decrease
Blessed Lord, I do not apprehend and do not observe whether physical forms increase or decrease

div.p:
and so on. Our own Lord Buddha and the tathāgatas together with their śrāvaka saṅghas and bodhisattva communities in as many world systems in the ten directions as there are sand particles in the Gaṅgā River teach the suchness of all the dharmas: the aggregates, constituents, sense fields, six contacts, six feelings, and six elements; the links of dependent origination; greed, hatred, and confusion; obsessions, obscurations, proclivities, fetters, and views; a self, a living being, a creature and so on (the thirteen); all the perfections; all the emptinesses; the dharmas on the side of awakening, gateways to liberation, four concentrations, four immeasurables, and formless absorptions; the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; morality; giving away; the gods; disgust at what is included in the body; The disgust is separate in the list in khri brgyad
; ’bum
; nyi khri ; PSP 1-1: 158, le’u brgyad ma ga 132b4 omit. breathing in and out; death; the five eyes, six clairvoyances, ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four detailed and thorough knowledges, eighteen distinct attributes of a buddha, and five appropriating aggregates that are like a dream, illusion, mirage, city of the gandharvas, echo, apparition, reflection in the mirror, and magical creation; isolation, calm, nonproduction, nonstopping, nonappearing, not occasioning anything, nondefilement, and nonpurification; suchness, unmistaken suchness, unaltered suchness, the true nature of dharmas, the dharma-constituent, the establishment of dharmas, the certification of dharmas, the very limit of reality, and the inconceivable element; the wholesome and unwholesome, basic immorality and not basic immorality, with outflows and without outflows, with afflictions and without afflictions, ordinary and extraordinary, compounded and uncompounded, defiled and purified, and saṃsāra and nirvāṇa dharmas; and the past, future, and present.
What is the difference between the terms

q.p: “suchness, unmistaken suchness,”
q.orig: the real nature, the unmistaken real nature

div.p: and so on? They are differentiated because the referent of the thoroughly established differs.
Here the mark of the thoroughly established is ninefold:

item.p: the thoroughly established that is indestructible,
the thoroughly established without error,
the thoroughly established that does not alter,
the thoroughly established that is the nature of things,
the thoroughly established that is the state causing all purification dharmas,
the thoroughly established that is constant,
the thoroughly established that is irreversible,
the thoroughly established that is true reality, and
the thoroughly established beyond the path of logic.

div.p: The thoroughly established that is indestructible is called suchness, because it always stays just like that without being destroyed.
The thoroughly established without error is called unmistaken suchness because it is without mistakes and is not a form of error.
The thoroughly established that does not alter is called unaltered suchness because it does not change.
The thoroughly established in its intrinsic nature is called the true nature of dharmas because it is the mark that all dharmas share—having emptiness for their intrinsic nature.

The thoroughly established that is the cause of all purification dharmas is called the dharma-constituent because it is the constituent and cause of all the buddhadharmas—the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so on.

The mark of the thoroughly established that is constant is called the establishment of dharmas because it remains constantly, because it says, PSP 1-2: 63 yā utpādād vā tathāgatānāṃ anutpādād vā sthitaivaiṣā dharmāṇāṃ dharmatā; khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Whether the tathāgatas arise or whether they do not arise this true nature of dharmas simply remains.”
q.orig: whether the tathāgatas arise or whether the tathāgatas do not arise, this true dharmic nature of dharmas simply remains

div.p: The thoroughly established that is irreversible is called the certification of dharmas because by breaking through to “Breaking through” (rab tu rtogs, prativyadh); alternatively, “awaken to” (rab tu rtogs, prabudh). the first level on up one goes forth to a state in which perfection is certain because one will have gone forth to perfect, complete awakening—to flawlessness.
The thoroughly established that is true reality is called the very limit of reality because it reaches its limit in reality, in the true reality that is without error.

The thoroughly established beyond the limit K, N mtha’; D lam (“path”). of logic is called the inconceivable element because it is inexpressible, self-reflexive analytic knowledge beyond the scope of all inference.
Furthermore, all imaginary phenomena are

q.orig: dreamlike
dreamlike

div.p: because they are not like that when awakening has happened. The opposite of those is called suchness, because suchness exists at all times.
All dharmas are like

q.orig: magical display
an illusion

div.p: because they are mistaken appearances, so the opposite of those is called unmistaken suchness, because it is an unmistaken nature.
All dharmas are like

because while they are one thing they look like something else, so the opposite of those is called unaltered suchness because it does not ever change. The Skt anya is rendered “one thing” (gzhan, anya), “something else” (gzhan, anya), “unaltered (mi ’gyur pa, ananya) suchness,” and “does not change” (mi gyur pa, anyathā-).
All dharmas are like

p.distinct: a reflection of the moon in water

q.orig: the moon in water
resemble the moon in water

div.p: because, while that is not the actual nature of that phenomenon, it appears as that phenomenon’s actual nature, so the opposite of those is called the true nature of dharmas, because it is the nature of the ultimate.
All dharmas are like
because they are meaningless. The opposite of those is called the dharma-constituent because it is the cause of the buddhadharmas and is meaningful.
All dharmas are like
because they are fleeting. The opposite of those is called the establishment of dharmas because its mark is lasting.
All dharmas are like

q.orig: an optical aberration
an optical aberration

div.p: because they have a nature that is not fixed. The opposite of those is the certification of dharmas because its nature is fixed.
All dharmas are like

q.orig: a reflection
a reflection

div.p: because they are a transference of consciousness. The opposite of those is the very limit of reality because it is the ultimate.
All dharmas are like

q.orig: a phantom emanation
a magical display[1]

div.p: because they are karmically created by mind. The opposite of those is the inconceivable element because it is beyond the entire scope of the thinking mind.
Ultimately these are all synonyms of the thoroughly established.

Having eliminated over-reification and over-negation by teaching that you cannot apprehend the waxing and waning of all phenomena, to teach that a name cannot be apprehended, he says, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Lord, whatever this designation bodhisattva that is a conventional term for the true nature of dharmas is, it cannot be said to be aggregates, or constituents, or sense fields,”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, the phenomena that the term bodhisattva might symbolize and the phenomena that it might designate cannot be expressed as anything at all—aggregates, sensory elements, sense fields
That which is…mental phenomena

div.p: and so on. This teaching is in two parts. I understand our author to be interpreting the version of the Sūtra he is reading as having three sections, the first two of which comprise the first section. He understands the passage as saying that the aggregates and so on that are the basis for designating a bodhisattva cannot be said to be wholesome, and so on, by saying the words dream and so on. LSPW renders the three as: (1) “anything to correspond to the word ‘Bodhisattva,’ ” (2) “to what, then, could that word ‘Bodhisattva[’] refer?” and (3) “the reality corresponding to ‘Bodhisattva.’ ”

The subsection of the passage ’gres renders hāraka; MW, s.v. hāraka, “a kind of prose composition.” saying “it cannot be said to be… at all” teaches that a name Golden 134b4 ming phung po; D ming dang phung po. is not included in the collection of dharmas—the aggregates, constituents, sense fields, and so on. The subsection of the passage saying “cannot be said to be anything” khri brgyad
, ’bum
, nyi khri all have gang gis kyang, not gang yang. teaches not being included in the true dharmic nature of

q.p: “wholesome or unwholesome or neutral, basic immorality or not basic immorality,”
q.orig: wholesome or unwholesome or neutral, to be basic immorality or not basic immorality
virtuous…untainted by inadmissible transgressions
virtuous or nonvirtuous, a basic transgression or not a basic transgression,

div.p: and so on.
The subsection of the passage saying “cannot be said by anything at all” teaches by saying the names for

q.p: “dream, illusion, mirage, city of the gandharvas, echo, apparition, a reflection in the mirror, and magical creation,”
q.orig: dream[1]…magical creation[1]
dream[1]…phantom emanation of the tathāgatas[1]
the term[1]…anything at all[7]

div.p: which are absolutely nonexistent but still are renowned in the world; for

q.p: “space, earth, water, fire, and wind,”
q.orig: space[1]…wind[1]
space[1]…wind[1]
space[1]…wind[1]

div.p: which are renowned as having the mark of just conceptualized phenomena; for

q.p: “suchness, unmistaken suchness, unaltered suchness, true nature of dharmas, dharma-constituent, establishment of dharmas, certification of dharmas, and very limit of reality,”
q.orig: suchness[1]…very limit of reality[1]
real nature[1]…very limit of reality[1]
real nature[1]…very limit of reality[1]

div.p: which are renowned as having the mark of the thoroughly established; for all the perfections that are renowned as the true dharmic nature of bodhisattvas; for

q.p: “morality, meditative stabilization, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and seeing of liberation,”
q.orig: morality[2]…knowledge and seeing of liberation[1]
[aggregate of] ethical discipline…[aggregate of] seeing the wisdom of liberation
ethical discipline[1]…knowledge and seeing of liberation[1]

div.p: all of which are renowned as the true dharmic nature of śrāvakas; and for

q.p: “stream enterer, once-returner, non-returner, worthy one, and pratyekabuddha”;
q.orig: stream enterer dharmas and the names once-returner, non-returner, worthy one, pratyekabuddha
entering the stream to nirvāṇa[1]…individual enlightenment[1]
one who has entered the stream[1]…pratyekabuddha[1]

div.p: and for

q.p: “stream enterer dharmas,”
q.orig: attributes of one entering the stream to nirvāṇa
attributes of one who has entered the stream

div.p: and so on; and for

q.p: “bodhisattva, bodhisattva dharmas… and buddha, and buddhadharmas.”
q.orig: bodhisattva[2]…buddha dharmas[1]
bodhisattva[2]…attributes of a completely awakened buddha

the term bodhisattva cannot be expressed as anything at all, and the term attributes of a bodhisattva cannot be expressed as anything at all; and the term perfectly complete buddha cannot be expressed as anything at all, and the term attributes of a perfectly complete buddha cannot be expressed as anything at all

div.p:
Then, at the end of just that practice free from the two extremes, again, in conclusion, to teach going forth, the passage, up to the end, says, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “You should know that bodhisattva great beings stand on the irreversible level by way of not taking their stand on it and will go forth to the knowledge of all aspects.”
q.orig: you should know that those bodhisattva great beings stand on the irreversible level by way of not taking their stand on it and will go forth to the knowledge of all aspects
abiding on the level of an irreversible bodhisattva. The expression abiding means in the manner of nondwelling
you should know that those bodhisattva great beings will certainly dwell on the level of an irreversible bodhisattva, dwelling in the manner of not dwelling.

div.head: Practice that does not stand
div.p: Having thus given the names and taught the dharmas of the practice free from the two extremes, after that, to teach the practice that does not stand, it says,

q.p: “Furthermore, Lord, bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom should not stand in form,”
q.orig: Furthermore, Lord, bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom should not stand in form
Moreover, Blessed Lord, when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom…they should not dwell in physical forms
Moreover, Blessed Lord, when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell in physical forms

div.p: and so on.
It also teaches this practice in two parts: not standing in dharmas and not standing in the true nature of dharmas.
Among these, not standing in dharmas is the passage from where it says

q.p: “should not stand in form,”
q.orig: should not stand in form
they should not dwell in physical forms
they should not dwell in physical forms

div.p:
up to, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Because of this one of many explanations, Lord, when bodhisattva great beings are practicing the perfection of wisdom they should not stand in syllables.”
q.orig: Because of this one of many explanations, Lord, bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom should not stand in syllables
Blessed Lord, those are the formulations explaining how, when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell in the syllables
Moreover, Blessed Lord, when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell in syllables

div.p: Not standing in the true nature of dharmas is the passage from where it says,

q.p: “Furthermore, Lord, bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom should not stand in ‘form is impermanent,’ ”
q.orig: Furthermore, Lord, bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom should not stand in… impermanent[1]
Moreover, Blessed Lord, when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell in the notion that physical forms are impermanent
Moreover, Blessed Lord, when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, they should not dwell in the notion that physical forms are impermanent

div.p:
and ending with khri brgyad
.

q.p: “and therefore do not fulfill the perfection of wisdom and go forth to the knowledge of all aspects.”
q.orig: Without perfecting the perfection of wisdom, they will not be emancipated in all-aspect omniscience
Without perfecting the perfection of wisdom, they do not go forth to all-aspect omniscience.

div.p:
At the end of listing the dharmas within the context of explaining the practice free from the two extremes, it says khri brgyad
. It is noteworthy that “will be near the knowledge of all aspects” is omitted here.

q.p: “[they] stand on the irreversible level by way of not taking their stand on it and will go forth to the knowledge of all aspects.”
q.orig: those bodhisattva great beings stand on the irreversible level by way of not taking their stand on it and will go forth to the knowledge of all aspects
abiding on the level of an irreversible bodhisattva. The expression abiding means in the manner of nondwelling.
those bodhisattva great beings will certainly dwell on the level of an irreversible bodhisattva, dwelling in the manner of not dwelling.

div.p: Because it says “by way of not taking their stand,” it should be taken as a segue to the category of the practice that does not stand.
Now an explanation has to be given that lists the dharmas within the context of explaining all the practices that do not stand, so, having taught that they do not stand in the five aggregates, with

q.orig: bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom should not stand in form; they should not stand in feeling, perception, volitional factors,…or consciousness
they should not dwell in physical forms… and they should not dwell in feelings, perceptions, formative predispositions, or consciousness

they should not dwell in physical forms, they should not dwell in feelings, they should not dwell in perceptions, they should not dwell in formative predispositions, and they should not dwell in consciousness;

div.p:
it then, taking form as its point of departure, also gives the reason why they do not stand in each of them separately, with, ’bum , nyi khri , and khri brgyad
. All differ slightly in unimportant details from the passage cited here.

q.p: “Lord, it is because form is empty of form… that emptiness of form is not form, and emptiness is not other than form. Form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form.”
q.orig: Lord, it is because…emptiness itself is…form[7]

Blessed Lord, it is because physical forms are empty of physical forms. The emptiness of physical forms is not physical forms, and emptiness does not exist elsewhere apart from physical forms. The nature of physical forms is indeed emptiness and emptiness indeed is physical forms

If you ask why, Blessed Lord, it is because physical forms are empty of physical forms. That emptiness of physical forms is not physical forms. Emptiness is not other than physical forms. The physical forms themselves are emptiness, and emptiness is the physical forms.

div.p: The intention is as follows: Earlier it said that they “should not stand in form,” and it said that it is “because form is empty of form.” There are three types of form: falsely imagined form, conceptualized form, and the true dharmic nature of form.
Among these, the form ordinary foolish beings take to be defined as an easily breakable or seeable real thing is imaginary form.
The aspect in which just that appears as real as an object of consciousness is conceptualized form.
Just the bare thoroughly established suchness separated from those two falsely imagined and conceptualized form aspects is the true dharmic nature of form. It is

q.p: “empty”

div.p: because it is empty of the definitions—being seeable and so on—of imaginary phenomena, and of any form conceptualized as a form appearing in the aspect of an object. This, like the earlier passage ( ), is important for understanding the discussion of the other-emptiness (gzhan stong) doctrine in fourteenth century Tibet.

When this is said, someone might entertain a doubt, thinking that that which is the true dharmic nature of form empty of the imaginary form and conceptualized form might have a definition of form that is quite other, and it might then also be called “form.” It therefore says

q.p: “that emptiness of form is not form.”
q.orig: that emptiness of form[3] is not form[4]
The emptiness of physical forms is not physical forms
That emptiness of physical forms is not physical forms.

div.p: This means the suchness K, N de bzhin nyid, D de nyid, “just that” (tad eva); also “true reality” (tattva). empty of imaginary and conceptualized form that is the true dharmic nature of form marking the thoroughly established does not have form for its intrinsic nature because it is totally isolated from form aspects.

When this is said, someone might entertain a doubt, thinking that if form is totally nonexistent, well then, that of which it is empty is called “emptiness,” and without the object there is no emptiness, so, a true dharmic nature that is other than a dharma is not tenable, and a dharma that is other than a true dharmic nature is not tenable either. Here “true dharmic nature” means the true nature that is the ultimate attribute, emptiness, and the dharma that is the possessor of that attribute (=dharmin) as something that can be said of everything, including even emptiness itself. It therefore says

q.p: “and emptiness is not other than form.”
q.orig: and emptiness is not other than form[5]
and emptiness does not exist elsewhere apart from physical forms
Emptiness is not other than physical forms.

div.p: What does this teach? It means that just as water that is not clear is called “dirty” when it is not clear, and “clear water” when it is clear, and just as space is called “cloudy” when it is not clear, and “clear space” when it is clear, similarly with this emptiness. In nonpure contexts you use the word “form” and so on for it, in order not to be different from ordinary fools, and in pure contexts you call it “emptiness.” Therefore the dharmas, form and so on, that are different from emptiness do not exist. Because a difference between dharmas and the true nature of dharmas does not exist, when you set forth a dharma as the true dharmic nature

q.p: “form itself is emptiness, and”
q.orig: form[6]…itself is emptiness, and
physical forms is indeed emptiness
The physical forms themselves are emptiness

div.p: when you have set forth the true dharmic nature as a dharma

q.p: “emptiness itself is form.”
q.orig: emptiness itself is…form[7]
emptiness indeed is physical forms
emptiness is the physical forms

div.p: Alternatively, in

q.p: “form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form,”
q.orig: physical forms is indeed emptiness and…emptiness indeed is physical forms
The physical forms themselves are emptiness, and emptiness is the physical forms.

div.p: take emptiness as suchness, as the true dharmic nature of form.
Thus, it says

q.p: “they should not stand in form,”
q.orig: bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom should not stand in form
they should not dwell in physical forms
they should not dwell in physical forms

div.p: because it is not suitable for them to stand in imaginary and conceptualized forms that are absolutely nonexistent, and it is also not suitable for them to stand in thoroughly established form.
Similarly, connect this with

q.p: “feeling”
q.orig: feelings
feelings

div.p: and so on.

q.p: “Should not stand in syllables”
q.orig: should not dwell in syllables
they should not dwell in syllables

div.p: and so on—they should not stand in seed syllables. A “seed syllable” (yi ge’i ’bru, vyañjana) here means an acronym.

q.p: “Should not stand in syllable accomplishment”—
q.orig: in syllable accomplishment
should not dwell in the words that these form
They should not dwell in syllable accomplishments.

div.p:
the term “syllable accomplishment” is used for the production of the knowledge of anutpāda (“nonproduction”) after resorting to the seed syllable a, and so on, used as a dhāraṇī. This teaches that they should not stand there either. That dhāraṇī knowledge is a product of such explanations as khri brgyad
. “Unproduced from the very beginning” renders ādy-anutpannatvād.

q.p: “a is the door to all dharmas because they are unproduced from the very beginning.”
q.orig: a[8]…is the gateway to all dharmas because they are unproduced from the very beginning
The letter…is the gateway to all phenomena for their being nonarising
the a is the gateway to all phenomena, because they have not arisen

div.p:
That statement, furthermore, becomes a condition for full awakening when certain bodhisattvas with sharp faculties resort to the single statement and enter into the meaning of nonproduction. It happens when those with middling faculties resort to two syllables and have become familiar with two statements. Many statements become a condition for full awakening when those with dull faculties resort to them and have become familiar with them. Hence it says khri brgyad
.

q.p: “should not stand… in a single explanation, in two explanations, or in a number of different explanations.”
q.orig: should not stand in syllables, in syllable accomplishment,…in a single explanation, in two explanations, or in a number of different explanations
should not dwell in singular expressions, dual expressions, or plural expressions
They should not dwell in singular expressions, dual expressions, or plural expressions

div.p:
Also, in the subsection of the passage about not standing in Golden 138a1; D chos nyid gnas, “the true nature of dharmas standing.” the true nature of dharmas, it says khri brgyad
.

q.p: “form that is impermanent is empty of the intrinsic nature of form that is impermanent.”
q.orig: form[2] that is impermanent…is empty of the intrinsic nature of form that is impermanent
the impermanence of physical forms is empty of the impermanence of physical forms
they should not dwell in the notion that physical forms are impermanent…If you ask why, Blessed Lord, it is because the impermanence of physical forms is empty of the impermanence of physical forms

div.p: The impermanence of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is marked by production and cessation, that is, is marked as a falsely imagined phenomenon. The nonexistent thing that is the meaning based on the bodhisattvas’ definition of impermanence is said to be “the meaning of impermanence.” Thus, existing permanently is called permanence. A permanently nonexistent thing, being nonexistent at all times, the opposite of that, is said to be the bodhisattvas’ impermanence. Hence it is saying that impermanence is ultimately marked by nonexistence. “Form that is impermanent is empty of the intrinsic nature of form that is impermanent”: that true reality, the ultimately “impermanent” of the bodhisattvas, is “empty of the intrinsic nature of the impermanent” marked by production and cessation that is conceptualized by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“And why?” It says, ’bum (ka 378a3), nyi khri (ka 136a4) gzugs mi rtag pa nyid kyi stong pa nyid, “emptiness of the impermanence of form.”

q.p: “Also, that which is the emptiness of form that is impermanent is not the impermanence of form.”
q.orig: The emptiness of the impermanence of physical forms is not the impermanence of physical forms
That emptiness of the impermanence of physical forms is not the impermanence of physical forms

div.p: This means that that which, ultimately, is the true reality that is the impermanence of form is not the intrinsic nature of the impermanence of imaginary form, and therefore the ultimate impermanence of form is empty of the impermanence of imaginary form.

To those who think, “In that case the true nature of a dharma is different from the dharma,” it says This exact wording is not found in khri brgyad
, nor in ’bum or nyi khri .

q.p: “and form that is impermanent is not other than emptiness.”
q.orig: emptiness does not exist elsewhere apart from the impermanence of physical forms
and emptiness is not other than the impermanence of physical forms

div.p: This means that there is no impermanence of a falsely imagined form other than suchness, like clean water and space.
Because they are not different, it says ’bum and nyi khri .

q.p: “and emptiness itself is form that is impermanent.”
q.orig: emptiness indeed is the impermanence of physical forms
and emptiness is the impermanence of physical forms

div.p: The idea is that emptiness is a word to convey the emptiness of form that is impermanent.
Connect this in the same way with all the rest.

div.head: Practice that does not fully grasp
div.p:
Having thus taught practice that does not stand, to teach the faults of standing, it says, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Furthermore, Lord, when bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means stand in form with a mind that has descended into grasping at ‘I’ and grasping at ‘mine,’ they practice an enactment “Enactment” renders abhisaṃskāra; Conze 1973a, s.v. anabhisaṃskāra, “put together, brought together.” of form, and they do not practice the perfection of wisdom,”
q.orig: Furthermore, Lord, if bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom without skill in means stand in form with a mind that has descended…into grasping at ‘I’ and grasping at ‘mine,’ they practice an enactment of form,…and they do not practice the perfection of wisdom.

Blessed Lord, if, when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, owing to their lack of skillful means, they dwell in physical forms with their minds maintaining notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ then they are engaging in the conditioning of physical forms, but they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom

Blessed Lord, if, when…bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, owing to their lack of skillful means, they dwell in physical forms with their minds maintaining notions of ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ then they are practicing the conditioning of physical forms, but they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom.

div.p: and so on. It means if, “without skill in means”—which is to say if, having incorrectly grasped dharmas without knowing that they are characterized as something that does not exist—they “stand in form,” and think, “I am, in my basic nature, form,” or “this form is me,” or “it is defined as being seeable,” then they “practice an enactment of form,” that is, a karmically formed phenomenon that ensues when there is the conception of form, “not the perfection of wisdom” that follows emptiness.
To teach the faults of practicing an enactment, it says

q.p: “practicing an enactment [they] do not cultivate the perfection of wisdom,”
q.orig: bodhisattva great beings practicing an enactment do not cultivate the perfection of wisdom
engage in conditioning do not grasp the perfection of wisdom
then they are engaging in the conditioning of physical forms, but they are not practicing the perfection of wisdom

div.p: and so on.

To those thinking, “Why, without such skill in means, when practicing an enactment of form and descending into grasping at ‘I’ and grasping at ‘mine,’ do they not attain the practice of the perfection of wisdom, and not attain the definite emergences nges par ’byung ba, niryāṇa. See to “practices that cause going forth” at . by becoming absorbed in ’jug means khri brgyad (ka 82a1) snyoms ’jug. and completing the yogic practice that does not fully grasp?” it says, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “It is because, Lord, form is not fully grasped,”
q.orig: It is because, Lord, form is not fully grasped
Blessed Lord, it is because physical forms cannot be appropriated
If you ask why, Blessed Lord, it is because physical forms are not grasped

div.p: and so on.
This is the “practice that does not fully grasp.” It teaches this practice in three parts as well:

item.p: not fully grasping dharmas,
not fully grasping causal signs, and
not fully grasping understanding.

div.p:
Among these, the subsection explaining not fully grasping dharmas is from khri brgyad
.

q.p: “form is not fully grasped, and…,”
q.orig: form is not fully grasped, and
physical forms cannot be appropriated
because physical forms are not grasped

div.p:
and from khri brgyad
.

q.p: “that knowledge of all aspects is not fully grasped, because of inner emptiness,”
q.orig: all-aspect omniscience cannot be appropriated, on account of the emptiness of internal phenomena
All-aspect omniscience is not grasped. All-aspect omniscience that is not grasped is not all-aspect omniscience, on account of the emptiness of its inherent existence.

div.p: up to

q.p: “because of the emptiness that is the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature.”
