Subhūti, emptiness is not one, not two, not three

div.p: up to

q.p: “ten.”

div.p: Summing up in conclusion by saying,

q.p: “Therefore, this is a vehicle… equally of the three time periods,”
q.orig: Therefore, this is the vehicle of the bodhisattva great beings equally of the three time periods

div.p: what does that intend? Take “vehicle equally of the three time periods” as the final Great Vehicle, a Great Vehicle that is, in its nature, one alone because it is free of all differentiation. In it, “time,” “the equality of time,” “Great Vehicle,” and “bodhisattva” are all just simply emptiness. It eliminates them all, because “in this” all falsely imagined dharmas are nonexistent.
Even having thus eliminated Here btsal is an archaism for sel, Mvy paryudasta. them, because all are, in their nature, one, it sums it all up in conclusion with,

q.p: “Therefore, this is the vehicle of the bodhisattva great beings equally of the three time periods.”
q.orig: So this is the vehicle of sameness that bodhisattva great beings possess

div.p: Having thus taught in brief, it gives a detailed explanation with,

q.p: “In this Great Vehicle you cannot apprehend same or not the same,”
q.orig: In this…not the same[2]
It does not apprehend [notions of] ‘same’ or ‘not same.’

div.p: and so on, eliminating all the branches.

q.p: “Same, or not the same,”
q.orig: same…not the same
same’ or ‘not same

div.p: that is to say, different. As for,

q.p: “you cannot apprehend greed or free from greed,”
q.orig: you cannot apprehend[2]…free from greed
It does not apprehend[2]…desire[2]

div.p: and so on, connect “greed” with “not the same,” and “free from greed” with “same.”
Having thus taught that all the dharmas are not, as entities, two, with

q.p: “a past form, Subhūti, is empty of a past form,”
q.orig: A past form, Subhūti, is empty of a past form
Subhūti, past physical forms are empty of past physical forms

div.p: and so on, it names each separately and teaches that they do not exist.

q.p: “Given that you cannot apprehend even emptiness because it is empty of emptiness, how could you ever apprehend a past form in emptiness?”
q.orig: Given that you cannot apprehend even emptiness because it is empty of emptiness, how could you ever apprehend a past form in emptiness?
Emptiness, too, is nonapprehensible because it is empty of emptiness. So how could past physical forms be apprehended in emptiness

div.p: This means “given that” when you describe an emptiness connected to form, as in “form is empty,” even that very emptiness is also falsely imagined and does not exist, “how could” there “ever” be “a form in” that “emptiness”?
Having taught that

q.p: “you cannot apprehend”
q.orig: does not apprehend

div.p: the dharmas—

q.p: “the perfection of giving”
q.orig: The perfection of generosity

div.p: and so on—

q.p: “in the equality”
q.orig: the sameness

div.p: of the three periods of time, what does is intend by

q.p: “given that you cannot apprehend even equality in the equality…”?
q.orig: In sameness, even sameness is nonapprehensible

div.p: At the level of the final Great Vehicle, all dharmas—the perfection of giving and so on—are in the nature of maturations and are fully engaged with emptiness, so even “the equality of the three periods of time” does not exist there, and the perfection of giving and so on included in the three periods of time do not exist either. Therefore, it says

q.p: “how could you ever apprehend the past, future, and present perfection of giving in the equality?”
q.orig: how could you ever apprehend the past, future, or present perfection of giving in the equality?
how could the past be apprehended in sameness, and how could the future and the present be apprehended

div.p: Similarly, connect this with them all.
As for the subsections of this passage, they should be understood as:

item.p: the section eliminating the equality of the three time periods;
the section eliminating all dharmas based on pairs;
the section eliminating the three time periods in the five aggregate dharmas;

the section eliminating emptiness in that [equality]; ’bum
ff. (Ghoṣa p. 1623), nyi khri ; khri brgyad
, Gilgit 383.14, PSP 1-2: 134 omit.
the section eliminating the applications of mindfulness and so on, up to, finally, the distinct attributes of a buddha in just that [equality];
the section eliminating an ordinary person; and
the section eliminating śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas.

q.p:
“Therefore, it is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva great beings.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Therefore, Lord, it is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva great beings
is the Great Vehicle of bodhisattva great beings

div.p: It explains through a creative etymology that because it is the vehicle of the great ones it is the Great Vehicle.

The elder Pūrṇa, setting the scene for what is going to be discussed next, says: khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Lord, tasked with the perfection of wisdom… this elder Subhūti thinks he has to give instruction in the Great Vehicle.”
q.orig: “Lord, tasked…with the perfection of wisdom by the tathāgata, worthy one, perfectly complete Buddha, this elder Subhūti thinks he has to give instruction in the Great Vehicle.”
Blessed Lord!…This elder Subhūti, who has been asked about the perfection of wisdom by the Tathāgata, Arhat, completely awakened Buddha, thinks of it just as teaching the Great Vehicle

div.p: Earlier, khri brgyad . at the start of the explanation of advice and instruction, “The Lord said to venerable Subhūti, ‘Subhūti, … be confident in your readiness to give a Dharma discourse to the bodhisattva great beings about how bodhisattva great beings go forth in the perfection of wisdom.’ ” He tasked him with the perfection of wisdom. Now [Pūrṇa’s] statement, prompted by Subhūti’s explanation of the Great Vehicle, wants, by means of that, to introduce the path that is going to be discussed next.

q.p: “Let it not be the case, Lord, that I am giving instruction in the Great Vehicle, having violated the perfection of wisdom”
q.orig: “Let it not be the case, Lord, that I am giving instruction in the Great Vehicle, having violated the perfection of wisdom.”
Blessed Lord, I hope that I have not contradicted the perfection of wisdom while teaching the Great Vehicle

div.p:
intends that the two—the perfection of wisdom and the Great Vehicle—are not different, so, by teaching the Great Vehicle, he has also taught the perfection of wisdom as well. So, it will make the statement at the end that khri brgyad
, Ghoṣa p. 1642, Gilgit 385.13.

q.p: “by giving instruction in the Great Vehicle you have given instruction in the perfection of wisdom, and by giving instruction in the perfection of wisdom you have given instruction in the Great Vehicle.”
q.orig: by giving instruction in the Great Vehicle you have given instruction in the perfection of wisdom, and by giving instruction in the perfection of wisdom you have given instruction in the Great Vehicle
you do indeed teach the Great Vehicle by teaching the perfection of wisdom…and you do indeed teach the perfection of wisdom by teaching the Great Vehicle

div.p:
The ten statements The ten statements (khri brgyad
–) are (1) “one does not assert a bodhisattva at the prior limit”; (2) one has to know the limitlessness of a bodhisattva through the limitlessness of form; (3) even such an idea as ‘form is a bodhisattva’ does not exist; (4) I, who thus do not see and do not find a bodhisattva great being as anyone at all in any way at all—to which bodhisattva great being will I give advice and instruction in which perfection of wisdom?; (5) you say ‘bodhisattva’ is just a word; (6) you say ‘self’ again and again, but it has absolutely not come into being; (7) given that all phenomena thus have no intrinsic nature, what is that form which has come into being?; (8) what has not come into being is not form; (9) Lord, you cannot apprehend those bodhisattva great beings who would practice for awakening other than those who have not come into being, so does what has not come into being give advice and instruction in a perfection of wisdom that has not come into being?; and (10) one should know when the mind of a bodhisattva given such instruction is not cowed.—

q.p:
“Lord, one does not apprehend nyi khri
mi dmigs. Ghoṣa p. 1642, Gilgit 385.14 nopalabhyate; PSP 1-2: 137 nopaiti; khri brgyad (ka 211a3) khas len, “assert.” a bodhisattva at the prior limit,”
q.orig: Lord, one does not assert a bodhisattva at the prior limit
Blessed Lord, bodhisattvas do not apprehend the limit of the past

div.p: and so on—teach the seed statements that are going to be discussed below.

Among them, “one does not apprehend a bodhisattva at the prior limit” teaches that one does not apprehend a bodhisattva in the three time periods: one that existed before, that will exist in the future, or that exists now.
One does not apprehend a bodhisattva at these three limits, so one is limitless. Therefore, having taught that a bodhisattva has no limits, it next says,

q.p: “Lord, one has to know the limitlessness of a bodhisattva through the limitlessness of form,”
q.orig: One has to know the limitlessness of a bodhisattva through the limitlessness of form
One should know that bodhisattvas are beyond all limits because physical forms are beyond all limits

div.p: and so on. This means that one should know that all dharmas, “form” and so on, do not have the three limits so they are in a limitless state; a bodhisattva is similarly limitless.
To someone who has the idea, “When one says that because form and so on are limitless a bodhisattva is limitless, well then, form and so on would become a bodhisattva,” it says,

q.p: “Lord, even such an idea as ‘form is a bodhisattva’ does not exist and is not found,”
q.orig: Lord, even such an idea as ‘form is a bodhisattva’ does not exist…and is not found
it cannot be discerned…and it cannot be apprehended that physical forms constitute a bodhisattva

div.p: and so on.

Because one cannot apprehend a bodhisattva in the three periods of time one cannot apprehend a bodhisattva entity in form and so on, so a bodhisattva cannot be found. Because one cannot be found, the two,

q.p: “advice and instruction,”
q.orig: teaching and instruction

div.p: do not exist either.

q.p: “So, Lord, I, who thus do not find a bodhisattva great being as anyone at all in any way at all,”
q.orig: So Lord, I, who thus do not see and do not find a bodhisattva great being as anyone at all in any way at all
Since in all respects, and in each and every way, I do not observe and do not apprehend a bodhisattva

div.p: and so on, is a teaching with just the meaning as the earlier teaching.

q.p: “You say this, Lord, that is, ‘bodhisattva.’ It is just a word.”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, this “bodhisattva” is a mere name

div.p: This is teaching that because bodhisattvas cannot be, they are simply just imaginary. Having thus taught that ultimately a bodhisattva does not exist, to give an example it says,

q.p: “To illustrate, Lord, you say ‘self’ again and again, but it has absolutely not come into being.”
q.orig: For example, Lord, you say “self” again and again, but it absolutely has not come into being
just as one speaks, Blessed Lord, of a self although the self has no coming into being

div.p: Having taught like that, next it teaches that form and so on, both marked by coming into being and marked by not coming into being, do not exist. Among them, about the nonexistence of the mark of coming into being, it says,

q.p: “Lord, given that all phenomena thus have no intrinsic nature, what is that form that has come into being?”
q.orig: Lord, given that all dharmas thus are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature, what is that form that has come into being
in phenomena that are without inherent existence, what physical form that has come into being

div.p: and so on. Form and so on are like an illusion, so they have nonexistence and nonproduction for their nature. Hence, they are not marked by coming into being.
After that, in order to teach the nonexistence of the mark of not coming into being, it says,

q.p:
“Lord, what has D, K, N, Golden 228a4 all read “has come into being”; khri brgyad
, nyi khri
“has not come into being.” come into being is not form,”
q.orig: what has not come into being is not form
Blessed Lord, something that has not come into being is not a physical form

div.p: Having thus taught that because bodhisattvas are falsely imagined phenomena they are not suitable to be given advice, now, based on the bodhisattva who is the ultimate true nature of dharmas, it says,

q.p: “Lord, you cannot apprehend those bodhisattva great beings who would practice for awakening other than those who have not come into being, so does what has not come into being give advice and instruction in a perfection of wisdom that has not K, N, Golden 228b1; D “has come into being.” come into being?”
q.orig: ‘Lord, you cannot apprehend bodhisattva great beings…who would practice for awakening other than those who have not come into being’?
One cannot apprehend bodhisattva great beings as other than not having come into being

div.p: What this means is the ultimate bodhisattvas have the dharma-constituent as their intrinsic natures, so they are marked by not having come into being, and because they are beyond all thought construction it is not feasible to give them advice and instruction.
Having thus taught the ultimate bodhisattva, with

q.p: “one should know that when the mind of a bodhisattva given such instruction is not cowed… then that bodhisattva great being is practicing the perfection of wisdom,”
q.orig: If when such teachings are given, the minds of bodhisattva great beings are not discouraged, not disheartened, not regretful, not frightened, and not terrified, then these bodhisattva great beings are indeed practicing the perfection of wisdom

div.p: it teaches the practice of the ultimate.

From here on, from among the twenty-nine questions and statements set forth earlier, Earlier ( ) it says there are twenty-eight questions. taking This is the Lord’s reply (khri brgyad
) to Subhūti when Pūrṇa asks why, having been told to talk about the perfection of wisdom, Subhūti talks about the Great Vehicle.

q.p: “you are giving instruction in the Great Vehicle in harmony with the perfection of wisdom”
q.orig: You are giving instruction in the Great Vehicle in harmony with the perfection of wisdom.
Subhūti, you do teach the Great Vehicle in conformity with the perfection of wisdom

div.p: as the point of departure, that array of twelve authoritative statements of specific instructions These are Subhūti’s answers to Śāriputra, nyi khri ff. (consistently mi dmigs, “does not apprehend”), khri brgyad (ka 212b) ff. (khas mi len, “does not assert”). must now be taught, and having been taught, must also be explained.

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, because beings are nonexistent one does apprehend a bodhisattva at the prior limit… at the later limit… or in the middle” nyi khri .
q.orig: “Venerable Śāriputra, because beings…are nonexistent, one does not assert a bodhisattva at the prior limit. Venerable Śāriputra, because beings are empty one does not assert a bodhisattva at the prior limit. Venerable Śāriputra, because beings are isolated one does not assert a bodhisattva at the prior limit. Venerable Śāriputra, because beings are nonexistent things one does not assert a bodhisattva at the prior limit.

Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is owing to the nonexistence of beings that bodhisattvas do not apprehend the limit of the past…It is owing to the emptiness of beings, the voidness of beings, and the lack of inherent existence in beings that bodhisattvas do not apprehend the intervening present

div.p: teaches that persons are without a self. Therefore, bodhisattvas did not exist at a time in the past, bodhisattvas will not exist at a time in the future, and bodhisattvas do not exist in the present time, and so

q.p: “one does not come close to a bodhisattva” “Does not come close to,” nye bar ’gro ba med do, is another rendering of nopaiti, rendered above by mi dmigs so (“does not apprehend”) and in khri brgyad by khas mi len (“does not assert”); LSPW pp. 244–46 “does not approach.” The closest to this is khri brgyad (ka 213a4–5).
q.orig: one does not assert a bodhisattva

div.p: in the three periods of time.
After that,

q.p: “because form is nonexistent one cannot find a bodhisattva at the prior limit,”
q.orig: because form is nonexistent one does not assert a bodhisattva at the prior limit
owing to the nonexistence of physical forms, bodhisattvas do not apprehend the limit of the past

div.p: and so on, teaches that dharmas are selfless.
They all

q.p: “are not two, nor are they divided”
q.orig: are all indeed not two things and are not to be divided into two

div.p: intends that all are marked as thoroughly established so all are the same.

q.p:
“Venerable Śāriputra, because suchness is nonexistent one does not come close to a bodhisattva at the prior limit,” Cf. khri brgyad
, which again has “assert” in place of “come close.”
q.orig: because suchness is nonexistent…and because the very limit of reality is nonexistent, the very limit of reality is empty, the very limit of reality is isolated, and the very limit of reality has no intrinsic nature, one does not assert a bodhisattva at the prior limit
Owing to the nonexistence of the real nature

div.p: and so on. The suchness of the three periods of time and the suchness of a bodhisattva is falsely imagined and therefore does not exist.

q.p:
Why, Venerable Śāriputra, should one know the limitlessness of a bodhisattva through the limitlessness of form…?” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Why, Venerable Subhūti, should one know the limitlessness of a bodhisattva through the limitlessness of form
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, you also asked why one should know that bodhisattvas are beyond all limits because physical forms are beyond all limits

div.p: teaches the second statement, because there is no prior limit and so on of those that are not limited.
The third statement,

q.p:
“Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty of form,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty of form.
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, physical forms are empty of physical forms

div.p: means form that is the thoroughly established true dharmic nature is empty of the falsely imagined form. Therefore, it says

q.p: “in emptiness form does not exist,”
q.orig: in emptiness form does not exist
in emptiness there are no physical forms

div.p: which means a falsely imagined form does not exist in the emptiness of form.
The fourth statement,

q.p:
“form is not found in form, form is not found in feeling,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: physical forms do not exist and cannot be apprehended in physical forms. Physical forms do not exist and cannot be apprehended in feelings

div.p: and so on, teaches that you do not find any dharmas when you seek for them in their own intrinsic nature or in something else’s intrinsic nature. This is explaining Śāriputra’s question was: “Why, Venerable Subhūti, do you say, ‘So Lord, I, who thus do not see and do not find a bodhisattva great being as anyone at all in any way at all—to which bodhisattva great being will I give advice and instruction in which perfection of wisdom?’ ”

q.p: “as anyone at all in any way at all.”
q.orig: in all respects, and in each and every way

div.p:
The fifth statement is khri brgyad
.

q.p: “this—that is, ‘bodhisattva’—is a name plucked out of thin air.”
q.orig: this—that is, ‘bodhisattva’—is designated by a name plucked out of thin air
this expression bodhisattva has been designated adventitiously

div.p: Given that the nature of a bodhisattva is the emptiness of ultimate reality, conventionally, in order to give it a label, it is given the name “bodhisattva” plucked out of thin air. “Out of thin air” means not there intrinsically.

q.p: “Because the words for all dharmas do not come from anywhere in the ten directions and do not go anywhere”
q.orig: Because, Venerable Śāriputra, the words for all dharmas do not come from anywhere in the ten directions and do not go anywhere
Such names do not come from anywhere, they do not go anywhere

div.p: teaches that they do not exist. In reality they “do not come from anywhere” when they arise and “do not go anywhere” when they stop.
Having taught that not only is a bodhisattva just simply a name like that, but that all dharmas also do not come from anywhere and do not go anywhere, it sums up in conclusion with

q.p: “so too the word for a bodhisattva does not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere.”

div.p: This means “the words for all dharmas,” “a bodhisattva,” and also “the word for a bodhisattva” do not exist.
Having thus taught that words do not exist, with

q.p: “because these—that is, ‘form,’ ‘feeling,’ ‘perception,’ ‘volitional factors,’ and ‘consciousness’—are simply just designated by names,”
q.orig: because these—that is, ‘form,’ ‘feeling,’ ‘perception,’ ‘volitional factors,’ and ‘consciousness’—are designated by names
physical forms…have been designated adventitiously

div.p: and so on, teaching that falsely imagined dharmas are simply words, it then, with thus

q.p: “that name”—
q.orig: That which is a mere name

div.p: the designation ‘form’—

q.p: “is not form,”
q.orig: is not form
is not physical forms

div.p: and so on, teaches that the form and so on that is the true nature of dharmas, and those names, are not different. It means “that”—the falsely imagined name “form”—is “ultimate form.” I understand our author to mean falsely imagined form “is” ultimate form because it is not different from it, because it is not there ultimately at all. Alternatively, if ultimate form is the name then it too is falsely imagined and hence not different.
Having taught that, next,

q.p: “because a name is empty of the intrinsic nature of a name. That which is empty is not the name,”
q.orig: because names are empty of the inherent existence of names, and that which is empty is not a name

div.p: teaches the reason that the name and emptiness are different. It means a falsely imagined name is empty of the intrinsic nature of a name, and its emptiness is not the intrinsic nature of a name. Thus, because names do not exist, and ultimate dharmas exist, those dharmas are the basic nature of the names. Hence the ultimate bodhisattva also does not have a name as its intrinsic nature. So, in order to teach that “bodhisattva” is a designation plucked out of thin air, it says

q.p: “so, one says ‘this, that is, “bodhisattva,” is just a word.’ ”
q.orig: one says ‘this, that is, “bodhisattva,” is just a word.’[2]
So it is that this bodhisattva is a mere name

div.p: Similarly, repeat “Repeat” renders bsgre par bya’o. A ’gre is a subsection of a longer connected passage. This is a voluntary, transitive (or causal) form of that. this in the same way with the constituents, sense fields, and dependent origination.
As for the perfections and so on being different, it says

q.p: “in that perfection of giving also there are no words and in those words there is no perfection of giving.”
q.orig: in those words there is no perfection of giving, and in that perfection of giving also there are no words.
this perfection of generosity is a mere name. The perfection of generosity does not exist in a name

div.p: The perfection of giving and so on are just falsely imagined, and the words are just falsely imagined too. The words are not lodged in the perfection of giving and the perfection of giving is not lodged in the words; both are like illusions because they are not real things. Therefore, it says

q.p: “both those words and that perfection of giving do not exist and cannot be found.”
q.orig: both the designation and the perfection of generosity do not exist and cannot be apprehended

div.p: Connect this with them all in the same way.
The sixth statement is,

q.p:
“Venerable Śāriputra, given that a self absolutely does not exist and is not found, how could it have ever come into being?” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Venerable Śāradvatīputra, you also asked why one speaks of a self although the self has absolutely not come into being

div.p: and so on. Given that persons—a “self” and so on—and dharmas—“form” and so on—“absolutely do not exist,” are not there, how could they “come into being” and originate? Hence it teaches all dharmas as marked by absolutely not coming into being. Take “does not come into being” as emptiness.
The seventh statement is,

q.p:
“An intrinsic nature arisen from a union does not exist.” Golden 230b6; at khri brgyad
’dus pa has accidentally been left out.
q.orig: there is no such thing as an essential nature of something arising from the conjuction of causes

div.p: “An intrinsic nature” is an essence. Just that which is its own, not something else’s, is its “essence.” All dharmas, form and so on, originate dependently, not independently. A person originates dependent on something else. They are just there because of something else; they are not there because of themselves. Therefore,

q.p: “given that all dharmas thus are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature, … an intrinsic nature… does not exist.”
q.orig: the essential nature of all phenomena is that of being nonentities…Venerable Śāradvatīputra, that is so! If you ask why, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is because there is no such thing as an essential nature of something arising from the conjuction of causes

div.p: Therefore, that which is the emptiness that serves to enable Golden 231a2 nus par gyur pa’i stong pa nyid; D nus par ’gyur ba’i stong pa nyid; K, N nus par byung stong pa nyid. falsely imagined form and so on is not a dependent origination; it is not contingent on something else, so it is feasible that just that is the intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Hence it says that “an intrinsic nature arisen from a union does not exist.” This means that what has arisen from a union is not an intrinsic nature. When everything has come together it arises, hence “arisen from a union.” This means arising from a collection of causes and conditions.

The explanation of that is in three subsections. One is “it has no intrinsic nature because it is arisen from a union”; one is “it has no intrinsic nature because it is impermanent and so on”; and one is “it has no intrinsic nature because it is unmoved and is not destroyed.”

q.p:
“Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, all dharmas are impermanent but not because anything disappears.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Moreover, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, all phenomena are impermanent, but that is not owing to the disappearance of anything at all

div.p: The Śrāvaka Vehicle takes as “impermanent” a dharma that has arisen, parted, and is destroyed. Here it teaches the mark of impermanence as not being like that; it is

q.p: “not because anything disappears.”
q.orig: but that is not owing to the disappearance of anything at all

div.p: In this Great Vehicle it says “the meaning of impermanence is the meaning of a nonexistent thing,” Pensa p. 60, tatrāsadartha ’nityārthaḥ; cf. khri brgyad (kha 86b1) ma mchis pa. so take the word impermanence as nonexistence. How so? The opposite of permanence is impermanence. Take something permanent to be something always there, and hence take impermanent to be something that is always not there. What is called impermanent is always, in all time periods, not there, therefore it says “the meaning of a nonexistent thing is the meaning of impermanence.” The Teaching of Akṣayamati (Akṣaya­mati­nirdeśa) blo gros mi zad pas bstan pa, Degé Kangyur (mdo sde, ma), (Braarvig and Welsh 2020), 168b.7 de la mi rtag pa’i don gang zhe na/ med pa’i don dang. What it means is because all falsely imagined dharmas, form and so on, are impermanent—that is, are not existent things—there is nothing at all that has changed from existing. If yod pa las gyur pa renders sadbhūta it would mean “there is nothing truly real at all.”
In

q.p:
“Venerable Śāriputra, it is because something impermanent is a nonexistent thing and has come to an end,” nyi khri ; PSP 1-2: 150 yad anityaṃ so ’bhāvaḥ kṣayaś ca; LSPW pp. 252–54 “nonexistence and extinction.” khri brgyad
“it is because that which is impermanent has come to an end, is a nonexistent thing.”
q.orig: Venerable Śāriputra, it is because that which is impermanent has come to an end, is a nonexistent thing
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is because phenomena that are impermanent are nonentities

div.p: take the word impermanent—not existing and not a real thing—as emptiness; construe the words come to an end with falsely imagined dharmas. Thus, it means an impermanence is an emptiness, falsely imagined dharmas have come to an end, a nonexistence. Thus “all dharmas are impermanent” is in fact teaching that “all dharmas do not exist as real things.” It is therefore teaching the thoroughly established nature of all dharmas marked by suchness—that “all dharmas are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature.”

q.p: “Similarly, all dharmas are suffering.”
q.orig: Similarly, all dharmas…are suffering
all phenomena are imbued with suffering

div.p: All falsely imagined dharmas—form and so on—when settled down on and appropriated in the form of real things, become the cause of the three sufferings, so they are said to be “suffering.” When falsely imagined forms are understood in their nature to be unreal things, are not settled down on and are forsaken, they become the cause of the nonexistence of suffering and are therefore pleasure. Therefore, suffering should be called falsely imagined dharmas. If the original compound is a bahuvrihi it would mean “suffering is called ‘what is on account of falsely imagined dharmas.’ ” “All dharmas are suffering” teaches that the falsely imagined phenomena are exclusively marked by not being real. Because they are not real in their nature all dharmas are “suffering.”

Here too construe suffering with “but not because anything disappears.” This means that suffering does not occur because anything that exists in the form of pleasure has disappeared; it is suffering because it is not real.
Similarly,

q.p: “suffering is a nonexistent thing and has come to an end.”
q.orig: has come to an end, is a nonexistent thing[2]
[and so forth] are nonentities, and extinct

div.p: This means falsely imagined dharmas that have come to an end, that are not real things and do not exist, but have been erroneously settled down on are “suffering.” Also, they are

q.p: “selfless,”
q.orig: without self

div.p: “not because anything disappears,” but because they are selfless and without an intrinsic nature.

q.p: “Something selfless is a nonexistent thing and has come to an end”
q.orig: has come to an end, is a nonexistent thing[2]
are nonentities, and extinct

div.p:
means just that nonexistence of dharmas that have come to an end is “selfless.” Construe them all like that. khri brgyad
“suffering, selfless, calm, empty, signless, and wishless, … wholesome, not a basic immorality, without outflows, without afflictions, extraordinary, purified, and uncompounded.”

q.p:
“All dharmas are neither unmoved nor destroyed.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: all phenomena are not eternal and they are not perishable

div.p: This also teaches a reason that they are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature. You can suppose falsely imagined phenomena have a certain intrinsic nature that might be “unmoved,” permanent, or might be “destroyed,” impermanent. Because, like an illusion of form, they have no intrinsic nature, they are not permanent and they are not impermanent. You cannot say of an illusion of form that it is “permanent” or “impermanent”; therefore, “all dharmas are neither unmoved nor destroyed.”

In the eighth statement, khri brgyad
. in regard to

q.p: “form has not occasioned anything,”
q.orig: form has not occasioned anything
physical forms have not come into being

div.p: “form” and so on have “not occasioned anything”

q.p: “because someone to enact them does not exist.”

div.p: Therefore they

q.p: “have not come into being.”

div.p: This is teaching that all dharmas have emptiness for their intrinsic nature.
In the ninth statement,

q.p: “Form is empty of a basic nature, and what is empty of a basic nature does not arise and does not pass away, and in what does not arise and does not pass away there is no transformation,”
q.orig: form is empty of a basic nature, and what is empty of a basic nature does not arise and does not pass away, and in what does not arise and does not pass away there is no transformation
physical forms are empty of inherent existence. That which is empty of inherent existence neither arises nor perishes, and that which neither arises nor perishes undergoes no change in its status

div.p: the “basic nature,” the intrinsic nature, of dharmas like form and so on is emptiness. Emptiness is the intrinsic nature of all dharmas.

q.p: “What is empty of a basic nature does not arise and does not pass away.”
q.orig: what are empty of a basic nature do not arise and do not pass away
That which is empty of inherent existence neither arises nor perishes[2]

div.p: In thoroughly established phenomena that are empty in their nature the two—arising and stopping—do not exist, and when those two do not exist, “there is no” aging or “transformation.” Thus, there is no intrinsic arising, stopping, and transformation, so that which is form and so on endowed with arising, stopping, and transformation, marked as a falsely imagined phenomenon, and coming into being, ultimately does not come into being and therefore does not exist. Therefore, it says

q.p: “what has not come into being is not form,”
q.orig: What has not come into being is not form
phenomena that are unconditioned are not physical forms

div.p: up to

q.p: “what has not come into being is not consciousness,”
q.orig: consciousness
consciousness

div.p: and so on.
In the tenth statement,

q.p: “what has not come into being is the perfection of wisdom, and the perfection of wisdom is what has not come into being,”
q.orig: that which has thus not come into being is the perfection of wisdom, and that which is the perfection of wisdom has not come into being

div.p: take the words “what has not come into being” as suchness, that is, as emptiness; take the words “the perfection of wisdom” as suchness too. So the two—something that has not come into being and the perfection of wisdom—are not different. Therefore, it says,

q.p: “Does what has not come into being give advice and instruction in a perfection of wisdom that has not come into being?”
q.orig: one who has not come into being should give teachings and instruction in the perfection of wisdom that has also not come into being

div.p: This means how will emptiness give advice to emptiness?
In the eleventh statement,

q.p: “do not see ‘what has not come into being as one thing and a bodhisattva as another,’ ”
q.orig: do not observe that something that has not come into being is one distinct thing and the bodhisattva another

div.p: it teaches that a bodhisattva great being is the emptiness of an intrinsic nature.

q.p: “What has not come into being and form are not two”
q.orig: what has not come into being and form are not two
not having come into being…are not two things

div.p: is teaching from the perspective of the true dharmic nature of form.
In the twelfth statement, it means when they examine

q.p: “all dharmas”
q.orig: all phenomena

div.p: they are similar to

q.p: “an illusion, a mirage,”
q.orig: like an illusion, like a mirage
a magical display

div.p: and so on, and

q.p: “they do not feel cowed by or tremble”
q.orig: they do not tremble, feel frightened, or become terrified
they will not be frightened and they will not be terrified

div.p: at anything.

div.head: The results of paying attention to the nonconceptual
div.p: Having thus first taught paying attention to the nonconceptual, it then teaches the result of those attentions, with

q.p: “they do not then grasp, do not accept, do not base themselves on, and do not settle down on form, and neither do they label anything ‘this is form.’ ” In place of ’dzin (“grasp”), khri brgyad (ka 224a3) has khas len (“assert”); nyi khri (ka 344a6) dmigs (“apprehend”). Gilgit 400.8–9 (na) upaiti.
q.orig: they do not then assert, do not accept, do not base themselves on, and do not settle down on form, and neither do they label anything ‘this is form’;
they do not apprehend, do not grasp, and do not dwell on physical forms as ‘physical forms

div.p: Thus, it makes five statements in order to teach the stages K, N rim pa; D rigs pa, “logic.” of grasping. At the start they do not grasp by forming an idea; they do not accept with the thinking mind; they do not base themselves on it with the intellect; then they do not settle down on it with a view; and then they do not label it for others with a word.

q.p:
“And why? Lord, it is because form is not produced, and the nonproduction of form is not form. Therefore form and nonproduction are not two nor are they divided. And why? Lord, it is because that nonproduction is not one nor is it many.” khri brgyad
, K, N; D “the nonproduction of form is form.”
q.orig: “And why? Lord, it is because form is not produced, and the nonproduction of form is not form. Therefore, form and the nonproduction of form are not two, nor are they divided. And why? Lord, it is because that nonproduction is not one, nor is it many.

why, Blessed Lord, it is because the nonarising of physical forms is not physical forms. That is to say, physical forms and nonarising are not two things and are not to be divided into two. If one were to ask why, Blessed Lord, it is because nonarising is not one, not two, not multiplicity

div.p: Here form that is “not produced” means the true dharmic nature of form that is not produced. “The nonproduction of form is not form”: suchness, “the nonproduction of” that true dharmic nature of “form,” “is not” in its intrinsic nature falsely imagined “form.”

In that case, what does “therefore form and nonproduction are not two nor are they divided” teach? There, the statement “form is not produced” teaches the thoroughly established, unproduced intrinsic nature. This “nonproduction of form is not form” teaches that the mark of the falsely imagined phenomenon is absent from nonproduction. Thus, it means the true dharmic nature of form, the intrinsic nature of which is nonproduction, is the intrinsic nature of nonproduction and also of the true nature of dharmas, so “form” and “not produced” are the same, that is, are not different.

The “nonproduction” in this “nonproduction is not one nor is it many” is suchness. There is no specific number “one” or “two” or “three” for that. So, it means that because specific particulars are absent from nonproduction, when thoroughly established, they all, form and so on, are a single nature.

Hence “the nonproduction of form is not form” means the true nature of dharmas that is the nonproduction of the true dharmic nature of form is not the intrinsic nature of falsely imagined form. If one leaves ngo bo nyid (svabhāva) untranslated, it means, simply, “the true nature of dharmas is not falsely imagined form.” I have rendered kun brtags pa’i gzugs kyi ngo bo nyid ma yin pa (na parikalpita­rūpa­svabhāva) literally to leave open the possibility that the author intends to say that the true nature of dharmas (dharmatā) does not have the falsely imagined (parikalpita) for its intrinsic nature, nor the falsely imagined the true nature of dharmas for its intrinsic nature.

q.p:
“Lord, suchness is not produced, and the nonproduction of suchness is not suchness. Therefore, suchness and nonproduction are not two nor are they divided.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Lord, it is because suchness is not produced, and the nonproduction of suchness is not suchness. Therefore, suchness and nonproduction are not two, nor are they divided.
Blessed Lord, the nonarising of the real nature is not the real nature. That is to say, the real nature and nonarising are not two things and are not to be divided into two

div.p: Construe this based on stained and unstained suchness.

q.p:
“Lord, it is because form is impermanent, so a decrease in form is not form. … Therefore, form and a decrease are not two nor are they divided. And why? Lord, it is because a decrease is not one nor is it many.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Lord, it is because form is impermanent, so a decrease in form is not form. A decrease in feeling…perception…volitional factors…and consciousness is not consciousness. Therefore, the aggregates and a decrease are not two, nor are they divided. And why? Lord, it is because a decrease is not one, nor is it many.

Blessed Lord, the perishing of physical forms is not physical forms. That is to say, physical forms and perishing are not two things and are not to be divided into two. If one were to ask why, Blessed Lord, it is because perishing is not one, not two, not multiplicity

div.p:
Here, because it says “the meaning of impermanence is the meaning of a nonexistent thing,” Cited above
. “impermanent” form means form that “is a nonexistent thing.” “A decrease in form is not form”—“a decrease” is because of a change in the falsely imagined aspect in the form that is a nonexistent thing. That which is “a decrease in” falsely imagined “form is not” the true dharmic nature of “form.”
“Therefore, form and a decrease are not two nor are they divided” means because both “form and a decrease” are falsely imagined and nonexistent things they are therefore just one.

“Lord, it is because a decrease is not one nor is it many.” A decrease does not exist, so, like an illusion of form, ultimately it has no specific particular number. Therefore, all falsely imagined things are just one as nonexistent things.
“So, a decrease in form is not form.” This means “a decrease in” falsely imagined “form is not” the intrinsic nature of the true dharmic nature of “form.”

q.p:
“Lord, suchness is impermanent, so a decrease in suchness is not suchness.” khri brgyad
ff. goes through categories of the thoroughly afflicted and purification dharmas but it does not explicitly include the “suchness, true nature of dharmas” category found at ’bum
– and nyi khri . However, both the longer versions omit the first “form… is impermanent” statement.
q.orig: the perishing of the real nature

div.p: Here also construe the particular stained and unstained suchness. Thus, it is “impermanent” because from the one that was stained before comes about an unstained one later. Thus construe it as: the “suchness that is impermanent”—the “decrease” that is “the suchness of form,” “the suchness of feeling,” and so on—“is not” the thoroughly established “suchness.”
Where it says,

q.p:
“Lord, anything called form is counted as not two,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Blessed Lord, whatever may be called physical forms, that may be counted among phenomena that are not two

div.p: “not two” is the true nature of dharmas, the ultimate. “Counted” in that ultimate are these, namely, “form,”

q.p: “feeling,”
q.orig: feelings

div.p: and so on. What is this teaching? It means that even while the ultimate is just one, is “not two,” with the words “form that is the true nature of dharmas, feeling that is the true nature of dharmas, perception that is the true nature of dharmas, volitional factors that are the true nature of dharmas, and consciousness that is the true nature of dharmas” it teaches the one nondual ultimate, having divided it into many aspects.
With that you should connect

q.p:
“then venerable Śāriputra inquired of venerable Subhūti” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Then the venerable Śāradvatīputra asked the venerable Subhūti

div.p:
as follows. In the immediately preceding teaching about the result of the attentions to the nonconceptual, the elder Subhūti gave an explanation in four connected sections: khri brgyad
,
,
,
. first,

q.p: “When bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom investigate those dharmas like that they do not then grasp, do not accept, do not base themselves on, and do not settle down on form, and neither do they label anything ‘this is form’ ”;
q.orig: When bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom investigate those dharmas like that they do not then assert, do not accept, do not base themselves on, and do not settle down on form, and neither do they label anything ‘this is form’

when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom and investigate those phenomena accordingly, at that time they do not apprehend, do not grasp, and do not dwell on physical forms as ‘physical forms.’ They are without fixation and do not designate them as such.

div.p: second,

q.p: “form is not produced, and the nonproduction of form is not form,”
q.orig: form is not produced, and the nonproduction of form is not form
the nonarising of physical forms is not physical forms

div.p: and so on; third,

q.p: “a decrease in form is not form”;
q.orig: a decrease in form is not form
the perishing of physical forms is not physical forms

div.p: and fourth,

q.p: “anything called form is counted as not two.”
q.orig: whatever may be called physical forms, that may be counted among phenomena that are not two

div.p: The elder Śāriputra, taking these four connected sections as his point of departure, asks the questions because he wants to hear a more detailed explanation.

Among these, in the first section, taking the three parts of the statement, “bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom investigate those dharmas like that,” as the point of departure, it asks three questions:

q.p: “What is a bodhisattva? What is the perfection of wisdom? What is it to investigate?”
q.orig: what is a bodhisattva great being? What is the perfection of wisdom? What is that investigation

div.p: They will be explained sequentially.
In

q.p: “they are called bodhisattvas because awakening is itself their state of being,”
q.orig: The term bodhisattva is employed because it designates a being (sattva) who is enlightened (bodhi)

div.p: take “awakening” as the dharma body. All “beings” have the dharma body as their nature, therefore bodhisattvas also have just “awakening” as their nature. So, it means they are called bodhisattvas because awakening is their nature, and because they are beings.

In that case, would not all beings then become bodhisattvas? There is not this fault here, because in the passage in general it wants to convey a special quality, so it is calling particular beings connected with awakening bodhisattvas. Thus, beings other than them who are not seeking for the knowledge of all aspects and who do not establish that state of being, are not connected in any way with awakening, so it is beings connected with awakening in particular who are being called bodhisattvas.
Therefore, it also teaches their special practice:

q.p: “And with that awakening they know the aspects of dharmas but they do not settle down on those dharmas.”
q.orig: It is on the basis of their enlightenment that bodhisattvas know the aspects of all phenomena, but they are without attachment to those phenomena

div.p: They “know” them as conventional truth, but ultimately “do not settle down on” them.

q.p: “Whatever the attributes, rnam pa (ākāra) is rendered “aspect” in the earlier line, and here by “attribute.” tokens, and signs on account of which”—
q.orig: the aspects, characteristics, and signs whereby phenomena are shaped

div.p: this teaches the “attributes” through which dharmas are formulated. The two—“tokens and signs”—are explaining those. Names, designations, conventional terms and so on are “tokens”; characteristic marks and behaviors are “signs.”

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, that which is called perfection of wisdom has gone far off.” The perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) has gone far off (āram itā).
q.orig: the expression perfection of wisdom denotes that which is far removed

div.p:
Because wisdom that has gone to the other side of all dharmas khri brgyad
“it has gone far off from the aggregates, constituents, sense fields, and dependent origination… all defilement… the six forms of life… the perfection of giving… inner emptiness… the applications of mindfulness… the knowledge of all aspects.” has gone far off from those dharmas, it

q.p: “is called wisdom gone to the other side.” nyi khri . “Gone to the other side” (pāram itā).
q.orig: the perfection of wisdom is far removed

q.p: “To investigate”
q.orig: that investigation

div.p: is realizing through skillful means and reasoning. “Skillful means” thabs (upāya) is part of the creative etymology of upaparīkṣa. K, N rigs pas brtags, “researching through skillful means and reasoning.”

After that, the second section is taught by, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Venerable Subhūti, why do you say, ‘…the nonproduction of form is not form…,’ ”
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti, why do you say that the nonarising of physical forms is not physical forms

div.p: and so on.

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty of form”
q.orig: Venerable Śāriputra,” replied Subhūti, “form is empty of form.
Venerable Śāradvatīputra,” replied Subhūti, “physical forms are empty of physical forms

div.p: means falsely imagined form does not exist as the real basis of form.

q.p: “The emptiness of form is not form, and is not production.”
q.orig: the emptiness of form is not form and is not production
That which is empty is not physical forms, nor does it arise

div.p: The emptiness of a basic nature that is the true dharmic nature of form is not the intrinsic nature of form, and it is also not the intrinsic nature of production.

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, because of this one of many explanations, the nonproduction of form is not form”
q.orig: Venerable Śāriputra, because of this one of many explanations, the nonproduction of form is not form
That, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, is the formulation explaining how the nonarising of physical forms is not physical forms

div.p: means because falsely imagined form does not arise skye ba med pa; K, N med pa, “does not exist.” and does not have arising as its intrinsic nature, therefore nonproduction is thus established as not form.
After that, with

q.p:
“Venerable Subhūti, why do you say, ‘It is because a decrease in form is not form,’ ” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti, why do you say, ‘It is because a decrease in form[1] is not form[2]
Venerable Subhūti, why do you say that the perishing of physical forms is not physical forms

div.p: and so on, it teaches the third section. Form and decrease are both

q.p: “not conjoined and not disjoined”—
q.orig: neither conjoined nor disjoined

div.p:
in the way explained before,
; also . form is a construct, and decrease is also a construct, so both

q.p: “have no mark.”
q.orig: no mark
without defining characteristics

div.p: In the fourth connected section,

q.p: “nonproduction is not one thing and form another; nonproduction itself is form, and form itself is nonproduction.”
q.orig: nonproduction[1]…nonproduction[3]
physical forms are not one distinct thing, and nonarising another…The nature of nonarising is indeed physical forms. The nature of physical forms is indeed nonarising

div.p:
In the way explained before,
. take “form” and “nonproduction” as the true nature of dharmas. Hence, they are

q.p: “not two.”

div.p: As for

q.p:
“they then view the nonproduction of form,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: they then view the nonproduction of form
they do observe the nonarising of physical forms

div.p: this means they directly realize suchness. As before, . it says “the nonproduction of form” because the true dharmic nature of form and suchness are the same.

div.head:
The questions and responses of the two elders
.
div.p: From here on there are the probing questions and responses of the two elders.
What does

q.p:
“Venerable Subhūti, if form is a nonproduction, up to the buddhadharmas are a nonproduction, then, Venerable Subhūti, will śrāvakas not have already gained śrāvaka awakening,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti, if form is a nonproduction, up to the buddha dharmas are a nonproduction, then, Venerable Subhūti, will śrāvakas not have already gained śrāvaka awakening

If that is so, Venerable Subhūti—if physical forms do not arise; if [all phenomena, and all the causal and fruitional attributes], up to and including the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas, also do not arise; if [the spiritual goals], up to and including all-aspect omniscience…then indeed those who follow the vehicle of the śrāvakas would have already attained the fruit of entering the stream to nirvāṇa, the fruit of being destined for only one more rebirth, the fruit of no longer being subject to rebirth, and arhatship

div.p: and so on, teach?

If “form,” and so on, and suchness were the same, in that case the understanding of form would be the understanding of suchness, and all beings would see the ultimate as well. Were they to do so, all beings would each properly reach their own respective awakening without having to concentrate on it. And then

q.p: “the five awakenings”
q.orig: the five degrees of enlightenment

div.p: would not be differentiable. stream enterer, once-returner, non-returner, worthy one, a pratyekabuddha’s awakening, and the knowledge of all aspects would be mixed up. Were that to be the case, stream enterers and so on would also be buddhas. Bodhisattvas would have already gained their awakening, so to

q.p: “undertake the difficult practices”
q.orig: practice austerity

div.p: and so on would be meaningless, and the knowledge of all aspects, complete awakening, and

q.p: “turning the wheel of the Dharma”
q.orig: turned the wheel of the Dharma
turn the wheel of the Dharma

div.p: would be meaningless as well.

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, I do not accept that an unproduced dharma has an attainment, or a clear realization. K, N mngon par rdzogs par yod pa (“is there manifestly and completely”) is an unusual rendering of abhisamaya. A later editor of the canon failed to replace it with mngon par rtogs pa, the reading in the following gloss. I do not accept that which is unproduced becomes a stream enterer. I do not accept that which is unproduced has the result of stream enterer.”
q.orig: The venerable Subhūti then replied to the venerable Śāradvatīputra as follows: “Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not hold that nonarising phenomena have attainments or comprehension. I do not hold that in nonarising there are…individuals…entering the stream to nirvāṇa

div.p: What does this teach? Nobody can attain or have a clear realization of an unproduced dharma. Given that it is unproduced, no one at all becomes a stream enterer. The elimination of mere falsely imagined obscurations, because the conceptualization of a grasper and grasped does not exist, are accepted to be the attainment and clear realization. So, it is teaching that “suchness does not realize suchness,” and hence the aforementioned fault that “the understanding of form and so on will be the understanding of suchness” is not a fault, because there are afflictive obscurations and obscurations to knowledge.

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, I do not accept that bodhisattvas are undertaking difficult practices.”
q.orig: Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not hold that bodhisattva great beings maintain the practice of austerity

div.p: It explains this because ultimately bodhisattvas do not have such conceptualizations. At the eighth level when bodhisattvas gain forbearance for dharmas that are not produced and do not apprehend any dharma at all, they undertake difficult practices free from production and so on. At that time bodhisattvas have a nonapprehending attention and do not have

q.p: “the idea of difficulty”
q.orig: the perception of hardship

div.p: when it comes to cutting off their heads and so on, or “any idea of suffering at all.” The concluding passage,

q.p: “bodhisattva great beings do not appropriate and do not apprehend any dharma as anything in any way at all,”
q.orig: bodhisattva great beings[4]…and do not apprehend any dharma as anything at all in any way at all
they neither acquire nor do they maintain any phenomena

div.p: teaches that.

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, in the absence of production I do not accept that there is the state of a tathāgata,”
q.orig: Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I do not hold that in nonarising there are tathāgatas

div.p: and so on—“in the absence of production” in the dharma body “I do not accept that there is” any tathāgata that is a second tathāgata realizing the absence of production. Hence this is teaching the unproduced state, that “a tathāgata” is the unproduced state, perfect complete awakening.

q.p: “I do not accept that an unproduced dharma attains an unproduced attainment.”
q.orig: there is nothing at all that would be obtained or that should be attained on the basis of phenomena that are nonarising

div.p: “I do not accept” that suchness realizes suchness is the meaning.

He says that, and then the elder Śāriputra asks about two alternatives: Given that something unproduced does not attain an unproduced attainment, does something unproduced attain a produced attainment, or does something produced attain an unproduced attainment?

q.p: “Well then, Venerable Subhūti, does an unproduced dharma attain a produced attainment, or does a produced dharma attain an unproduced attainment?”
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti, do you hold that attainment will ensue on the basis of phenomena that are arising, or else do you hold that attainment will ensue on the basis of phenomena that are nonarising

div.p: If something in the nature of suchness were to attain the falsely imagined results of stream enterer and so on, then “an unproduced dharma would attain a produced attainment.” Were falsely imagined persons to attain the results of stream enterer and so on that are in the nature of suchness, then “a produced dharma would attain an unproduced attainment.”
Since he is unable to accept either of them he says,

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, I do not accept that a produced dharma attains an unproduced attainment,”
q.orig: nor do I hold that attainment will ensue on the basis of phenomena that are nonarising

div.p: and so on.

q.p: “There is an attainment and there is a clear realization, but not in a dual way.”
q.orig: there is indeed attainment and there is clear realization, but not on the basis of either of those two

div.p: This is teaching that even though both an attainment of the unproduced by the produced, and an attainment of the produced by the unproduced, do not exist, still, on the mere abandonment of afflictive obscurations and obscurations to knowledge,

q.p: “attainment and clear realization are labeled by ordinary convention,”
q.orig: attainment or clear realization is designated in accordance with worldly conventions

div.p: and the person is labeled

q.p: “stream enterer, tathāgata,”
q.orig: A stream enterer, or once-returner, or non-returner, or worthy one, or pratyekabuddha, or bodhisattva—even a buddha
Those entering the stream to nirvāṇa, those destined for only one more rebirth, those who will no longer be reborn, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas

div.p: and so on.

q.p: “Venerable Subhūti, is the unproduced similar to the attainment and clear realization that, as ordinary convention, is formless, cannot be pointed out, does not block, and has only one mark—that is, no mark?”
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti, is the unproduced similar to an attainment and a clear realization that, as ordinary convention, is formless, cannot be pointed out, does not obstruct, and has only one mark—that is, no mark

div.p: Śāriputra is asking if the unproduced is, like attainment and clear realization, also ultimately nonexistent.

q.p: “Exactly so, Venerable Śāriputra”

div.p: teaches that because, ultimately, an unproduced cannot be grasped and cannot be expressed, it does not exist in an unproduced form.
Now, because even production is eliminated, it says,

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, because of this one of many explanations neither is production produced nor is nonproduction produced.”
q.orig: “Exactly so, Venerable Śāriputra, exactly so,” Subhūti replied. “Because of this one of many explanations, neither is production produced nor is nonproduction produced.”
Those, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, are the formulations explaining how arising does not arise, nor does nonarising arise

div.p: This means the “unproduced” is the thoroughly established so it is not produced; the “produced” is the falsely imagined so it is nonexistent and therefore not produced, so in “this one of many explanations… production” also does not exist.

q.p: “Venerable Subhūti, you are confident in your readiness to say again and again that ‘dharmas are unproduced’? You are also confident in your readiness to say there is no production of unproduced dharmas?”
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti, are you confident in your readiness to say again and again that ‘dharmas are unproduced’? Are you also confident in your readiness to say there is no production of unproduced dharmas

Venerable Subhūti, if are you inspired to say that nonarising phenomena are indeed nonarising phenomena, then, Venerable Subhūti, are you inspired also to say that there is no arising with respect to nonarising phenomena?

div.p: Both the terms “unproduced” and “no production” are well-known synonyms for suchness. When those two are differentiated as particulars qualifying the word “dharma”—“an unproduced dharma” and “a dharma of which there is no production”—they become words for falsely imagined dharmas.
When asked if it is appropriate to say that, the elder Subhūti again, having thought about whether the two terms “unproduced” and “no production” are well known as falsely imagined words, says,

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, I have no ready confidence to say again and again that dharmas are unproduced. I have no ready confidence to say there is no production of unproduced dharmas.”
q.orig: I have no confident readiness to say again and again that dharmas are unproduced. I have no confident readiness to say there is no production of unproduced dharmas

Venerable Śāradvatīputra, I am not inspired…to say that nonarising phenomena are indeed nonarising phenomena. Nor am I inspired…Venerable Śāradvatīputra, to say that there is no arising with respect to nonarising phenomena

div.p: Then, teaching that the two—unproduced and no production—are just falsely imagined, it says,

q.p: “And why? Because, Venerable Śāriputra, an unproduced dharma, nonproduction, ready confidence, saying something, and a state of production—all those dharmas are not conjoined and not disjoined, are formless, cannot be pointed out, do not obstruct, and have only one mark—that is, no mark.”
q.orig: And why? Because, Venerable Śāriputra, an unproduced dharma, nonproduction, confident readiness, saying something, and a state of production—all those dharmas are not conjoined and not disjoined, are formless, cannot be pointed out, do not obstruct, and have only one mark—that is, no mark.

If you ask why, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is because nonarising phenomena, the absence of arising, the act of inspired speech, the statements that are expressed, and the phenomena that do not arise are all neither conjoined, nor disjoined, and they share a single defining characteristic in that they are all immaterial, unrevealed, unimpeded, and without defining characteristics

div.p: In this statement about a ready confidence to say something about unproduced dharmas and no production, these six dharmas are indicated: unproduced, nonproduction, the absence of a state of production, a dharma, ready confidence, and saying something. That they are all falsely imagined and hence do not exist is the meaning.

You can suppose dharmas that exist are mental factors, not conjoined with mind, with form, or uncompounded. There, “those dharmas are not conjoined” teaches that they do not exist as real mental factors; they “are not disjoined” teaches that they do not exist as real things not conjoined with mind; they “are formless” teaches that they do not exist as existent things with form like the eleven The other ten are (1) the five objects of the senses and (2) the five senses. forms that are nonrevealing and so on; they “cannot be pointed out” teaches that they do not exist as things like colors that can be pointed out; they “do not block” teaches that they do not exist with the mark of the form of a sense faculty; This means the eye faculty and so on are blocked from seeing forms and so on. Alternatively, if apratigha means “unobstructed,” it means the sense faculties are not obstructed from knowing their object in the way an inert material object is. and they “have only one mark—that is, no mark”—teaches that they do not exist with the mark of the uncompounded, which is to say, there is no dharma at all that is “the mark of the uncompounded.” This means it does not exist, so they are liberated from the mark of existence and nonexistence and hence are without a mark, that is, they “have one mark”—marked by being without a mark.
Then the elder Śāriputra asks if saying something and so on are also nonproductions.

q.p: “Venerable Subhūti, is there is no production of saying, is there also no production of ready confidence, and is there also no production of a dharma? Are those dharmas that are the point of departure for a ready confidence to say something also not produced?”
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti…also not produced

Venerable Subhūti, is it then the case that those statements are nonarising, that the act of inspired speech is also nonarising, and that those phenomena about which you were inspired to say what you said are also nonarising

div.p: This means: Do “saying,” “ready confidence,” and all “dharmas” and dharmas that have to be said have nonproduction as their intrinsic nature?
Then the elder Subhūti says

q.p: “exactly so,”
q.orig: it is so

div.p: asserting that they all have nonproduction as their intrinsic nature.
Having said,

q.p: “There is no production of saying, there is also no production of ready confidence, and there is also no production of a dharma. Those dharmas that are the point of departure for a ready confidence to say something are not produced,”
q.orig: There is no production of saying, there is also no production of confident readiness, and there is also no production of a dharma. Those dharmas that are the point of departure for a confidence giving a readiness to speak are not produced
Those statements are nonarising, the act of inspired speech is nonarising, and those phenomena about which I was inspired to say what I said are also nonarising

div.p: with

q.p: “there is no production of form,”
q.orig: there is no production of form
physical forms are nonarising

div.p:
and so on, it teaches that they all have nonproduction as their intrinsic nature, teaching just what has been taught before in the section on nonproduction. Also, in this teaching it gives a reminder of the aforementioned faults—“in that case will the five forms of life not be differentiable” and so on—and gives a response to them. The section on nonproduction, including the objections and responses, is khri brgyad
–. As for

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, just as attainment and clear realization exist as ordinary conventions, similarly,”
q.orig: Just as attainment and clear realization are designated according to worldly convention

div.p: and so on, it means “just as” ultimately both “attainment and clear realization” do not exist, and “stream enterer” and so on also do not exist, “similarly,” because the three vehicles are also simply just suchness, there are ultimately no differences in the results.

There are those who have gone wrong, thinking, “But earlier, when accumulating the accumulations during three incalculable eons, there are the particular different actions, there are particular different maturations corresponding to those, and similarly, during the result period there are different afflictive obscurations and obscurations to knowing that have been produced and not produced, so, based on just those, there are differences in defilement and purification.” So it says,

q.p:
“Venerable Śāriputra, it is because ultimately there is no maturation of karma, there is no production, there is no cessation, there is no defilement, and there is no purification.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Venerable Śāradvatīputra, in…ultimate reality[2]…there are no past actions, no ripening of past actions, no arising, no ceasing, no affliction, and no purification

div.p: This means they are all falsely imagined phenomena and do not exist, so suchness does not become different on account of them.
Having thus eliminated an unproduced dharma, to eliminate a dharma that arises again it starts by asking a question:

q.p: “Venerable Subhūti, is an unproduced dharma produced or is a produced dharma produced?”
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti, do nonarising phenomena arise, or else do arising phenomena arise

div.p: Here it is asking, given that a seedling and so on is produced from a seed, is that production of a seedling the production of one that has not come into being—is it “unproduced”—or is it the production of one that has come into being—is it already “produced”?

Having been asked that, the elder says that if an unproduced seedling is produced, everything unproduced would also be produced indeterminately, and if the already produced is produced, it would come to be produced repeatedly again and again, so, because being produced and so on is contradicted by these lines of reasoning, it is not appropriate to say it is like either:

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, I do not accept that an unproduced dharma is produced, nor do I accept that a produced dharma is produced.”
q.orig: Venerable Śāradvatīputra,” replied Subhūti, “I do not hold that nonarising phenomena arise, nor do I hold that arising phenomena arise.

div.p: This means the unproduced does not exist because it is in a state of nonexistence, and because it is nonexistent it is not produced. Furthermore, the produced, because it is already in a produced state, does not arise again. Ultimately, therefore, the attribute of arising is just nonexistent.
Saying that prompts these questions: “Are certain unproduced attributes—a rabbit’s horns and so on—not produced? Or are past productions not produced?” So there are these two questions:

q.p:
“Venerable Subhūti, what unproduced dharma do you not accept is produced?” nyi khri , ; khri brgyad
and differ slightly.
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti, what nonarising phenomena do you hold not to arise

div.p: and

q.p: “What produced dharma do you not accept is produced?”
q.orig: what arising phenomena do you hold not to arise

div.p: To eliminate arising, again it says,

q.p: “Venerable Subhūti, is a dharma that has not been produced, produced; or is a dharma that has been produced, produced?”
q.orig: Venerable Subhūti, is an unproduced dharma produced, or is a produced dharma produced?
Venerable Subhūti, does arising arise, or else, does nonarising arise

div.p: A nonproduction is not produced because it is an uncompounded phenomenon, and a production is not produced because it is a falsely imagined phenomenon and does not exist, so the elder says,

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, the unproduced is not produced, and the produced is not produced either,”
q.orig: Venerable Śāradvatīputra, arising does not arise, nor does nonarising arise

div.p: and as the reason for that says,

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, it is because both produced and unproduced dharmas are not conjoined and not disjoined because there is no production,”
q.orig: Venerable Śāriputra, it is because both produced and unproduced dharmas are neither conjoined nor disjoined because there is no production
Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is because both phenomena that arise and phenomena that are nonarising are neither conjoined, nor disjoined

div.p: having in mind that both are nevertheless ultimately simply just suchness.

Having taught that, it teaches just what has been taught before in the section on nonproduction. khri brgyad
–. Thus, there is the teaching from

q.p: “there is no production of form,”
q.orig: there is no production of form
physical forms are nonarising

div.p: up to

q.p: “there is no production of the knowledge of all aspects.”
q.orig: the distinct qualities of the buddhas are nonarising

div.p: It sums up in conclusion with,

q.p: “Venerable Śāriputra, because of this one of many explanations, there is no production of saying, there is also no production of ready confidence, and there is also no production of a dharma; those dharmas that are the point of departure for a ready confidence to say something are not produced.”
q.orig: Venerable Śāriputra, because of this one of many explanations, there is no production of saying, there is also no production of confident readiness, and there is also no production of a dharma; those dharmas that are the point of departure for a confidence giving a readiness to speak are not produced

Those, Venerable Śāradvatīputra, are the formulations explaining how these statements are indeed nonarising, how the act of inspired speech, too, is nonarising, and how those phenomena about which there is the inspiration to make statements are also nonarising

q.p:
“Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty of a basic nature” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Venerable Śāriputra, form is empty of a basic nature
physical forms, being empty of inherent existence

div.p: teaches the true dharmic nature of form, so it says,

q.p: “It has no fixed position inside, it has no fixed position outside, and it cannot be apprehended without both.”
q.orig: are internally without support, they are externally without support, and there is no support apprehended outside these two [extremes]

div.p: Were it to have a “fixed position” in something, you can suppose it would have a fixed position either “inside, outside,” or in something other than “both.” Because ultimately it does not exist in all three, therefore “it has no fixed position.”
Having taught that, it elaborates excellently the marks of just that fixed position and no fixed position and teaches the means to

q.p: “purify the awakening path”
q.orig: refine the path to enlightenment?

div.p: with

q.p:
“there is an ordinary… and there is an extraordinary” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: is both mundane and supramundane

div.p: one and so on.

q.p:
“It does not move from, does not transcend, and does not pass beyond the ordinary world,” khri brgyad
. “Ordinary world” renders loka (“ordinary,” “world,” “person”). Generally, loka means both a world and a person, in the sense suggested by John Dunne’s “No man is an island, entire of itself.” The “ordinary” is the opposite of the “extraordinary,” that is, the path and the result. The ordinary is the location of a person, the five aggregates, conveyed by the standard Tib rendering of loka as ’jig rten, “perishing basis.”
q.orig: Because it does not move from the ordinary, does not transcend the ordinary, and does not pass beyond the ordinary
it does not move beyond, sublimate, or transcend the mundane

div.p:
beyond falsely imagined phenomena. The three are based on the small, middling, and big forbearance. The “forbearance” (kṣānti) can be the third division of the aids to knowledge that penetrates true reality (nirvedha­bhāgīya) or the “path of seeing” (prayogamārga). Here the context suggests a threefold division of the eighth bodhisattva level, or, alternatively, the last three bodhisattva levels. The meaning of the rest is clear. khri brgyad
–. This is the explanation of each of the six perfections as ordinary and extraordinary based on whether the bodhisattvas apprehend or do not apprehend anything.

As for the seven statements khri brgyad
.

q.p: “as which the world (as subject) exists,”
q.orig: ordinary…worldly

div.p: and so on, there

item.p: in some places it is to be taken as the world as inhabitants;
in some places the container world;
in some places the world of ordinary beings;
in some places the cycle of existences;
in some places falsely imagined dharmas; and
in some places as the five sorts of sense object.

q.p: “On account of them the world is here” This section is explaining the usage of laukikī, a secondary derivative (“worldly, to do with the world”) from loka (itself perhaps from a root like ruc, “to shine”). The explanation relates laukikī to loka by putting loka in each of the seven cases, nominative and so on. Each explanation should be understood as, for instance in the first of the seven, “[the aggregates are laukikī because it is] on account of them the loka is here. PSP 1-2:171 kena kāraṇena laukikī? loko yābhir bhavati, lokaṃ vā yābhir nivartayati, lokena vā yāḥ samāḥ, lokāya vā yābhir dīyate, lokād vā yābhir [na?] niḥsarati, lokasya vā yā bhavāya, loke vā bhavā yās tā laukikasyaḥ. “Why are they laukikī? They are called laukikī because they are those on account which the world (nominative) exists; or on account of which [afflictive emotion and karma] the world (accusative) is established; or which are the same as the world (instrumental); or on account of which [five sense objects] something is given to the world [of the six senses]; or on account of which, [the links of dependent origination and so on, they do not] escape from the world (ablative); or [ordinary beings] who are for the coming into existence of the world (genitive); or [beings] who come into being in the world (locative).” —

div.p: the world as aggregates;

q.p: “on account of them the world is established”—

div.p: the container world;

q.p: “the world is the same as them”—

div.p: the same as falsely imagined phenomena;

q.p: “on account of them there is something given to the world”—

div.p: the five sorts of sense objects are given to the world;

q.p: “on account of them they do not escape the world”—
q.orig: on account of them[3]…they do not escape the world

div.p: from the world that is the cycle of existences;

q.p: “they are for the coming into being of the world”—

div.p: the world as ordinary beings, because to come into being is to increase; This is a speculative translation based on the idea that ordinary beings procreate and increase in the world. and

q.p: “they come into being in the world”—

div.p: the world as inhabitants comes into being in the container world.

q.p: “On account of them the world goes free” This section again puts loka in each of the seven cases, nominative and so on, and explains the usage of lokottara (“extraordinary, transcendental, supramundane”) a compound word composed of loka and uttara (“higher”). In most of the following explanations, however, the word uttara is derived not from uttara, but from uttṝ (“to escape”)—for instance, the first of the seven, “[the parts of noble eightfold path are lokottara because] on account of them the loka (“person”) (nominative) escapes.” PSP 1-2:171 tatra katamā lokottarā? loko yābhir uttarati, lokaṃ vā yābhir uttārayati, lokena vā yābhir uttāryate, ālokāya vā yā bhavati, lokād vā yābhir niḥsarati, lokasya vā yā uttaraṇāya, loke vā yā uttarās tā lokottarā iti: “There, what are the lokottaras? They are called lokottaras [because they are those] on account of which the world (nominative) escapes; or on account of which [compassion and wisdom] they free the world (accusative); or on account of which [compassion and wisdom], a world [=a person] (instrumental) causes an escape; or which are there for illumination (dative); or on account of which they escape the world (ablative); or who are for the emancipation of the world (genitive); or who are the emancipators in the world (locative).” —
