Subhūti, that is due to absolute purity

div.p: Earlier it was teaching the pure perfection of wisdom, now it is teaching the purity of selflessness.

q.p:
“Because knowledge is not found and is not discarded, Subhūti.” khri brgyad
; ’bum nya 166b4, nyi khri
omit.
q.orig: Because knowledge is not found and is not discarded, Subhūti,

div.p: They do not obtain or find a transcendent knowledge that was not there before, and a transcendent knowledge that is found is also not lost, so, because there are neither, there is not even awakening. Even “awakening” is falsely imagined.

q.p:
“Nonduality and purity” khri brgyad
, ’bum nya 166b4–5, nyi khri
.—

div.p: because the two—defilement and purification—do not exist, it is pure in its intrinsic nature even before, so like space it has no defilement. And even at the period of the final outcome, it is like space that has no purity that was not there before.
Having thus completed the explanation of purity, it begins the explanation of the unlimited to inculcate belief in the deep, with

q.p: “because form is unlimited.”
q.orig: form is unlimited
the limitlessness of physical forms

div.p: It is “unlimited” because it is not permanent and not annihilated, and is not at the prior limit, later limit, or in the middle. Therefore, it says

q.p: “because of the emptiness of what transcends limits and the emptiness of no beginning and no end, Subhūti.”
q.orig: That is due to the emptiness of the unlimited and the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end

div.p: Why does the elder Subhūti ask,

q.p: “Lord, why is such a realization as that the perfection of wisdom of bodhisattva great beings?”
q.orig: Blessed Lord…why is it the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattva great beings through which this is realized

div.p: He is asking why, if the perfection of wisdom is so deep a topic as that, is it just an object of bodhisattvas, not of buddhas. It says,

q.p: “Because it is the knowledge of path aspects, Subhūti.”
q.orig: Subhūti, it is so owing to knowledge of the path

div.p: Thus, this perfection of wisdom is not the final one, is not when the work is done. It is an aspect of the path of the knowledge of all aspects, hence it is “just of bodhisattvas.”

q.p:
“Lord, you cannot apprehend the perfection of wisdom of bodhisattva great beings on this side, on the farther side, or on neither.” khri brgyad
; cf. Abhi­samayālaṃkāra 3.1.
q.orig: Lord, you cannot apprehend the perfection of wisdom of bodhisattva great beings on this side, on the farther side, or on neither,
they do not dwell on the near shore, the far shore, or the midstream between these two, this denotes the perfection of wisdom that bodhisattva great beings have

div.p: What does this intend? You can suppose “perfection” (pāramitā) is on the way to the other side (para), has arrived at the other side, or is the essential nature of the other side. It says this because, even when taken to be the perfection of wisdom of bodhisattvas, it is not positioned on this side, it is not positioned on the farther side, and cannot be apprehended on some other that is not included in those sides. “This side” incorporates the compounded; “the farther side” incorporates the uncompounded.
After saying that,

q.p: “Because it is extremely pure,” said the Lord.
q.orig: “Because it is extremely pure, Subhūti,” said the Lord.
that is due to absolute purity,” replied the Blessed One

div.p: Were any side to be apprehended, then, in that case, it would not be purity. This means it is extremely pure because there are none, and, because it is extremely pure, it is not positioned on either side or anywhere else either.

q.p: “Because of the sameness of the three time periods, Subhūti”—
q.orig: Subhūti, this is owing to the sameness of the three times

div.p: this means that with the comprehension of the sameness of the three time periods, because of the emptiness of no beginning and no end, there is no notion of this side and no notion of a farther side, and hence “it does not stand on this side and it also does not stand on the farther side.”

div.head: Attachment and nonattachment
div.p: In order to build trust that the perfection of wisdom is deep, it then again sets the scene for the explanation of attachment and nonattachment from the perspective of practices that apprehend and do not apprehend, with

q.p:
“they are attached to a name and attached to a causal sign,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: attachment to names and attachment to signs

div.p: and so on. Seizing on a dharma, form and so on, as a word is falsely imagining. Seizing on a causal sign as a conventional term is conceptualizing. Both are obscurations, so they are “attachment.”

q.p: “Subhūti, even though all dharmas are without causal signs and without names”

div.p: is teaching that they are within the range of the perfection of wisdom.

q.p: “Lord, such an excellent exposition and excellent definitive teaching of this perfection of wisdom… to bodhisattva great beings is amazing”—
q.orig: Blessed Lord, how wonderful it is that this perfection of wisdom has been eloquently explained and excellently revealed in that manner to bodhisattva great beings

div.p: this is teaching of the knowledge of path aspects.

q.p:
“When… they perceive that form is ‘empty,’ they are attached” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: when sons of a good family or daughters of a good family in the Bodhisattva Vehicle without skillful means perceive that form is ‘empty,’ they are attached
if noble sons or noble daughters who follow the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, lacking in skillful means, perceive that physical forms are empty, then they are attached

div.p: is thinking like that by way of apprehending something.

q.p:
“Not perceive form as ‘form’ ” nyi khri , ’bum nya 185a7, le’u brgyad ma nga 151a5; cp. khri brgyad
: “Form does not perceive form.”—
q.orig: Form does not perceive form
do not perceive that physical forms are physical forms

div.p: this is the bodhisattva’s knowledge of path aspects.

q.p: “Not perceive… dharmas as… ‘dharmas’ ”—
q.orig: nor do past dharmas not perceive past dharmas, nor do future dharmas not perceive future dharmas, nor do present dharmas not perceive present dharmas

They do not perceive that phenomena of the past are phenomena of the past. They do not perceive that phenomena of the future are phenomena of the future. They do not perceive that phenomena of the present are phenomena of the present

div.p: they do not appear.

q.p:
“Kauśika, it is because the basic nature of form cannot be dedicated” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Kauśika[2]…it is because the basic nature of form cannot be dedicated.
Kauśika, they are incapable of dedicating the intrinsic nature of physical forms

div.p: means dharmas should not be dedicated to awakening by way of apprehending something, because they stay in the same state and do not undergo transformation.

q.p:
“Subhūti, I will teach you other sorts of attachment even more subtle than those” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: I will also explain to you more subtle modes of attachment than these.

div.p: that obscure the knowledge of path aspects.

q.p:
“Lord, the perfection of wisdom is deep.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Blessed Lord, the perfection of wisdom is profound

div.p:
Earlier,
, explaining khri brgyad
,
, and
. to build trust, the elder Śāriputra set the scene for the explanation of the perfection of wisdom being deep, and for it being hard to believe in. Now, to demonstrate that he himself has comprehended that it is deep, the elder Subhūti says, “Lord, … [it] is deep.”

q.p: “Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are isolated in their basic nature.”
q.orig: Subhūti, that is because all phenomena are naturally void

div.p: Thus all phenomena are always deserted by all attachments, are deserted by a basic nature, are isolated in their basic nature. But falsely imagined attachment is still apprehending, and even though falsely imagined attachment is apprehending, still all dharmas are untainted, that is, are isolated in their intrinsic nature so they are deep.

q.p: “The perfection of wisdom… is unmade and does not cause anything to come into being.”
q.orig: the perfection of wisdom because it is unmade and has not caused anything to come into being.
the perfection of wisdom is unfabricated and unconditioned.

div.p: In it there is nothing to be established and nothing is caused to come into being because it is the intrinsic nature of the dharma body.

q.p: “The basic nature of a dharma is not two; it is simply one.”
q.orig: so it is that the nature of phenomena is without duality. The nature of phenomena is exclusively singular

div.p: As the intrinsic nature that is suchness, all dharmas are a single entity, but still they appear with different identities. This is difficult to clearly realize. Because suchness is the intrinsic nature of all dharmas it is called their “basic nature.” That suchness, moreover, is not the cause of any other true nature of dharmas, so it

q.p: “is not a basic nature.”
q.orig: this singular nature of phenomena is without inherent existence

div.p: This suchness is uncompounded; it is not made by anybody, so it

q.p: “is unmade.”
q.orig: is unfabricated

div.p: Just that

q.p: “has not caused anything to come into being”
q.orig: is unconditioned

div.p: because no enactment of merit or demerit whatsoever has occasioned it.

q.p: “Nobody has seen, heard, thought about, been conscious of, or fully awakened to the perfection of wisdom,”
q.orig: the perfection of wisdom has not been seen, realized, cognized, or acquired in manifest buddhahood by anyone at all

div.p: because the perfection of wisdom is not the object of seeing consciousness and so on, nor of thought constructions such as those, because an apprehender and an apprehended object are the same in their intrinsic nature.

q.p: “The perfection of wisdom is inconceivable”

div.p: means you cannot conceive of it through another dharma, like fire indicated by smoke. Therefore, it says

q.p: “it is not known through form”
q.orig: It is not known through form
it has not been known by physical forms

div.p: and so on. It

q.p: “is the nonapprehender of all dharmas.”
q.orig: agents are nonapprehensible

div.p: It makes all dharmas known as the mark of what cannot be apprehended.

div.head: Explanation of Chapters 37 and 38

q.p: “How do [they]… practice the perfection of wisdom?”
q.orig: how do bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom?
How then should bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom

div.p: that is, the knowledge of path aspects.

The section of the text to teach that if those conscious of a basic nature practice all dharmas they do not practice the perfection of wisdom is The first section (khri brgyad
) is “if one does not practice form, one practices the perfection of wisdom” and so on, and the second, “if one does not practice with the idea ‘form is permanent’ and so on, one practices the perfection of wisdom.”

q.p: “if they do not practice form,”
q.orig: if they do not practice form
if they do not engage with physical forms

div.p: and so on. The second section is to teach that when those conscious of special insight practice the marks of dharmas, they do not practice the perfection of wisdom.
It says,

q.p: “ ‘form is completed’ or ‘not completed,’ ”
q.orig: form is completed’ or ‘not completed,
the notion that physical forms are unperfected

div.p: intending when meditation is completed.

q.p:
“ ‘Form is not attached’ ” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: form is not attached,
the notions that physical forms are with attachment, or that they are without attachment

div.p: is the unobstructed true dharmic nature of form. When they practice like that

q.p: “they do not perceive ‘form is not attached.’ ”
q.orig: they do not perceive ‘form is not attached’
they do not perceive that physical forms are with attachment, or that they are without attachment

div.p: This means that if, when practicing, they have set out like that, then when they awaken to the knowledge of all aspects they will have a realization like that.

div.head: Benefits of purity
div.p:
Subhūti’s statement that he is amazed, the statement of some monk or other, the statement by Śatakratu, and the statement that guarding, protecting, and keeping safe are not possible are all alike. The statements (khri brgyad
,
,
, finishing ) all say that the perfection of wisdom is like space, or like a dream and so on, but is the origin of benefits.

q.p:
“They do not falsely project form” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: do not falsely project form
they do not give rise to conceits based on physical forms

div.p: as a functioning thing that is real and a defining mark and so on;

q.p: “do not falsely project form as ‘mine’ ”
q.orig: do not project form as ‘mine,’
do not give rise to conceits on account of physical forms

div.p: as a real thing, like a master’s servant;

q.p: “do not falsely project anything onto form”
q.orig: do not project anything onto form
do not give rise to conceits about physical forms

div.p: as a real thing on a foundation or basis; and

q.p: “do not falsely project a causal sign of form”
q.orig: do not project a causal sign of form

div.p: as a basis of a designation that is a conventional term.
The description of

q.p:
“the thousand buddhas” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: a thousand buddhas
the thousand buddhas

div.p: is because those thousand buddhas cause faith to arise in that perfection of wisdom.
The question about

q.p: “Maitreya”

div.p:
teaching the Dharma khri brgyad
. is to make it known that during the three periods of time the explanations are of just this perfection of wisdom.

Then, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is pure because form is pure.”
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Lord, “the perfection of wisdom is pure because form is pure
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “the perfection of wisdom is absolutely pure owing to the absolute purity of physical forms

div.p: The dharmas, form and so on, that have been apprehended are stainless, so the knowledge of path aspects is also pure.

q.p: “Subhūti, form… is unproduced and unceasing, without defilement and without purification.”
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Lord, “form that is unproduced and unceasing, without defilement and without purification,
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “physical forms are absolutely pure because they neither arise nor cease, and they are neither afflicted nor purified

div.p: When form abides in its intrinsic nature—the true nature of dharmas—and does not appear as produced, ceasing, defiled, or purified, that

q.p: “form is pure,”
q.orig: is pure form
physical forms are absolutely pure

div.p: not otherwise.

q.p: “Because space is pure”—
q.orig: Because space is pure[1]
owing to the absolute purity of space

div.p:
this is teaching that just as space does not become impure even if there are clouds and haze because it is pure in its nature, so too with the perfection of wisdom. The six khri brgyad
.—

q.p: “pure… untainted… cannot be grasped… does not say anything… does not converse about anything… cannot be apprehended”—
q.orig: untainted
unsullied

div.p: teach that it is comparable to space.

q.p: “Because space does not say anything”—
q.orig: because space is inexpressible

div.p: even though in space something other than that space says something, in space nothing is said and there is no conversation,

q.p:
“just like the two sounds of an echo, as an analogy,” Cf. khri brgyad
, nyi khri , ’bum nya 334a2.
q.orig: just like the two sounds of an echo, to give an analogy,
like the resonance of a double echo

div.p: reverberate in space, but it is not suitable to say that space says something.

q.p: “Because space does not converse about anything”
q.orig: because space is inexpressible

div.p: means that because of its intrinsic nature there is no conversation in space. Alternatively, “saying something” is mere sound; “conversing” is naming.

q.p:
“Subhūti, … because form is extremely pure, cannot be apprehended, is unproduced and unceasing, and without defilement and without purification” khri brgyad
.—
q.orig: Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is pure because…and without defilement and without purification.
Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom is absolutely pure because all phenomena neither arise nor cease, and are neither afflicted nor purified

div.p: when this perfection of wisdom sees all dharmas, it sees the “pure” aspect of form and so on because the stains of falsely imagined afflictions and conceptualizations constructed in thought do not exist; the aspect that “cannot be apprehended” because it is separated from all apprehending; the “unproduced and unceasing” aspects because it is a thoroughly established phenomenon; and the aspects “without defilement and without purification” because it is isolated from an intrinsic nature. At that point it is called

q.p: “pure”

div.p: in its nature.
Having thus taught that the perfection of wisdom is extremely pure, then, to engender faith in it, they

q.p: “will not contract diseases of the eye,”
q.orig: will not contract diseases of the eyes
will not suffer ailments of the eyes

div.p:
and so on, teaches its benefits in the here and now and in future lives. khri brgyad
.

q.p: “In the perfection of wisdom there is no dharma that is produced or ceases, is defiled or purified, or is appropriated or rejected at all”
q.orig: In this precious perfection…there is nothing at all that arises or ceases, nothing that is defiled or purified, nothing that is to be retained or forsaken

div.p: teaches that production, cessation, and so on do not appear in the perfection of wisdom.

q.p: “Thus, do not form a notion, and thus do not conceive”—
q.orig: thus do not form any notion and thus do not conceive
do not perceive in that manner, do not conceptualize in that manner

div.p: they do not even conceive of the perfection of wisdom as such

q.p: “a great jewel”
q.orig: precious

div.p: endowed with those good qualities.

q.p:
“Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom does not establish any dharma, or teach it.” Cf. khri brgyad (kha 84b2) has thob par byed pa ma yin in place of sgrub pa’am; ’bum nya 338a2 and nyi khri
both omit sgrub pa. The “this perfection of wisdom” here is seyaṃ punaḥ, “And again, this,” at both PSP 2-3: 183 and Aṣṭa (Wogihara p. 441); le’u brgyd ma nga 166b7 rab ’byor yang shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa ’di ni chos gang yang mthong bar byed pa ma yin. Abhi­samayālaṃkāra 3.16 and the AAV (Sparham 2006–11 vol. 2, p. 63) relate the repetition of “[And again] this perfection of wisdom” with the first three of the Abhi­samayālaṃkāra’s eight chapters, respectively.
q.orig: Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom does not cause any dharma to be gained, does not teach it,
Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom does not teach

div.p: All dharmas are thoroughly established phenomena that do not alter, so at the time they are thoroughly established phenomena this perfection of wisdom appears like that, which is to say, there is no false projection of having to establish any special dharma; there is no false projection of taking hold of or bestowing any special dharma; there is no false projection of producing dharmas without outflows or stopping bad dharmas; there is no false projection of annihilating the dharmas of cyclic existence or of making purification permanent; Emend brtag par bya to rtag par bya (PSP 2-3:180 śāśvatikā). there is no false projection of being one or being different things; there is no false projection of coming about through the power of bodhisattva activities not there before or being separated from all obscurations; there is no false projection of having earlier become defiled by afflictions, secondary afflictions, and so on, and later being purified; there is no false projection of making dark dharmas decline and making bright dharmas increase; there is no false projection of being included in the three periods of time; there is no false projection of being established in the three realms or of having to transcend them; and there is no false projection of bestowing the perfection of giving and so on, or of removing their opposing sides of miserliness and so on.

q.p:
“Subhūti, whether the tathāgatas arise or whether the tathāgatas do not arise” khri brgyad
, ’bum nya 339a7, nyi khri
omit “Subhūti.”
q.orig: whether the tathāgatas arise or whether the tathāgatas do not arise,
regardless of whether the tathāgatas have appeared or not

div.p: is teaching the mark of all dharmas that remain in the same state, nothing doing anything at all. Those “tathāgatas,” so called because they know just this state in which dharmas remain, appear in the world. It means just this is their clear realization, just this is

q.p: “the wheel of Dharma.”
q.orig: the wheel of the Dharma
the wheel of the Dharma

q.p:
“Subhūti… it is not a second turning of the wheel of Dharma and it is not a first turning either.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Subhūti[2]…it is not a second turning of the wheel of Dharma and it is not a first turning either.
Subhūti, owing to the emptiness of the essential nature of nonentities, this turning of the wheel of the Dharma is not the first [in Jambudvīpa], nor is it the second

div.p: It says this because ultimately all dharmas are beyond counting. It

q.p:
“has not been made available in order to turn or not turn any Dharma” nyi khri
, ’bum nya 338b5; khri brgyad
differs.
q.orig: has not been made available in order to turn forward or turn backward any Dharma?
is not at all established as a doctrine that is to be set in motion or not set in motion

div.p: removes the notion or idea that it is turning or not turning the wheel of Dharma.

q.p: “Given the emptiness that is the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature”
q.orig: the emptiness that is the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature
the emptiness of the essential nature of nonentities

div.p: means the perfection of wisdom grasps all dharmas as the mark of the emptiness that is the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature.

q.p: “The perfection of wisdom is a great perfection,”
q.orig: this perfection of wisdom that bodhisattva great beings have is great

div.p: and so on. With the ninety-five statements the elder Subhūti explains at length that this perfection of wisdom engages with all dharmas. ’bum nya 339b6–341a1 says of the six perfections, eighteen emptinesses, thirty-seven dharmas on the side of awakening, and the twenty-five other dharmas that they are empty. The total of ninety-five is perhaps reached by taking each of the ten powers separately.

There “the perfection of wisdom is a great perfection” teaches that it is a great object, and a great secret in the form of an object. It says about such a secret that it is three: a secret engagement with dharmas, a secret awakening, and a secret turning of the wheel of Dharma.
There, for dharmas, governed by the conventional and ultimate, it engages with perceiving dharmas as dharmas and also engages with perceiving them as not dharmas as well, so it says

q.p: “all dharmas are empty of the intrinsic nature of all dharmas.”
q.orig: all phenomena are empty of all phenomena

div.p:
It teaches awakening but also sees the nonexistence of awakening, so it says nyi khri , ’bum nya 341a2–3; cf. khri brgyad
.

q.p: “but still, bodhisattva great beings abiding in this perfection of wisdom fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening without fully awakening to any dharma at all.”
q.orig: but still bodhisattva great beings, thanks to this perfection of wisdom, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening without fully awakening to any dharma at all,
although bodhisattva great beings dwell in the perfection of wisdom and attain consummate buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete enlightenment, there is nothing at all that attains consummate buddhahood

div.p:
Teaching the secret turning of the wheel of Dharma, it says Cf. khri brgyad
, nyi khri
, ’bum nya 341a3.

q.p: “will turn the wheel of the Dharma but will not turn or not turn any Dharma.”
q.orig: will turn the wheel of the Dharma even though any Dharma that has to be engaged in or backed away from does not exist
Although they indeed turn the wheel of the Dharma, there is nothing at all that is set in motion, not set in motion, or further set in motion

div.p:
Then there is the section with the eightfold turning of the wheel of Dharma: khri brgyad
–. the nonexistence of the Dharma, the nonexistence of the wheel, the nonexistence of the turning, the nonexistence of the intrinsic nature of an explanation, the nonexistence of one who explains, the nonexistence of one who listens, the nonexistence of realization, and the nonexistence of a noble person.
There, about the nonexistence of the Dharma, it says

q.p: “will not see any Dharma at all, and will not not see any Dharma at all either.”
q.orig: will not see any Dharma at all, and will not…see any Dharma at all either.
There is nothing at all that they see or do not see

div.p: About the nonexistence of the wheel, it says

q.p: “because a Dharma that will be turned or will not be turned cannot be apprehended.” Cp. khri brgyad , nyi khri , and ’bum.
q.orig: Because a dharma that engages or backs away cannot be apprehended,
because anything that set it in motion, did not set it in motion, or further set it in motion cannot be apprehended

div.p: About the nonexistence of turning, it says

q.p: “emptiness does not turn it, nor does it not turn it. The signless and the wishless also do not turn it, nor do they not turn it.”
q.orig: emptiness does not engage, nor does it back away; the signless and the wishless also do not engage, nor do they back away.

emptiness does not set in motion or not set in motion anything at all. Signlessness does not set in motion or not set in motion anything at all. Wishlessness does not set in motion or not set in motion anything at all

div.p: About the nonexistence of an explanation, it says

q.p: “therefore, this teaching of the perfection of wisdom, this illumination,”
q.orig: That which describes, explains, proclaims, establishes, posits, analyzes, interprets, mentions, elucidates, introduces, and reveals the perfection of wisdom

div.p: up to

q.p: “is the teaching of the perfection of wisdom that is perfectly pure.”
q.orig: is the absolutely pure exposition of the perfection of wisdom

div.p: About the nonexistence of one who explains, it says

q.p: “nobody teaches that teaching of the perfection of wisdom.”
q.orig: This exposition of the perfection of wisdom has neither been explained by anyone at all

div.p: About the nonexistence of one who listens, it says

q.p: “and nobody receives it.”
q.orig: nor has it been grasped by anyone at all

div.p: About the nonexistence of realization, it says

q.p: “nobody has directly realized it.”
q.orig: nobody has directly realized
has not been brought into being by anyone at all

div.p: And about the absence of a noble person, it says

q.p: “nobody has entered into nirvāṇa either. And in this Dharma teaching there is also nobody who becomes worthy of offerings.”
q.orig: there is no passing into final nirvāṇa…Nor is there anyone at all who is worthy of offerings on account of this exposition of the Dharma.

div.head: Glosses

q.p:
“Because space is a nonexistent thing, Subhūti” In the Sūtra (khri brgyad
–), Subhūti makes a brief statement and the Buddha gives a corroborating reason. In this first instance Subhūti says, “This perfection of wisdom is a nonexistent thing (alternatively, “not truly real”) (asat) and the Buddha says, “Because space is a nonexistent thing.” In the Abhi­samayālaṃkāra’s system this marks the beginning of the fourth chapter, the explanation of the practice (prayoga) proper, beginning with a listing of its one hundred and seventy-three ākāras (“aspects,” “cognitive-subjective states”). Our author only glosses those he feels need clarification. —
q.orig: This is owing to the nonexistence of space

div.p: like space, it is not truly real in a form you can apprehend, and not not truly real in a form that cannot be apprehended.

q.p: “Because all dharmas are equally nonapprehendable, Subhūti”—
q.orig: This is owing to the nonapprehension of all phenomena

div.p: all dharmas are equally imaginary with a nature that cannot be apprehended.

q.p: “Because of not having a name and body”—
q.orig: This is owing to namelessness and noncorporeality

div.p: this means formless dharmas and form dharmas are not in the form of names.

q.p: “Because the movement of breath in and out is unfindable”—
q.orig: This is owing to the nonexistence of the exhalation and inhalation of breath

div.p: this is because upon analysis there is no movement of breath in and out because the body is empty like space.

q.p: “Because applied and sustained thought is unfindable”—
q.orig: This is owing to the nonapprehension of ideation and scrutiny

div.p:
it says this because the two, applied and sustained thought, occasion words, because it is said, “Having applied their mind and thought in a sustained way earlier, later on they deliver a speech.” This is in response to Subhūti’s rhetorical question (khri brgyad
), “Lord, this is a perfection without language?” I have not been able to identify the citation.

q.p: “Because the feeling, perception, volitional factors, and consciousness aggregates are unfindable.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nonapprehension of feelings, perceptions, formative predispositions, and consciousness

div.p: Because they have no form they are in their nature just a collection of names. nāmarūpa (“name and form”) is the fourth of the twelve links of dependent origination.

q.p: “Because all phenomena do not go away.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nonmoving of all phenomena

div.p: Because all phenomena are separated from going.

q.p: “Because all dharmas cannot be seized.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nongrasping of all phenomena

div.p: Dharmas do not seize dharmas, so it

q.p:
“is not stolen.” khri brgyad
: “Lord, this perfection of wisdom is a perfection that is not stolen.”
“Because all dharmas have come to an end in extreme purity.”
q.orig: Because all dharmas have come to an end in extreme purity
This is owing to the absolute exhaustion of all phenomena

div.p: Because all dharmas appear as an extreme purity they do not arise and are not stopped, and hence appear to have come to an end.

q.p: “Because all dharmas do not arise and do not stop.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nonarising and nonceasing of all phenomena

div.p: All dharmas are empty. They appear as not arising and as not stopping.

q.p: “Because death and rebirth are unfindable.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nonapprehension of death and rebirth

div.p:
It khri brgyad
: “Lord, this perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not change places.” knows that the time of deaths and rebirths appear based on false imagination, not ultimately.

q.p: “Because all dharmas are indestructible in their nature.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nondisintegration of all phenomena

div.p: It is indestructible because the nature of all dharmas is suchness, so it does not change.

q.p:
“Because a dream that has been seen cannot be apprehended.” nyi khri
.
q.orig: Because a dream that has been dreamed cannot be apprehended
This is owing to the nonapprehension of the perception of dreams

div.p: Just as that thing existent in a dream which has been seen in a dream cannot be apprehended and does not exist, so too all phenomena are there as nonexistent things. Golden 289a5. D: “Just as that human seen in a dream, who is an existent thing in a dream, cannot be apprehended and does not exist, so too all phenomena are there as nonexistent things.”

q.p:
“This is a perfection without purification… because the presence of defilement cannot be apprehended.” khri brgyad
. The separate statements by Subhūti and the Buddha are combined into a single statement in this and some of the following glosses.
q.orig: this perfection of wisdom is a perfection without purification
This is owing to the nonexistence of afflicted mental states

div.p: There can be purification if there is defilement, but all phenomena are pure in their nature so there is no defilement and there is no purification either.

q.p: “This is a perfection that does not stand… because all phenomena cannot be apprehended.”
q.orig: this perfection of wisdom is a perfection that does not stand
This is owing to the nonapprehension of a basis

div.p: Because all phenomena cannot be apprehended they therefore are not apprehended as standing anywhere.

q.p: “Because it is a full awakening to all dharmas as unmistaken suchness.”
q.orig: This is owing to the incontrovertible, genuinely manifest buddhahood of all phenomena

div.p:
All phenomena are the intrinsic nature of unmistaken suchness, which is to say, they make manifest that unmistaken intrinsic nature so they make available the wisdom that knows “all phenomena are calm.” At khri brgyad
, ’bum nya 343a7, and nyi khri this is the response to Subhūti’s, “Lord, this perfection of wisdom is a detached perfection.” Below Subhūti will say, “Lord, this perfection of wisdom is a calm perfection.”

q.p: “Because the causal sign of greed cannot be apprehended.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nonapprehension of…desire

div.p: There is no causal sign that is a basis to become attached to.

q.p: “Because hate is not real.”
q.orig: This is owing to the absence of hatred

div.p: Because the causal sign that serves as a cause of hate does not exist.

q.p: “This perfection of wisdom is a perfection that is not a means of measurement… because all phenomena do not fully arise.”
q.orig: this perfection of wisdom is a perfection that is not a means of measurement
This is owing to the nonarising of all phenomena

div.p: It might be supposed that all phenomena are caused to fully arise on account of a means of measurement. “Not a means of measurement” or, alternatively, “immeasurable” renders tshad ma mchis pa (apramāṇa); it has the sense of “not a valid cognition” of something. “Fully arise” renders kun nas ldang ba (paryutthāna), which has a negative sense, like a rage that arises in somebody and totally takes them over. But this perfection of wisdom does not see the emergence of a basis for the measurement of any phenomenon, therefore it is “not a means of measurement.”

q.p: “Because all phenomena are distinct.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nonassociation of all phenomena

div.p: Because all dharmas are isolated.

q.p: “Because the measure of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nonapprehension of the dimensions of all phenomena

div.p: There might be a means of measurement were there something to be measured. “Something to be measured” renders gzhal bya (prameya). But because a means of measurement of all phenomena, were there to be something measured, cannot be apprehended and does not exist, therefore something to be measured does not exist either.

q.p: “Because all phenomena are without attachment like space.”
q.orig: This is owing to the absence of attachment with regard to all phenomena

div.p: All phenomena, similar to space, are without attachment.

q.p: “This… is an impermanent perfection
q.orig: this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is impermanent

div.p:
Because all dharmas are unproduced, like horns on a rabbit and so on, they are not destroyed. Therefore, they do not exist. They are impermanent because they are not existent things, because scripture says that “the meaning of a nonexistent thing is the meaning of impermanence.” Cited earlier
.

q.p: “Because all phenomena are not suitable to be clung to.”
q.orig: This is owing to the absence of preoccupation with all phenomena

div.p:
All phenomena are not suitable to be clung to, or to be stayed with, or to be made use of, so it is suffering. This is the response to khri brgyad
, “Lord, this perfection of wisdom is a suffering perfection.”

q.p: “This… is a perfection of the empty This is partially supported by AAVN 63a2 śūnyatākāreṇa sarva-dharmānupalabdher iti, AAV ka 122b4, Sparham 2006–11 vol. 2, p. 63. khri brgyad kha 89b1, nyi khri kha 219b3, ’bum nya 344b2 omit. … because an intrinsic nature of all phenomena cannot be apprehended.”
q.orig: “Lord, this perfection of wisdom is a perfection that is emptiness,
this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is emptiness

div.p: Those intrinsic natures—easily breakable, experience, These are the definitions of the form and feeling aggregates. and so on—do not ultimately exist. Therefore, those phenomena are empty of those intrinsic natures.

q.p: “This… is a selfless perfection… because all phenomena are not settled down on.”
q.orig: This… is a selfless perfection
this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is not a self

div.p: The “phenomena,” form and so on, do not exist. They are therefore not suitable to be “settled down on.” Since that is the case, the nonexistence of all the phenomena is selflessness. Even though there is no difference in the meaning of emptiness and selflessness, based on being designated they are differentiated. “The empty” is being without something else. To illustrate, you say “an empty pot” when it has no water. Similarly, because they are without an intrinsic nature, their “defining mark” and so on, those phenomena are thought of as “empty.” As for “selfless,” it is the nonexistence of the phenomena, like, to illustrate, the magically produced illusion of elephants and so on. You say “empty” when you want to say those phenomena are separated from their defining marks and so on. You say “selfless” when you want to say that “they are not existent”—they are not existent things.

q.p: “Because all phenomena have no causal sign.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nonestablishment of all phenomena

div.p: Given that a causal sign is a defining mark and there is no such defining mark they are

q.p: “without a defining mark.”
q.orig: without defining characteristics

q.p: “Because the emptiness of emptiness cannot be apprehended.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nonapprehension of the emptiness of emptiness

div.p: This means there is just no second emptiness in emptiness. The empty is said to be “emptiness.” An “empty” that is a different attribute called “emptiness” does not exist at all.

q.p: “The great emptiness cannot be apprehended.”
q.orig: This is owing to the nonapprehension of the emptiness of great extent

div.p: “Great emptiness” is said of the immensity of just the nonexistence of forms for all the directions. A different attribute called “the great emptiness” does not exist at all.

You should construe them all like this as well. khri brgyad
– goes through the entire list of emptinesses.

q.p: “This… is a perfection that is the emptiness of a basic nature… because compounded and uncompounded dharmas cannot be apprehended.”
q.orig: This… is a perfection that is the emptiness of a basic nature
this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that constitutes the emptiness of inherent existence

div.p: This means if compounded and uncompounded dharmas were findable, their basic nature would be not empty, but all dharmas are empty, hence their “emptiness of a basic nature.”

q.p: “This… is a perfection that is giving… because miserliness cannot be apprehended.”
q.orig: This… is a perfection that is giving
this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of generosity

div.p: The miserliness that cannot be apprehended in the perfection of wisdom is the mark of giving.

You should construe the others like this as well. khri brgyad
–.

q.p:
“This… is a perfection that is the ten powers… because all the aspects of all dharmas cannot be apprehended.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: This… is a perfection that is the ten powers
this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that constitutes the ten powers

div.p: All the aspects of all dharmas would fall within the range of the ten knowledges—the power that is knowledge of the possible and impossible and so on. But they are not within their range, they are unreal aspects. So, because those aspects do not ultimately exist, therefore the aspects that serve as the objects of the ten powers are seen not to exist, hence it is “a perfection that is the ten powers.”

q.p:
“Because the knowledge of path aspects is not cowed.” At nyi khri
, ’bum nya 347b3 Subhūti says the “four fearlessnesses” are the perfection because “the knowledge of a knower of paths is not cowed.” khri brgyad
says it is “a perfection that is fearlessness” because the knowledge of paths cannot be apprehended.
q.orig: Because the knowledge of path aspects cannot be apprehended
This is owing to their undauntedness concerning knowledge of the path

div.p: The knowledge of path aspects of bodhisattvas is not cowed by any phenomenon. Therefore, the knowledge of path aspects, which in its nature is uncowed by anything, is

q.p: “a perfection that is fearlessness.”
q.orig: this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that constitutes the four fearlessnesses

q.p: “Because knowledge is totally unattached and unimpeded.”
q.orig: This is owing to the absence of attachment and absence of obstruction with respect to all-aspect omniscience

div.p: Because the knowledge of bodhisattvas is totally unattached and unimpeded, therefore it is

q.p: “a perfection that is detailed and thorough knowledge.”
q.orig: the perfection that constitutes the four kinds of exact knowledge

q.p: “Because it has gone beyond all śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha attributes.”
q.orig: This is owing to the transcendence of all the doctrines of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas

div.p: Because śrāvakas and so on do not have this perfection of wisdom it is therefore counted as

q.p: “a perfection that is the… attributes of a buddha.”
q.orig: the perfection that constitutes the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas

q.p:
“This… is a perfection that is the realized one… because what has been spoken by all the buddhas is reality.” Golden 289a5. “Realized one” renders tathāgata, “reality” tathatā, and “thus” tathā. D: “This is a perfection that is the realized one, because what has been said by all the buddhas is indeed the realized one.” At nyi khri
, ’bum nya 347b7: “This perfection of wisdom is a perfection that is the realized one because it is the reality of all that has been said.” khri brgyad
: “Lord, this perfection of wisdom is a perfection that is suchness… because it is the suchness of all that has been said.” Note that the Sanskrit tathatā/Tibetan de bzhin nyid is generally rendered "suchness" throughout. See also .
q.orig: this perfection of wisdom is the perfection of the tathāgatas

div.p: By a creative explanation, the realized one is so called because of having spoken thus, which is to say, the perfection of wisdom that observes thus—what has been spoken by all the buddhas—is called the “perfection that is the realized one.”

q.p: “This… is a perfection that is self-originated… because it is in control of all dharmas.”
q.orig: This… is a perfection that is self-originated
this perfection of wisdom is the perfection that is naturally arisen

div.p: Because all dharmas are under its control, therefore it predominates among all dharmas so it is a “self-originated perfection.” svayambhū, “self-originated” = “intrinsic”; abhibhū, “predominate.”

div.head: Absence of a practice and signs of completion
div.p:
It is easy to explain Śatakratu’s praise passage, the elder Śāriputra passage, and the Lord’s rejoicing passage so they are just as they are in the Sūtra. khri brgyad
–.

q.p: “When practicing the perfection of wisdom [they] do not stand in form, and when they do not stand in form they practice the yoga of form.” ’bum nya 353a5–6, nyi khri , le’u brgyad ma nga 177b4. I have rendered brtson par byed in line with khri brgyad (kha 95a1) rnal ’byor du byed pa yin no (PSP 4: 11 yogam āpadyate). LSPW pp. 301–2, “does not stand in form, etc. and in consequence makes no endeavor about form.”
q.orig: bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom do not stand…they practice the yoga of form

when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not dwell in physical forms, and when they do not dwell in physical forms, at that time they do not persevere…with physical forms

div.p: The bodhisattvas’ transcendental knowledge of a knower of path aspects does not stand in any phenomenon, therefore just that not standing is their “practice of the yoga.”

q.p:
“Furthermore, Kauśika, they do not practice the yoga of a bodhisattva’s form, and thus not practicing the yoga of form like that, they practice the yoga of form.” Cf. khri brgyad
, nyi khri , ’bum nya 361a5.
q.orig: Furthermore, Kauśika, bodhisattva great beings do not apply themselves to form, and because they do not apply themselves to form like that, they practice the yoga of form.

Moreover, Kauśika…when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, they do not engage with or differentiate physical forms, and when they do not engage with or differentiate physical forms, at that time they do persevere with physical forms

div.p: The earlier subsection of the passage refutes standing; here it refutes what is established by not standing. Here “stand on X” means, from a negative perspective, to keep on entertaining the idea of X as real, and from a positive perspective to have one’s feet solidly on the ground of reality. Even the second is ultimately negated.

q.p: “Do not apprehend form as past,”
q.orig: do not apprehend form as past
do not apprehend physical forms in the limit of past time

div.p: and so on, teaches that they do not apprehend it in any of the three time periods.

q.p:
“Śāriputra, it is because the depth of form is not form.” nyi khri , “It is because the depth of form is not form” and so on, up to “the depth of the knowledge of all aspects is not the knowledge of all aspects.” It does the same with “hard to fathom” () and “immeasurable” (); ’bum nya 386a7 to ’bum ta 4b1 is the same but fills in all the details; khri brgyad
ff. differs.
q.orig: the profundity of physical forms is not physical forms

div.p: It says this because “the depth” is falsely imagined, so form itself ultimately does not exist.

The interpretation of the depth subsection, hard to fathom subsection, and immeasurable subsection; the Śatakratu passage and obtaining a prediction; the wilderness analogy, the spring analogy, and the pregnant woman analogy; and the passage on taking care of and teaching others is easy. khri brgyad
–. The section goes up to ’bum ta 11a, and nyi khri .
There are two signs that

q.p: “the meditation on the perfection of wisdom… is completed”—
q.orig: the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom that bodhisattva great beings have will be perfected

div.p: when they

q.p: “do not see… an increase… or a decline in”
q.orig: do not observe the enhancement of

div.p:
all dharmas, and when they see the marks of dharmas. khri brgyad
–, ending “what marks dharmas as dharmas is irreversibility, vanity, hollowness, pointlessness, and fraudulence.”
That the inconceivable has been taught and that they do not conceptualize the inconceivable are also signs that

q.p:
“the meditation on the perfection of wisdom… is completed.” khri brgyad
–.
q.orig: then meditation on the perfection of wisdom… is completed[2]
the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom that bodhisattva great beings have will be perfected

div.p:
The sign that they are practicing the six perfections is that they khri brgyad
.

q.p: “do not mentally construct and do not conceive of form, do not mentally construct and do not conceive of a causal sign of form, and do not mentally construct and do not conceive of an intrinsic nature of form.”
q.orig: do not mentally construct and do not conceive of form, do not mentally construct and do not conceive of a causal sign of form, and do not mentally construct and do not conceive of an intrinsic nature of form.
do not imagine or construe physical forms, they do not imagine or construe the indications of physical forms, and they do not imagine or construe the inherent existence of physical forms

div.p: With the meditative stabilization on emptiness they do not mentally construct dharmas; with the meditative stabilization on signlessness they do not mentally construct causal signs; and with the meditative stabilization on wishlessness they do not mentally construct an intrinsic nature. They do not conceptualize falsely imagined phenomena; they do not conceptualize dependent phenomena.

Earlier Cf. khri brgyad
. Here (Bṭ3 ) Subhūti says, “Lord, the perfection of wisdom is deep because form is deep.” it said that it is deep because of the depth of suchness; here, having superimposed the mark of suchness onto form and so on, and saying that it is deep, is because of the various dispositions of trainees.

q.p: “Lord, the perfection of wisdom is an aggregate of the purity of all dharmas”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, the perfection of wisdom is a mass of purity owing to the purity of physical forms

div.p:
means it is pure and it is the aggregate of all dharmas. khri brgyad
. The gloss explains the tatpuruṣa compound śuddharāśi.

q.p:
“Lord, that… would not give rise to many hindrances would be amazing.” khri brgyad
: “Lord, that such an exposition of this deep perfection of wisdom would not give rise to many hindrances would be amazing,”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, it would be so astonishing if many obstacles do not arise

div.p: It says this having in mind that there are many obstacles to something excellent.

Next, the explanation of the teaching about the merit from reciting the good Dharma is easy. khri brgyad
– explains the hindrances and merit.

div.head: Last of the five hundreds

q.p:
“During the last of the ‘five hundreds’ ” khri brgyad
, ’bum ta 58a6, nyi khri (kha 245b1) lnga brgya tha ma; Harrison (2006, p. 144, n. 40) “final five hundred years”; PSP 4: 29–30, le’u brgyad ma nga 193a1 ff. omit; Aṣṭa (Wogihara p. 487) saddharma­syāntardhānakāle. There are a number of ways to explain “last of the five hundreds,” one of which is that the Dharma lasts five thousand years, divided into ten periods of five hundred years (Nattier 1999, Yuyama 1992).—
q.orig: during the future, this perfection of wisdom will perform the activities of the buddhas in the south, the east, and the north for the final five-hundred

div.p: a “five hundred” incorporates five one hundreds. It is said that the time the doctrine of the Tathāgata lasts is five thousand years. If you break up and subdivide the five thousand years into five-hundred-year periods, there are ten five hundreds. For these there are ten chapters: “Chapter” renders le’u. Skt parivarta means not only “chapter” but also a period of time. The literal translation of le’u (“chapter”) is retained here because it conveys the sense of “a chapter in our history,” and connects the history to scripture. first, three chapters (the Understanding chapter, Practice chapter, and Scripture chapter). There the Understanding chapter is again subdivided into three chapters (the Worthy One chapter, Non-returner chapter, and stream enterer chapter); the Practice chapter too is subdivided into three chapters (the Insight chapter, Meditative Stabilization chapter, and Morality chapter); and the Scripture chapter is also subdivided into three (the Abhidharma chapter, Sūtra chapter, and Vinaya chapter). These nine chapters and the Mere Signs chapter K, N; D rtags tsam ’jigs pa’i le’u “Fear of Mere Signs chapter”; Mañjuśrīkīrti’s Kīrtimālā commentary chos thams cad kyi rang bzhin mnyam pa nyid rnam par spros pa’i ting nge ’dzin gyi rgyal po zhes bya ba theg pa chen po’i mdo’i ’grel pa grags pa’i phreng ba, Degé Tengyur (mdo ’grel, nyi), 116b2, has rtags tzam ’dzin pa’i (“Grasping Mere Signs”). are the ten chapters.
There, each of the ten chapters lasts five hundred years, so, the ten chapters comprise ten five hundreds that become the five thousand years.

There, in the first of all the five hundreds are the worthy ones; in the second five hundred, the non-returners; in the third, the stream enterers; in the fourth five hundred, insight; in the fifth, meditative stabilization; in the sixth, morality; in the seventh, the abhidharma; in the eighth, the sūtras; in the ninth, the vinaya; and in the tenth five hundred, a mere sign. It is just this that is called “the last of the five hundreds.”

Some say Braarvig (1993, vol. II, pp. 587–89) cites the passage from Vasubandhu’s Akṣaya­mati­nirdeśa­ṭīkā, ’phags pa blo gros mi zad pas bstan pa rgya cher ’grel pa, Degé Tengyur (mdo ’grel, ci), 268a4–269a3, in a note and has an excellent translation. The entire passage in a slightly different wording is found in Mañjuśrīkīrti’s work cited in the previous note (mdo ’grel, nyi), 116a6–116b4. “the measure of a human lifespan can be one hundred years. There in the earlier fifty years the color, shape, strength, intellect and so on increase, and in the later fifty years they wane. Similarly, the end of the time period, the time of the waning of the teaching, is like the later fifty years and hence is labeled ‘the last of the five hundreds.’ ”

*When formulated like that, Vasubandhu’s Akṣaya­mati­nirdeśa­ṭīkā. the duration of the lasting of the Tathāgata’s teaching is two thousand five hundred years. The two commentaries appear to be contradictory. Śāntarakṣita’s intention is that the good Dharma lasts from the Worthy One chapter up to the Meditative Stabilization chapter. There is the explanation in the explanatory tradition and there is this other expanation. In general there is agreement on five thousand years.* I have included this paragraph (between the two asterisks) even though it is omitted from the Degé Tengyur. In K, N, and Golden 293b4–6 it reads de de ltar byas na de bzhin gshegs pa’i bstan pa gnas pa’i dus lo nyis stong lnga brgyar ’gyur te/ TI ka ’di dang gnyis ’gal bar snang ba/ shanta rak+Shi ta’i bsam pa ni/ dgra bcom pa’i le’u dang/ ting nge ’dzin gyi le’u’i bar la dam pa’i chos gnas so zhes bya bar bsam pa yin te/ ’chad pa’i lugs la ji skad ’chad/ la la ji skad du ’chad de/ spyir lo lnga stong mthun no. If this is part of our original text, it is clearly problematic to assert that our author is Vasubandhu.

The explanation of the teaching of all the benefits of the good qualities is easy. khri brgyad
–.

div.head: Explanation of the work of Māra
div.p: The work of Māra:

q.p:
“When it takes a really long time to have the confidence to speak” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: when it takes a really long time to have the confidence giving a readiness to speak
if inspired speech arises after a very long lapse of time

div.p: it becomes an impediment; and,

q.p: “when the confidence to speak happens too fast,”
q.orig: when the confidence giving a readiness to speak happens too fast
if their inspired speech arises too quickly

div.p: bodhisattvas become arrogant and act with disrespect. There is

q.p: “yawning”

div.p: and being arrogant;

q.p: “laughing”—

div.p: laughing or joking with each other when the Dharma is being explained; and

q.p: “fooling ’bum ta 64a4, nyi khri (kha 250a7). steg is an old word for sgeg and rol. with each other”
q.orig: sneering at one another

div.p: when they make the other want to laugh.

q.p: “Attached to each other as friends” The reading is uncertain, as our author makes clear. PSP 4: 35, Aṣṭa (Wogihara p. 500) anyonya­vijñāna­samaṅgino, le’u brgyad ma nga 197b6 phan tshun rnam par shes pa chags shing, “they feel an attraction for each other”; khri brgyad (kha 114a3) phan tshun sems ’thun par byed, “harmonize their thoughts with each other.” Haribhadra’s Illumination of the Abhisamayālaṃkāra, rgyan gyi snang ba, Degé Tengyur (shes phyin, cha), 194a6, cites this with the translation rnam par shes pa phan tshun dang ldan pas, which is to say, they both have the same attractive object in mind. Gilgit 486.12 anya­vyañjanasasaṅgo, ’bum ta 66a5–6 and nyi khri (kha 250b1) yi ge gzhan la chags shing tshig gi don myi /mi shes par, “attached to other readings while not knowing what the meaning is”; ŚsPN3 4518.10 anyo na vyañjana­samāṅganaḥ padārtham ajānā; Bṭ1 pa 87a4–5 explains that it means quibbling over the correct grammatical form in place of looking at the meaning; LSPW p. 316 “with their minds on other kinds of talk.”—
q.orig: harmonize their thoughts with each other
while being attached

div.p: they do it to protect each other’s minds; they do not do it out of faith. There is also the reading “attached to other readings while not knowing what the meaning is.”

q.p: “While if they yawn while… taking it up”—
q.orig: if they yawn while reciting it, or taking it up
If they yawn while disseminating, upholding

div.p: in regard to these five, yawning and so on, The five are yawning, laughing, sneering, being distracted, and being attached to each other’s ideas (“harmonizing their minds”). the earlier five are when they are writing it out; here it is when they are taking it up in their minds.

q.p:
“As many thoughts as they have to leave, they appropriate that many eons of practice.” khri brgyad
; cf. ’bum ta 67b1–2, nyi khri ; LSPW p. 316 “have to take to (Birth-and-death).”
q.orig: the more those who have set their minds on enlightenment think they should depart and the more they step away, the more eons of time they will continue to be imprisoned

div.p: They have to practice the yoga of the perfection of wisdom again for as many eons as the thoughts they have to leave, because they do not reach maturity for that many eons, since their thought is confused.

q.p:
“Those… would reject the root of the tree of the knowledge of all aspects.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: those bodhisattvas…would reject the root of the tree of the knowledge of all aspects.
those noble sons and noble daughters who follow the vehicle of the bodhisattvas have abandoned the roots of the tree of all-aspect omniscience

div.p: To illustrate, if you get rid of the root of a tree you will not get

q.p: “the branches, petals, and leaves”
q.orig: its branches, leaves, and foliage

div.p: as the outcome you aim for. Similarly, without the tree of the knowledge of all aspects you will not get śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas that are like the branches and leaves and so on. That is the meaning.
Connect this here in the same way: it is just as

q.p: “a dog might spurn”
q.orig: a dog may well spurn

div.p: its master’s tasty

q.p: “food”

div.p: that is easy to get, and go looking for

q.p: “food from a servant”
q.orig: morsel from a servant

div.p: that it either does not get, or only gets a bit of.
Similarly, connect this in the same way: it is just as when

q.p: “somebody finds an elephant,”
q.orig: find the elephant
some person who wants an elephant, after finding the elephant

div.p: rejects it, and makes the absurd statement, “I am interested in

q.p: ‘the track’
q.orig: track
the tracks

div.p: of the elephant, I am not interested in the elephant.”
The illustration of

q.p: “the hoofprint left by a bull,”
q.orig: the hoofprint of a bull

div.p: and the analogy of the

q.p: “contractor who wants to build a Vaijayanta palace”
q.orig: a contractor or contractor’s apprentice might want to build a palace on the scale of the Vaijayanta palace
builder…or a builder’s apprentice wished to build a house the size of [Śakra’s divine] Vaijayanta Palace

div.p: who looks for a

q.p: “celestial mansion circle,”
q.orig: celestial mansion circles
celestial palace

div.p: thinking a Vaijayanta palace is also just that measure, are similar.

q.p:
“Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom does not give confidence to speak” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Subhūti, it is because the perfection of wisdom does not give confidence giving a readiness to speak

div.p: because it does not conceptualize;

q.p: “is inconceivable”

div.p: because it is beyond the range of speculative thought;

q.p: “is without production and without cessation”
q.orig: neither arises nor ceases

div.p: because it is thoroughly established as a final outcome that does not alter;

q.p: “is without defilement and without purification”
q.orig: neither afflicted nor purified

div.p: because it is pure in its basic nature;

q.p: “is without distraction”
q.orig: is undisturbed

div.p: because it is always in meditative equipoise;

q.p: “is not something that can be spoken out loud”
q.orig: is inexpressible

div.p: because it is self-reflexive analytic knowledge;

q.p: “is not part of a conversation”

div.p: because it is beyond language;

q.p: “is not something that can be talked about”

div.p: because it is beyond applied thought and sustained thought; and

q.p: “cannot be apprehended”
q.orig: is nonapprehensible

div.p: because it is separated from apprehending anything as an existent thing. If they

q.p:
“form the notion ‘this deep perfection of wisdom is not an existent thing,’ Subhūti, they should know that this too is the work of Māra.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: form the notion ‘this deep perfection of wisdom is not an existent thing,’ Subhūti, they should know that this too is the work of Māra.
perceive that this profound perfection of wisdom is a nonentity, that too should be known as the work of Māra

div.p: If they explain the perfection of wisdom with the notion that it does not exist, there is the fault of not honoring it.

q.p:
“The perfection of wisdom is without letters,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: the perfection of wisdom is unwritten

div.p: because it is not something that can be spoken out loud and is not something that can be heard. K, N mnyam du med pa, “without equal.”

The rest of the works of Māra are easy to understand. The section goes up to khri brgyad
.

div.head: Revealing this world

q.p: “Subhūti… this deep perfection of wisdom gives birth to a tathāgata’s ten powers,”
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “this perfection of wisdom gives birth to the ten powers of the tathāgatas

div.p:
and so on, khri brgyad
; PSP 4: 58 anayā subhūte gambhīrayā prajñā­pāramitayā daśa­tathāgata­balāni janitāni. teaches that it gives birth to the ultimate tathāgata because it gives birth to the buddhadharmas.

q.p: “Reveals this world”—
q.orig: reveals the world

div.p:
it says it “reveals this world” in eleven forms: khri brgyad
–. it reveals the world of the aggregates; it reveals that the basic nature of all dharmas cannot be designated or apprehended; it reveals the thought activities of all beings and the divisions and so on; khri brgyad
–?. it reveals the suchness of all phenomena; it reveals that the mark of all phenomena is no mark; it reveals the power of being cognizant of what has been done, and acknowledging what has been done, Cf.
ff., explaining khri brgyad
. The words kṛtajñatā (byas pa bzo ba, or, alternatively, byas pa shes pa) and kṛtaveditā (byas pa tshor ba) usually mean “appreciation” and “gratitude.” and the nonexistence of one who knows and the nonexistence of one who sees; it reveals all unseen dharmas; and This is eight to eleven of the ways the perfection of wisdom reveals the world to bodhisattvas. it reveals the power of one who knows, one who understands, one who is aware of, and one who reveals a description of the world as empty, and who reveals this world as inconceivable and isolated, without an interior and so on, and at peace on account of the nonexistence of a perception of this world or the world beyond.
Among those,

q.p:
“Subhūti, the Tathāgata has said that the five aggregates are the world… the perfection of wisdom does not reveal those five aggregates as being destroyed, nor does it reveal them as being really destroyed.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Subhūti, the Tathāgata has said that the five aggregates are the world
Subhūti, the five aggregates are the world of which the tathāgatas speak

div.p: The perfection of wisdom sees only the suchness of the aggregates, not the falsely imagined aggregates. Take “destroyed” and “really destroyed” as getting used up and becoming ruined.

q.p: “If even this very perfection of wisdom does not exist and is not apprehended in this deep perfection of wisdom, how could form ever exist or be apprehended?” khri brgyad kha 130a2–3 omits “ever exist or.”
q.orig: if even this very perfection of wisdom does not exist and is not apprehended in this deep perfection of wisdom, how could form, feeling, perception, and volitional factors ever be apprehended

if even the perfection of wisdom itself does not exist and is not apprehended in the perfection of wisdom itself, how could physical forms, feelings, perceptions, formative predispositions, and consciousness exist and be apprehended

div.p: This means that if even this very perfection of wisdom does not appear to the nonconceptual perfection of wisdom when an apprehended and an apprehender have become equally the same, it goes without saying form and so on do not.

q.p:
“Subhūti, the tathāgatas know those collected thoughts and distracted thoughts of those beings for what they are through the true nature of dharmas.” ’bum ta 113a2–3 ff.; cf. khri brgyad
, nyi khri .
q.orig: Subhūti, that the tathāgatas correctly and definitively know the collected and diffused thoughts of those beings through reality itself

div.p: To “know collected thoughts and distracted thoughts” is to know collected thoughts and distracted thoughts as not what they are, as nonexistent, by seeing the true dharmic nature of thought. Then it says,

q.p: “How do they know those collected thoughts and distracted thoughts?”
q.orig: how, Subhūti, do they know collected thoughts and distracted thoughts
how the tathāgatas, arhats, completely awakened buddhas correctly and definitively know the collected and diffused thoughts

div.p: And it teaches that they are

q.p: “inexhaustible… free from greed… cessation,”
q.orig: inexhaustible[2] … free from greed… cessation

the extinction of contaminants. Subhūti, the tathāgatas, arhats, completely awakened buddhas correctly and definitively know the collected and diffused thoughts of those beings as aspects of nonattachment, cessation

div.p: and so on, saying to “know those thoughts” is to know all thoughts as being in their true dharmic nature “inexhaustible,” in their true dharmic nature

q.p: “an abandonment,”
q.orig: abandonment
rejection

div.p: and

q.p: “isolated”
q.orig: voidness

div.p: from an intrinsic nature.

Then, with khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Subhūti, a mind that is greedy is not a mind as it really is,”
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Lord, “a mind that is greedy is not as it really is.
thoughts that are afflicted with desire are not the genuine and definitive reality of thought

div.p: it teaches that they This is responding to the question “how do the tathāgatas, worthy ones, perfectly complete buddhas know a greedy thought?” know a thought that is greedy and so on.
Here, in regard to

q.p:
“know a greedy thought… for what it is, a greedy thought,” Cf. khri brgyad
.
q.orig: know that the thoughts of those beings who are afflicted with desire are thoughts afflicted with desire

div.p: if there is such knowledge of greed, thought, and greediness, then the “greedy” thought is not a phenomenon as it really is. A phenomenon “as it really is,” a thought that is a phenomenon “as it really is,” is a phenomenon isolated from an intrinsic nature. The Tathāgata has an extremely pure consciousness and has not grasped thought, or greed, or a dharma that is a mental factor, or being greedy and so on, because falsely imagined temporary states when there are greedy thoughts and so on do not exist at all. Therefore, the passage here should be understood as follows: a thought that is greedy is not as it really is, is not a truth, so, having abandoned it, they “know it” in the form it is really in. That is the meaning.
So it again teaches that they know a mind free from greed for what it is, with

q.p:
“therefore, Subhūti, a mind that is free from greediness is not a mind that has greediness.” nyi khri . khri brgyad
reverses the statement.
q.orig: Subhūti, it is in this manner that the tathāgatas correctly and definitively know that the thoughts of those beings that are free from desire are thoughts free from desire

div.p: What is this teaching? Minds free from greed and minds with greediness are not only ultimately nonexistent, you cannot even say about a temporary state of a falsely imagined nature free from greed that “it is greedy,” because the two—free from greed and greedy—are impossible in one thought; two thoughts do not arise simultaneously. Therefore, not only is it unreal, but even in a falsely imagined form a mind free from greed cannot properly be “greedy,” so it says “free from greediness.” Similarly, connect this with

q.p: “free from hatred… and free from a confusion.”
q.orig: free from hatred is not a mind with hate…a mind that is free from a confused state is not a mind with confusion. And why? Because, Subhūti, two thoughts do not come together. Therefore, Subhūti, the tathāgatas know a mind of those beings free from confusion for what it is, a mind free from confusion.
free from hatred

q.p: “An inclusive thought… as an inclusive thought”
q.orig: an inclusive thought of other beings or other persons for what it is, an inclusive thought
the extensive thoughts of other beings and other persons are extensive thoughts

div.p: and

q.p: “Subhūti, here the tathāgatas know that a thought of those… beings is not inclusive, … that a thought is not constricted,”
q.orig: Subhūti, here the tathāgatas know that a thought of other beings or other persons is not inclusive, that a thought is not constricted,
Subhūti, the tathāgatas, arhats, completely awakened buddhas know that the thoughts of other beings and of other persons do not increase and their thoughts do not decrease

div.p: and so on, teach as follows: They do not view this one’s thought as “inclusive,” or another’s thought as “constricted”; that this one’s thought

q.p: “increases,”
q.orig: increase
enhanced

div.p: or another’s thought

q.p: “is reduced”;
q.orig: reduced
diminished

div.p: or that this one’s thought

q.p: “pervades,” Alternatively, “this one’s thought comes, another’s does not come.” In khyab par ’gro ba, the khyab pa may render Skt ā (“from all sides”), or else is alerting a reader to an a+ā sandhi. If so, khyab pa is being used (like rnam pa as a sign for vi-) in a mechanical translation (tshig ’gyur), not a translation conveying what the words mean (don ’gyur). khri brgyad (kha 132a5) sems ’ong ba ma yin / sems ’gro ba ma yin, and similarly, nyi khri , ’bum ta 114b3–4 (“that a thought does not come, and that a thought does not go”), supported by ŚsPN3 4538r7, PSP 4: 61–62 nāgacchati na gacchati; Gilgit 506.1 anāgacchati tac cittaṃ na vigacchati.
q.orig: does not come
do not come

div.p: or another’s thought

q.p: “does not pervade.”
q.orig: does not go
do not go

div.p: It teaches that they

q.p: “know, thanks to this deep perfection of wisdom,”
q.orig: thanks to this deep perfection of wisdom, know
know this profound perfection of wisdom

div.p: that that inclusive thought is a nonexistent thing, that it is does not exist, and that it is without an intrinsic nature; they thoroughly know

q.p: “an inclusive thought as an inclusive thought,”
q.orig: an inclusive thought of other beings or other persons for what it is, an inclusive thought[3]
the extensive thoughts of other beings and other persons are extensive thoughts[3]

div.p: knowing it

q.p: “for what it is,”
q.orig: for what it is[3]
definitively[3]

div.p: a nonexistent thing.
Similarly, with

q.p: “that has become great.”
q.orig: are grand thoughts

div.p: Here also,

q.p: “Subhūti, here the tathāgatas view a thought of other beings or other persons as not coming, as not going, as not lasting, as not arising, and as not stopping,”
q.orig: Subhūti, here the tathāgatas do not view the intrinsic nature of a thought of other beings or other persons as coming, going, being stationary, being produced, stopping, or as lasting
Subhūti, the tathāgatas, arhats, completely awakened buddhas do not see that the thoughts of other beings and of other persons come or go. They do not see that they arise or cease

div.p:
and so on, khri brgyad
, nyi khri, and ’bum all omit the negation of “coming” and so on, and have mi gzigs. explains this. “Great” here is in the sense of arising, in the sense of lasting for an extended period, and in the sense of changing into something else marked by lasting and having an extended period. As for “has become,” “Has become” renders gyur pa (-gata). Whitney’s Sanskrit Grammar 1273c, 435: “gata… is used in a loose way… to express relation of various kinds.” The compound mahāgata (chen por gyur pa) just means “great.” it is in the sense of “coming and going.” A tathāgata’s wisdom does not view it like that; it views it solely as the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature. Since this is the case, it is saying that where “a thought has become big” its becoming big does not exist, so they “thoroughly know” of it that it is a nonexistent thing.

q.p: “Immeasurable thought”
q.orig: immeasurable thoughts

div.p: is explained by saying they

q.p: “view that thought of… beings… as not there, as not interrupted, as not fixed, and as not not fixed,” Cf. the slight difference from the translations at ’bum ta 115b2, nyi khri , le’u brgyad ma nga 218b7; the forms of sthita at PSP 4: 62, ŚsPN3 4538r10, and Gilgit 506.9 all differ slightly; LSPW p. 330: “He does not review that it is, nor that it is not, nor does He review it as discontinuous, or as not discontinuous.”
q.orig: view that thought of other beings or other persons as not there, as not…fixed.
observe that the thoughts of other beings and of other persons are stable, and do not observe that they are they are unstable, accomplished, or established

div.p: and so on. This teaches the following: You can suppose it is “immeasurable” in the sense that it is pervasive or is a basic element. “Basic element” renders dbyings (dhātu). Alternatively, “entire cosmos,” “vast expanse.” The tathāgatas do not view an immeasurable thought like that; rather, they view all thoughts as having no fixed position and being without a foundation. When they view it like that, they

q.p: “know an immeasurable thought… for what it is.”
q.orig: know an immeasurable thought of other beings[3]…or other persons for what it is[3].
definitively know, dependent on this perfection of wisdom, that the immeasurable thoughts of other beings and other persons are immeasurable thoughts[2]

q.p: “[They] view that thought… as without a mark and separated from an intrinsic nature.”
q.orig: view that thought of other beings or other persons as without a mark and separated from an intrinsic nature.
know that thoughts without defining characteristics are thoughts without defining characteristics, owing to the emptiness of their own defining characteristics

div.p: Because it has no intrinsic nature and no mark it cannot show itself, so they view it as

q.p: “a thought… that does not show itself.”
q.orig: a thought that does not show itself
are undefinable thoughts

q.p: “Those thoughts… are not even visible to the five eyes”—
q.orig: those thoughts of other beings and of other persons do not appear to the five eyes of the tathāgatas

div.p: a thought forms, This derives citta from root ci, “to gather.” gsags from gsog (K, N brtsags?) (the prefixed g in place of b is not attested in the bod rgya tshig mdzod chen mo) means to get everything together, as in “accumulate the equipment,” tshogs gnyis bsags te rdzogs sangs rgyas, or to accumulate in the sense of possession: “The water drops all together form the ocean,” chu thigs bsogs na rgya mtshor ’gyur. Cf. Laṅkāvatāra­sūtra (Nanjio edition, p. 46) citteṇa cīyate karmam, (Suzuki translation, p. 158) “Karma is accumulated by thought.” so take it as falsely imagined; furthermore, because that does not exist in itself, it is a nonexistent thing, so it does not appear to the eyes of those who see true reality. Hence,

q.p: “an invisible thought.”
q.orig: an invisible thought[5]
are imperceptible thoughts[3]

div.p: That is the meaning.

q.p:
“Thoughts that are clear, dull, abridged, and expanded” Our author cites the words (probably unmiñjita, nimiñjita, saṃmiñjita, and prasārita) as derived from miñj (“to say, to shine”), a derivation that fits the context well. The translators at khri brgyad kha 133b1 (lhag par g.yo ba, bral bar g.yo ba, bsdus par g.yo ba, rgyas pa), and, less obviously, in part at least, at ’bum ta 116b1, nyi khri kha 275b2, le’u brgyad ma nga 219b3 (’phro ba, ’du pa, bkram pa, bcum pa) understood some of the words as derived from iñj. The four categories are those under which the wrong views (khri brgyad
–) are explained. Cf. the sixty-two wrong views set forth in detail in the Brahma­jāla­sūtra (tshangs pa’i dra ba’i mdo). —
q.orig: the thoughts of other beings or other persons that have moved excessively, are freed from movement, have moved to abridge, or are expanded
thoughts of other beings and of other persons that are diffused or absorbed, and expansive or narrow

div.p: they know “clear” thoughts in the sense of those of tīrthikas who make philosophical errors grasping at permanence; the “dull” in the sense of those grasping at nihilism; the “abridged” in the sense of those who over-negate; and the “expanded” in the sense of those who over-reify

q.p: “for what they are.”
q.orig: definitively

q.p:
“Based on form” khri brgyad
: “When the thoughts of beings that have moved excessively are freed from movement, have moved to abridge, and are expanded, arise, whichever of them arises they all arise based on form, or based on feeling, or based on perception, or based on volitional factors, or based on consciousness.”
q.orig: based on form
dependent on physical forms

div.p: explains arising based on the five aggregates.

q.p: “Refers to form”
q.orig: refers to form
refers to physical forms

div.p: means a thought has “been emitted” This ’phro ba (from iñj) (if derived from miñj the translation is “been beamed out”) is an alternative translation of the first of the four categories (gsal ba, rendered “clear”). with form as its reference point, and they have settled down on it and say, “I am form.”

q.p: “Connect this in the same way also with”

div.p: refers to

q.p: “feeling”
q.orig: feelings

div.p: and so on.

Similarly, having taught that thoughts that have arisen from wrong views have “been emitted” and so on, now, to reveal those that have been emitted and so on from conceptual thought constructions, it says, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Furthermore, Subhūti, thanks to this deep perfection of wisdom the tathāgatas know form. How do they know form? They know it just as they know suchness—without distortion, without conceptualization,”
q.orig: Furthermore, Subhūti, thanks to this deep perfection of wisdom the tathāgatas know form. How do they know form? They know it just as they know suchness without distortion, without conceptualization,

Moreover, Subhūti, the tathāgatas perceive physical forms through this profound perfection of wisdom. If you ask how they perceive physical forms, they perceive them as the real nature, the unmistaken real nature, unchanging, nonconceptual

q.p: “without a causal sign,”
q.orig: signless

div.p: because of the very limit of reality;

q.p: “without effort,”
q.orig: effortless

div.p: because there is no illumination;

q.p: “without thought construction,”
q.orig: unelaborate

div.p: because they are isolated from an intrinsic nature;

q.p: “and without apprehending anything,”
q.orig: nonapprehensible

div.p: because of the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature.
