Now, because all phenomena with outflows and without outflows, that are ordinary and extraordinary, and all superior persons and all superior dharmas, even the tathāgatas, are not broken apart in suchness, with

q.p: “therefore, Subhūti, the suchness of thoughts… that are clear, dull, abridged, and expanded is the suchness of the aggregates, constituents, sense fields, dependent origination,”
q.orig: Therefore, Subhūti, the suchness of the thoughts of other beings or other persons that have moved excessively, are freed from movement, have moved to abridge, or are expanded is the suchness of the aggregates, constituents, and sense fields.

Subhūti, it is in that manner that the tathāgatas definitively know, dependent on this profound perfection of wisdom, the real nature of the thoughts of other beings and other persons that are diffused or absorbed, and expansive or narrow, and that they definitively know their unmistaken real nature

div.p: and so on, it reveals that as suchness, their intrinsic nature, all phenomena are not different.

div.head: Marks

q.p:
“Gods, this perfection of wisdom is deep because it is marked by emptiness.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Divine princes,” replied the Blessed One, “this profound perfection of wisdom…has the defining characteristic of emptiness

div.p: The separation from falsely imagined phenomena that are the objects in the range of fools is “marked by emptiness.” The absence and total extinguishing of the causal signs of mental construction and conceptual thought projections is

q.p: “marked by signlessness.”
q.orig: has the defining characteristic of signlessness

div.p: Not joining up later with what has been wished for, because all conceptualized wishes have been forsaken, is

q.p: “marked by wishlessness.”
q.orig: has the defining characteristic of wishlessness

div.p: The uncompounded state is

q.p: “marked by the absence of production and stopping”
q.orig: marked by the absence of production, marked by the absence of stopping,
has the defining characteristic of nonarising. Divine princes, this profound perfection of wisdom has the defining characteristic of noncessation

div.p: because all thought constructions conceiving of cause, condition, and result are severed. It is separated from production and so on. The absolutely purified state when there is a transformation of the basis through the four transformations is These are perhaps the transformations (parāvṛtti) of the ālaya, kliṣṭamanas, and pravṛtti­vijñānas into the three bodies and a fundamental purity. Cf. the transformations in Ratnākaraśānti’s Prajñā­pāramitopadeśa , shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa’i man ngag, Degé Tengyur (sems tsam, hi), 141a7, and Khasamā­nāma­ṭīkā, nam mkha’ dang mnyam pa zhes bya ba’i rgya cher ’grel pa, Degé Tengyur (rgyud, wa), translated and explained by Seton (pp. 97–101).

q.p: “marked by the absence of defilement and the absence of purification.”
q.orig: marked by the absence of defilement, marked by the absence of purification,
has the defining characteristic of nonaffliction. Divine princes, this profound perfection of wisdom has the defining characteristic of nonpurification

div.p: Like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, and so on, which are not thoroughly established and are nonexistent, a nonexistent thing is

q.p: “marked by the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature.”
q.orig: marked by an intrinsic nature
has the defining characteristic of the essential nature of nonentities

div.p: What has no standing anywhere, like space separated from all false imagination and thought construction, ultimately inexpressible, is

q.p: “marked by the absence of a foundation.”
q.orig: has the defining characteristic of nondwelling

div.p: Because a prior limit, a later limit, and a middle This means the time of birth, the time of death, and the duration of a life in between. have been abandoned, the natural state of nirvāṇa separated from an existent thing and a nonexistent thing is

q.p: “marked by the absence of annihilation and of going on and on forever.”
q.orig: marked by the absence of a foundation, marked by the absence of annihilation, marked by the absence of going on and on forever,

div.p: The nondual state separated from difference and unity is

q.p: “marked by the absence of unity and the absence of difference”
q.orig: marked by the absence of unity, marked by the absence of difference,

div.p: because all conceptualizations of difference have stopped. The state separated from coming and going is

q.p: “marked by the absence of coming and absence of going”
q.orig: marked by the absence of coming, marked by the absence of going,

div.p: because all effort has been abandoned, illuminating does not exist, and an act of doing something does not exist. Because everything is totally separated from all of its own characteristic marks, the place constituted by the unmarked is

q.p: “marked by space.”
q.orig: has the defining characteristic of space

div.p: Furthermore,

q.p: “the Tathāgata uses the conventional label as an ordinary conventional term, but not as an ultimate one”
q.orig: the tathāgatas have expressed it in worldly conventional terms, but that is not the case in ultimate truth

div.p: says it is marked by being inexpressible.

q.p:
“Gods, the world with its gods and humans cannot alter those marks” ’bum ta 121a6, nyi khri
. Gilgit 510.7 vigopayati, cf. Edg, s.v. avikopana, LSPW “alter.” khri brgyad (kha 136b5) ’khrug; le’u brgyad ma nga 223a4 dkrugs; PSP 4: 68 vikopayati, “disturb.”
q.orig: Gods, the world with its gods, humans, and asuras cannot disturb those marks.
Divine princes, these defining characteristics cannot be altered by the world with its gods, humans

div.p: is saying that it is marked as thoroughly established because it is thoroughly established as being without alteration and thoroughly established as being without error.

q.p:
“Gods, a mark does not make a mark into something else” ’bum ta 121a7, nyi khri
.
q.orig: a mark does not disturb a mark
defining characteristics do not alter defining characteristics

div.p: means suchness does not disturb suchness.

q.p: “A mark does not know a mark.”
q.orig: Defining characteristics do not cognize defining characteristics

div.p: Suchness does not know suchness, just as space does not know space.

q.p: “A mark does not know the absence of a mark.”
q.orig: Defining characteristics do not cognize the absence of defining characteristics

div.p: Suchness does not know a falsely imagined phenomenon, just as space does not know a rabbit’s horns.

q.p: “The absence of a mark does not know a mark.”

div.p: A falsely imagined phenomenon does not know suchness, just as a rabbit’s horns do not know space.

q.p: “And the absence of a mark does not know the absence of a mark.”
q.orig: The absence of defining characteristics does not cognize the absence of defining characteristics

div.p: A falsely imagined phenomenon does not know a falsely imagined phenomenon, just as a rabbit’s horns do not know a rabbit’s horns.

q.p:
“Therefore that mark, and that absence of a mark, and also both, do not have… the intrinsic nature of that which might cause knowing.” Similar to khri brgyad
; cf. ’bum ta 121b1–2, nyi khri , Twenty-Five Thousand translation: “Therefore, as far as defining characteristics, absence of defining characteristics, both presence and absence of defining characteristics, and neither presence nor absence of defining characteristics are concerned, it is impossible for them to be known by anyone, for any of them to be known, or for them to know anything”; le’u brgyad ma nga, 223a5–6 … gang gis shes par bya ba’am/ gang shes par bya ba mi srid do (“to know or to be known”); Gilgit 510.8, ŚsPN3 4540v6 lakṣaṇaṃ cālakṣaṇaṃ ca lakṣaṇālakṣaṇaṃ ca tayor ubhayo[r] nāsti saṃbhavo yena prajānīyād yo vā prajānīyād (“something that might know or someone that might know”).
q.orig: Therefore, in that mark, and in that absence of a mark, and also in them both that which makes known, or who makes known, or to whom it is made known, or the intrinsic nature of whom it is made known to do not exist.

Therefore, as far as defining characteristics, absence of defining characteristics…both the presence and absence of defining characteristics, and neither the presence nor absence of defining characteristics are concerned, it is impossible for them to be known by anyone, for any of them to be known, or for them to know anything

div.p: An intrinsic nature of perceiving does not exist because suchness is nonconceptual, effortless, and does not stir, because a falsely imagined phenomenon does not exist. “That which might make known” is consciousness and so on.

q.p: “Who might know”
q.orig: who[1]…makes known[2]
for them to be known by anyone

div.p: is a person or a dharma.

q.p: “To whom it might be made known”
q.orig: to whom it is made known
for any of them to be known

div.p: is another person or a dharma.

q.p: “Gods, those marks are not occasioned by form,”
q.orig: Gods, those marks are not occasioned by form
Divine princes, these defining characteristics have not been conditioned by physical forms

div.p: and so on, reveals that it The perfection of wisdom is the subject. is marked by not occasioning anything.

q.p: “Because all marks have no mark”—

div.p: because the aforementioned emptiness, signlessness, and so on, and all compounded and uncompounded phenomena, are marked as falsely imagined phenomena is the meaning.

q.p: “Whether the tathāgatas arise or whether the tathāgatas do not arise,”
q.orig: whether the tathāgatas have appeared or whether the tathāgatas have not appeared

div.p: and so on, is speaking about the defining mark of phenomena remaining in the same state. chos gnas pa’i mtshan nyid is similar to the term chos gnas pa nyid (dharmasthititā): “the establishment of dharmas,” “the abiding of phenomena.”

q.p: “The element of marks simply remains as it really is, the element of no marks. A tathāgata has perfectly and fully awakened to that.”
q.orig: the expanse that is without defining characteristics dwells in that manner. The tathāgatas are called tathāgatas because they have unerringly attained consummate buddhahood

div.p: It is called “the element of no marks” because all conceptualizations of a mark are absent.

q.p: “Therefore a tathāgata is called a ‘tathāgata.’ ” The sense of tathāgata here, a synonym of the perfection of wisdom, is that all the doctrines have properly been included (tathā āgata) in it, or that it properly understands (tathā gata) all phenomena, or that all the doctrines that might be included in it do not ultimately exist (tathā a-āgata), or that all that might be properly understood is not ultimately understood (tathā a-gata) with the corresponding negative senses.
q.orig: The tathāgatas are called tathāgatas

div.p: Through a creative explanation they are called “tathāgatas” because they have realized as suchness or because they have realized suchness. “Suchness” renders tathatā and “realized” renders gata.

q.p: “The Tathāgata has given an exposition of K, N; D yang dag par rab tu mkhyen, “knows.” all marks by giving an exposition of the perfection of wisdom”
q.orig: the Tathāgata has given an exposition of all marks by giving an exposition of the perfection of wisdom.
they continue to reveal these defining characteristics by revealing the perfection of wisdom

div.p:
is indicating the earlier statement, khri brgyad
ff. “Gods, this is deep because it is marked by emptiness, it is marked by signlessness,” and so on.

q.p: “Having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening… [he] has differentiated all the marks”
q.orig: having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, has differentiated all the marks
after attaining consummate buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete enlightenment, they continue to distinguish between all defining characteristics

div.p: means that even though they have fully awakened to such a nonconceptual ultimate they still explain the conventional marks for the benefit of beings.

q.p: “The mark of form is something that can show itself,”
q.orig: The mark of form is something that can show itself
physical forms have the defining characteristic of being perishable

div.p: and so on, teaches the conventional defining marks.

div.head: Appreciation and gratitude
div.p: [The tathāgatas]

q.p:
“have appreciation and a feeling of gratitude” nyi khri , Twenty-Five Thousand translation: “Subhūti, if you ask how the tathāgatas appreciate it and are thankful for it, it is, Subhūti, because the tathāgatas serve, respect, honor, worship, and protect that very vehicle by which the tathāgatas, arhats, completely awakened buddhas reach, and that very path by which they attain, consummate buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete enlightenment. In this sense, Subhūti, it should be recognized that the tathāgatas appreciate it and are thankful for it.” Cf. khri brgyad
. The words kṛtajñatā and kṛtaveditā usually mean “appreciation” or “one who has appreciation,” and “gratitude” or “one who feels gratitude,” but here the Tib literally renders them as “cognizant of what has been done” and “acknowledge what has been done.” ’bum ta 126a6–7, nyi khri kha 281b3 render kṛtajñatā by byas pa mkhyen pa and byas pa shes pa, and kṛtaveditā by byas pa dgongs pa and byas pa dran pa.
q.orig: Subhūti, the Tathāgata is cognizant of what has been done, and acknowledges what has been done.
appreciate it and are thankful for it

div.p: for this [perfection of wisdom]. They think ‘We have done this and we have asserted this’ because they realize what they have done and achieved.

q.p: “Fully awakened to all dharmas as not done and not changed” D: “Fully awakened as not done (akṛta) and not changed (avikṛta).”—
q.orig: fully awakens to all dharmas as not done and not changed
They have attained consummate buddhahood [knowing] that [all phenomena] are uncreated

div.p: they have “fully awakened” to dharmas constituted by what has not been done—that nobody has done. As for “not changed,” they have fully awakened without distortion; they know them as unchanging.

q.p: “Because there is no body”—
q.orig: because they have no corporeality

div.p: this is the nonexistence of a body, the nonexistence of an interior, formlessness. Therefore, Subhūti, the nonexistence of a body, this interior, is

q.p: “the Tathāgata’s cognizance of what has not been done, and acknowledgment of what has not been done.”
q.orig: the tathāgatas have attained consummate buddhahood dependent on the profound perfection of wisdom, [knowing] that all phenomena are inactive

div.p: He is cognizant of what has not been done because he is cognizant of the mark of uncompounded phenomena.

q.p:
“Furthermore, Subhūti, thanks to the perfection of wisdom, on account of the force of ultimately not originating, the unmade transcendental knowledge has engaged with all dharmas.” Cf. khri brgyad
; ’bum ta 126b6–7 sangs rgyas kyi ye shes byas pa med pa/ chos thams cad la ’jug pa med pa’i brdas ’jug ste, “the unmade transcendental knowledge engages with all dharmas through the convention of not engaging;” nyi khri
, Twenty-Five Thousand translation: “symbolically engage with the uncreated wisdom, which does not engage with anything.”
q.orig: Furthermore, Subhūti, thanks to the perfection of wisdom, on account of being ultimately unoriginated, the Tathāgata has engaged with all the dharmas of the unmade transcendental knowledge.

Moreover, Subhūti, it is dependent on this perfection of wisdom that the tathāgatas, arhats, completely awakened buddhas symbolically engage with the uncreated wisdom, which does not engage with anything

div.p: “On account of the force of ultimately not originating” means based on the ultimate being unproduced and unoriginated. It is teaching that the transcendental knowledge of the tathāgatas is the mark of the thoroughly established dharma body and hence is “unmade,” so the Tathāgata cognizes what has not been done. Alternatively, “the Tathāgata does not have appreciation.”

q.p:
“Lord, when all dharmas are not producers and are not seers” khri brgyad
“not producers and not revealers”; nyi khri , ’bum ta 127a1 “not knowers and not seers.”
q.orig: Lord, when all dharmas are not producers and are not revealers,
Blessed Lord, if there is no knowing and no perceiving of any phenomena

div.p: is teaching that there has been no production so there is no producer, therefore it is not feasible K, N; here and in the following D has ma mthong, “it is not seen.” that

q.p: “the perfection of wisdom gives birth”;
q.orig: the perfection of wisdom give birth
the perfection of wisdom give birth

div.p: it does not cause seeing so there is no seer, so it is not feasible that it

q.p: “reveals the world.”
q.orig: reveal the world
reveal this world

q.p: “Exactly so, Subhūti, exactly so!”
q.orig: Subhūti, it is so! It is so

div.p: and so on is teaching

q.p: “because all dharmas are empty, ring hollow, are in vain… are not producers and are not revealers,”
q.orig: all phenomena are empty, vacuous, hollow, powerless, and essenceless. This is the formulation, Subhūti, that explains how there is no knowing and no perceiving of any phenomena

div.p: that it is true, and in the ordinary world there is nobody who knows such a reality. It is teaching “Still, he, Literally “I.” The Lord is speaking. thanks to the perfection of wisdom, has fully awakened to this reality as it actually is, therefore it has given birth to him and reveals the world.” He intends this as a statement of praise.

q.p: “It reveals it, moreover, because form is not seen.”
q.orig: It reveals it, moreover, because form is not seen.
It also reveals the world because there is no perceiving of physical forms

div.p: Because he does not see form, therefore it reveals it. Were he to have seen form, he would have seen reality imperfectly, like somebody with a visual distortion, so it also would not reveal it.

q.p: “Subhūti, when a consciousness with form as objective support does not arise”—
q.orig: “Subhūti,” replied the Lord, “when a consciousness with form as objective support does not arise,
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “it is when there is no consciousness arising that apprehends physical forms

div.p: when a consciousness with bristly strands of hair and so on as its objective support arises in somebody with a visual distortion, and then later on does not arise, you say sight has become clear. Similarly, here too, there is the locution

q.p: “it reveals”

div.p: because “consciousness and so on with form as objective support does not arise.”

q.p:
“Reveals… [that the world] is inconceivable” khri brgyad
: “Furthermore, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom reveals to the tathāgatas that the world is inconceivable.”—

div.p: because suchness is beyond the range of speculative thought.

q.p: “Subhūti, form is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, uncountable, and equal to the unequaled because it does not appear.” In place of “does not appear,” khri brgyad (kha 142a3–4) shes par byar med pa’i phyir ro, “not something to be known”; nyi khri (kha 286b5) mnyam pa dang mi mnyam pa mi dmigs so, Twenty-Five Thousand: “with regard to physical forms, why can that which is inconceivable, inestimable, unappraisable, and equal to the unequaled not be apprehended”; PSP 4: 76 rūpaṃ hi subhūte acintyam atulyam aprameyam asaṃkhyeyam asamasaman na prajñāyate, “…does not make itself known”; le’u brgyad ma nga 230ba2 shes su ma mchis pa lags, “cannot be known.”
q.orig: Subhūti, form is inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, uncountable, and equal to the unequaled because it is not something to be known.
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “with regard to physical forms, that which is inconceivable, inestimable, unappraisable, and equal to the unequaled cannot indeed be apprehended.

div.p: “Form” does not appear. And why? Falsely imagined form does not exist, like a rabbit’s horns, so “it does not appear”; the true dharmic nature of form cannot be apprehended by any consciousness so “it does not appear,” and because it thus does not appear it is therefore “inconceivable,” “incomparable,” “immeasurable,” and so on.

The teaching about “inconceivable” and so on is easy to understand as found in the scripture. khri brgyad
. In it,

q.p:
“all mental and mental factor dharmas are not apprehended” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: all[1]…mind and mental factor dharmas are not apprehended.

div.p: means cannot be grasped by “all mental and mental factor dharmas,” so it says that “it does not appear.”
Why does Subhūti, with

q.p: “it is made available to serve a great purpose,”
q.orig: has been made available through tremendous work
this perfection of wisdom is established for a great purpose

div.p: and so on, again introduce an exposition of a part of the text that has already been explained?Earlier nyi khri (kha 285a3), and here (288a7–b1) don chen po slad du (Twenty-Five Thousand: “is established for a great purpose”); khri brgyad (kha 141a3) mdzad pa chen pos, (143b7) bgyid pa chen pos is the corresponding reading (“is made available through the tremendous work”). He says that in order to gather a retinue, and also because, having introduced just that, he wants a greater enthusiasm. Earlier it taught that it benefits the practice prior to a buddha; now it is teaching that it does the work of a buddha.

q.p:
“This deep perfection of wisdom is made available so that you do not hold on to and do not settle down on form.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: this deep perfection of wisdom is made available so you do not hold on to and do not settle down on form
this profound perfection of wisdom is established in order that one might not appropriate or become fixated on physical forms

div.p: Because from seeing the perfection of wisdom they do not on account of craving come to “hold on to” and on account of a view “settle down on form” and so on—the dharmas—therefore it is put into words as “this deep perfection of wisdom is made available so you do not hold on to and do not settle down,” which is to say, it teaches that it is for a truly great purpose.

q.p:
“Subhūti, I too…” khri brgyad
: “Subhūti, I too do not see that form which you might hold on to and might settle down on, or which itself holds on and settles down. Subhūti, I too do not see… up to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.”
q.orig: Subhūti, I also

div.p: He is saying he himself is in full control.

q.p:
“That knowledge and abandonment of faith-followers, dharma-followers, up to worthy ones, and pratyekabuddhas, is the forbearance of bodhisattvas who have gained forbearance for the nonproduction of all dharmas” khri brgyad
, K, N; D has spros pa, “enthusiasm.” prahāna, “abandonment,” also means pradhāna (=spros pa), “effort.”
q.orig: that knowledge and effort of faith followers, Dharma followers, the eighth, and stream enterers, as well as the knowledge and effort of once-returners, non-returners, worthy ones, and pratyekabuddhas, is the forbearance of the bodhisattva great beings who have gained forbearance for the nonproduction of dharmas.

the exertion of those who have become followers through faith, and those who have become followers of the Dharma, who have reached the eighth level, who have entered the stream to nirvāṇa, who are destined for only one more rebirth, who are no longer subject to rebirth, who have attained arhatship, and who have become pratyekabuddhas, is subsumed in the receptivity of bodhisattva great beings who have accepted that phenomena are nonarising

div.p: teaches that a bodhisattva’s wisdom is greater. Just by merely having entered into the eighth level and gained the forbearance for dharmas that are not produced, the knowledges and the abandonments of all afflictions that are the result of the path to all śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha worthy ones are completed. Their knowledge and abandonment do not exceed that forbearance. From here the bodhisattvas are totally without afflictions. Up to here the bodhisattvas described as those “who have gained forbearance for the nonproduction of dharmas” are the ones without afflictions.

q.p:
“Before they had gone very far disappeared” khri brgyad
. —
q.orig: Having gone not very far, they disappeared

div.p: this explanation teaches that their work has been completed.
Then the elder Subhūti, to engender respect in persons with perfect belief in this explanation and so on, asks about their birth. It says,

q.p: “Where did they die, Lord, the bodhisattva great beings who have taken birth here and believe in this deep perfection of wisdom the moment they hear it?”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, if bodhisattva great beings who have heard this perfection of wisdom, immediately afterward are inclined toward it, and, as mentioned before, commit it to writing, take up, uphold, recite, master, and focus their attention correctly on it, from where will they pass away and be reborn into this [human world]

div.p: and so on. Here it also gives an exposition of the three bodhisattvas that make up the bright side and the three that make up the dark side. Those who

q.p: “have died a human and taken birth as a human”
q.orig: have died as humans and taken birth as humans
pass away among humankind and be reborn among humankind

div.p: are good. The second who,

q.p: “having died in other buddhafields, take birth”
q.orig: in other buddhafields and, having died there, takes birth
have venerated other lord buddhas, and then passed away to be reborn

div.p: among humans are good. The third who

q.p: “have died among the Tuṣita gods and taken birth here”
q.orig: have died among the Tuṣita gods and, having taken birth here
who have [previously] been born equal in fortune to the gods of Tuṣita, and who, on passing away from that [divine realm], have been reborn

div.p: are also good. As for the three on the dark side, there are those who are not endowed with having

q.p: “heard or asked about it in the past [and] have taken birth here,”
q.orig: heard or asked about the perfection of wisdom in the past have taken birth in the human world
have not had an opportunity to pose questions and investigate it

div.p: but do not believe in the explanation; the second, who are also not endowed with having heard and so on, hear it here just because of faith, but

q.p: “get robbed”

div.p: and become uncertain; and the third, who have asked about this explanation in the past just because of faith but still are not endowed with taking it up and so on, and who later fall into

q.p: “the Śrāvaka and the Pratyekabuddha”
q.orig: the śrāvaka level or the pratyekabuddha
the level of the śrāvakas and the level of the pratyekabuddhas

div.p:
Vehicles. khri brgyad
.
Here the analogy of

q.p: “the boat on the ocean,”
q.orig: a boat has broken up on the ocean
a ship is wrecked at sea

div.p: the analogy of

q.p: “the pot,”
q.orig: pot[1]
unbaked clay jar

div.p: and then the analogies of

q.p: “the ship”
q.orig: ship[1]
an ocean-going ship

div.p: and

q.p: “the very old man”
q.orig: a very old, decrepit, one hundred and twenty-year-old man
an aged and decrepit old man

div.p:
are easy to understand as found in the scripture. khri brgyad
–.

To teach that when they do not have such a perfection of wisdom and skillful means they fall into the two vehicles, and that when they do have them they reach unsurpassed, complete awakening, Subhūti asks how it is that they do not have those two, and asks how it is that they do not not have those two. khri brgyad
–. Subhūti asks, “How is it, Lord, that those sons of a good family or daughters of a good family who have set out in the Bodhisattva Vehicle have not been assisted by the perfection of wisdom and have not been assisted by skillful means and even fall to the śrāvaka level and the pratyekabuddha level?” Our author, based on the Lord’s long reply, construes the question from both the conventional and ultimate perspectives.

At that time the Lord puts into words that not having the six perfections is because of the power of apprehending and because of the power of pride, and that they fall to one of the two deficient levels. He teaches that those who do not apprehend the six perfections and have no pride

q.p: “reach unsurpassed, complete awakening.”
q.orig: attain unsurpassed, complete enlightenment

q.p:
“It is because the perfection of giving has gone to the near shore.” Cf. khri brgyad
(kha 154a3), ’bum ta 255a7, nyi khri (kha 301b2–5), le’u brgyad ma nga 242b5: “The perfection (pāramitā, pha rol tu phyin pa) of giving has gone to the farthest limit (āram itā, pha mthar phyin/ring du song).” Our author, or at least his Tibetan translators, perhaps understood a-āraṃ / apāraṃ.
q.orig: Because that‍—namely, the perfection of giving‍—has gone to the farthest limit
The perfection of generosity is far removed

div.p: The side that is the knowledge of path aspects of bodhisattvas—the absence of conceptualization—is “gone to the near shore.” The side that is the knowledge of all aspects of buddhas is “gone to the farther shore,” because it is the perfection of the absence of conceptualization. Therefore, it says

q.p: “knows the near shore and knows the farther shore.” Cf. le’u brgyad ma nga 242b6–7 de ltar yin yang gang zag byang chub sems dpa’i theg pa pa des tshu rol yang mi shes/ pha rol yang mi shes te; LSPW p. 347: “and he knows neither the not-beyond nor the Beyond.” khri brgyad (kha 154b5), pha mtha’ yang shes/ pha rol yang shes, “knows the farthest limit and knows the farther shore.”
q.orig: know the farthest limit and know the farther shore
understand that which is far removed and that which is transcendent

div.p:
Then the section of the text to do with skillful means is in just that sequence as well. The immediately preceding citation ends the section. It begins at khri brgyad
and goes up to ; nyi khri
up to
.

div.head: How those new to the bodhisattva vehicle train
div.p:
Having thus heard that those who do not have the perfection of wisdom and skillful means fall into the two vehicles, thinking, “How, then, do they become those who have newly set out in the vehicle and are beginning the work,” Subhūti asks, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Lord, how should bodhisattva great beings beginning the work train in the perfection of wisdom?”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, how should those bodhisattva great beings who are beginners train in the perfection of wisdom

div.p: And the Lord, because those who are beginning the work definitely have to have spiritual friends, therefore teaches that they

q.p: “should attend on spiritual friends.”
q.orig: should rely upon and venerate spiritual mentors

q.p: “You should not hold as an absolute,” PSP 4: 94, ŚsPN3 4594 mā … rūpataḥ parāmrākṣīḥ / parāmṛkṣaḥ. Cf. khri brgyad (kha 155b1), nyi khri (kha 305a2) rtog par ma byed, “should not form an idea.”
q.orig: you should not form an idea
you should not misconstrue unsurpassed, complete enlightenment as physical forms

div.p: and

q.p:
“you should not produce a longing for form” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: you should not produce a longing for form
do not generate desire for physical forms

div.p: means do not, because of conceptual views and attachment to an ultimate, set your hopes on something.

div.head: Nine qualities of the doers of the difficult
div.p:
Then the elder Subhūti said, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Lord, those bodhisattvas who want unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, even while all phenomena are empty of their own marks, are doers of the difficult.”
q.orig: Lord, those bodhisattva great beings who want unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, yearning for unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, even while all phenomena are empty of their own marks, are those who do what is difficult.

Blessed Lord…those bodhisattva great beings who aspire to unsurpassed, complete enlightenment, and who wish to attain consummate buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete enlightenment, are engaged in a difficult task, inasmuch as all phenomena are empty of their own defining characteristics.

div.p: In that context the Lord makes nine statements:

q.p: “ ‘May I for the world’s benefit and happiness… become the protector nyi khri (kha 307a5); khri brgyad (kha 156b5) skyob.… refuge… resting place… final ally… island… leader and… support. May I become the benefit and happiness of the world: its protector, refuge, resting place, final ally, island, leader, and support,”
q.orig: for the benefit and happiness of the world. They have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, thinking, ‘May I become the world’s protector.’ They have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, thinking, ‘May I become the world’s refuge, the world’s resting place, the world’s final ally, the world’s island, the world’s leader, and the world’s support.’
for the benefit, well-being, and happiness of the world. So, they set out for unsurpassed, complete enlightenment, saying…and a guide for the world!

div.p:
which he then explains in detail, discussing each separately. khri brgyad
–. “The benefit” is the intention to liberate beings from all forms of life and establish them in a place without fear; “the happiness” is the intention to liberate them from suffering and establish them in happiness; “the protector” is the intention to teach the doctrine in order to protect them from suffering; “the refuge” is the intention to liberate those afflicted by suffering from that suffering and establish them in the nirvāṇa without any aggregates remaining; “the resting place” is the intention to explain the doctrine in order that they will have no attachment; “the final ally” is the intention to explain by way of all phenomena, form and so on, the father shore of phenomena; “the island” is the intention to explain the doctrine in a delimited form like an island that is circumscribed; “the leader” is the intention, because of great compassion for beings, to explain the doctrine that leads Emend ’dres to ’dren. to nirvāṇa; and “the support” is the intention to understand analytically the places supporting life that are, in brief, eighty-five. Those are the successive contents of the passage.

q.p:
“Lord, how are all phenomena not mingled?” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: How are all phenomena not mingled?
Blessed Lord, in what manner do they not embrace anything

div.p: During saṃsāra, when the falsely imagined and the thoroughly established are as one, are there not broken apart, at that time, when the two are undifferentiable, they are “mingled.” When there has been a gradual transformation through the force of listening, thinking, and meditating in harmony with the extremely pure dharma-constituent as cause, at that time, when the two—the falsely imagined and the thoroughly established—have become differentiated and a transformation into the extremely pure, stainless, intrinsic nature has come about, they are “not mingled.”

q.p: “The nonconnection… the nonproduction… the noncessation,”
q.orig: nonassociation of physical forms. The nonassociation of physical forms…nonceasing

div.p: and so on, are synonymous with just that.

q.p:
“The farther shore of form is not form.” khri brgyad
. The Sūtra explains parāyana (“finally ally”) with pāra (“farther shore”).
q.orig: The farther shore[1]…form[2]
The transcendence of physical forms is not physical forms

div.p: This is saying that suchness is the farther shore of form because in it the mark of form has been eliminated. Therefore, that suchness that serves as the farther shore of form is not the intrinsic nature of falsely imagined form.

q.p: “Subhūti, as form really is, so too are all dharmas.”
q.orig: Subhūti, as form really is, so too are all dharmas.
Subhūti, just as this applies to physical forms, so indeed it applies to all phenomena

div.p: It says this because all phenomena have suchness as their intrinsic nature, not because they are connected with it.
What is intended by,

q.p: “Will not bodhisattva great beings have indeed fully awakened to the knowledge of all aspects?”
q.orig: bodhisattva great beings would attain consummate buddhahood with respect to all phenomena

div.p: It intends to say that if all dharmas are as form really is, well then, with the clear realization of form comes the clear realization of all dharmas and hence the attainment of the knowledge of all aspects.

q.p: “Lord, on the farther shore of form there is no thought construction whatsoever.”
q.orig: on the farther shore of the knowledge of all aspects there is…thought construction whatsoever.
Blessed Lord, in the transcendence of physical forms there is no conceptual notion at all

div.p: Were there to be a thought construction of form in the suchness that is the farther shore of form, then, with the realization of the farther shore of form there would not be the realization of all phenomena, there would just be the realization of form alone. But, because it is suchness, there is no thought construction of form on the farther shore of form, hence the realization of just that is established as the realization Emend rtog to rtogs. of all phenomena.
Because phenomena are seen to be like islands, they are “islands.”

q.p: “Form is delimited by a past and a future.”
q.orig: form is delimited by a past and a future.
physical forms are confined by the limit of past time and the limit of future time

div.p: Ultimately form has never arisen in the past and ultimately will never arise in the future because it does not exist during all periods of time.

q.p: “Subhūti, that delimitation of all phenomena by a past and a future… is calm, it is sublime.”
q.orig: Subhūti, that which confines all phenomena by the limit of past time and the limit of future time is peaceful; it is excellent

div.p: This is teaching that the nonapprehension of all phenomena, because of the emptiness of time, is the ultimate, is viable. D rigs pa; K, N rig pa.

q.p:
“Form has space as its way of being.” khri brgyad kha 159a7 nam mkha’i tshul can (ākāśagatika); ’bum ta 311a1, nyi khri kha 314a4 ngang tshul can; LSPW p. 353 “situated in space”; Ten Thousand, khri pa
“have the modality of space.” This explains “support” (rten), that in turn renders gati, the last of the nine words describing the “doers of the difficult.” The author here takes it as the “eighty-five” places (ecosystems), but it is more often understood as a form of life, or as life itself as continual movement.
q.orig: form has space as its way of being
physical forms are of the nature of space

div.p: This means ultimate form, like space, is untainted and unchanging.

q.p: “The emptiness of form does not go and does not come”
q.orig: the emptiness of form does not go and does not come
that the emptiness of physical forms is without movement, that is to say, it neither goes nor comes

div.p: means the emptiness of form does not go anywhere, even when together with thought construction, and also does not come from anywhere later on when there is no thought construction.

q.p: “Subhūti, all phenomena have emptiness as their way of being”
q.orig: Subhūti, it is because all phenomena have emptiness as their way of being,
all phenomena are of the nature of emptiness

div.p: means they have emptiness as their intrinsic nature.

q.p: “Because they do not pass beyond that way of being”
q.orig: They do not transgress this nature

div.p: is saying that the intrinsic nature is not removed from those phenomena. They

q.p: “have the unborn and unreal as their way of being”—

div.p: they are not born—have not arisen—through the force of causes and conditions, and are not real things because in their intrinsic nature they are not produced.

q.p:
“Subhūti, all phenomena have the limitless” khri brgyad
.—
q.orig: Subhūti, all phenomena have a nature that is limitless

div.p: they are not destroyed so they are “limitless”; they are immeasurable, so they are

q.p: “boundless.” nyi khri ; khri brgyad (kha 160a3) mu med pa.

div.p: Alternatively, they are “limitless” because they do not go on and on forever and are not annihilated, and “boundless” because they are not embodied. They

q.p: “have the absence of being taken away from and the absence of being added to as their way of being.”
q.orig: have a nature that is without subtraction and addition

div.p: “The absence of being taken away from” is because there is no over-negation of what exists; “the absence of being added to” is because there is no over-reification of what does not exist. They

q.p: “have not going and not coming as their way of being.”
q.orig: have not going and not coming as their way of being.
have a nature that is without coming

div.p: They are “not coming” because they have not come from anywhere, and they are “not going” because they are not going anywhere. They

q.p: “have not bringing in and not sending out as their way of being.”
q.orig: have a nature that is without acceptance and rejection

div.p: At the time of the action they are “not bringing in,” and at the time of karmic maturation they are not “not sending out.” They

q.p: “have not joining, not not joining, not mingling, and not not mingling as their way of being.”
q.orig: have not joining, not…mingling as their way of being.
have a nature that is without conjunction, disjunction, embracing, and nonembracing

div.p: Even when there is thought construction the falsely imagined is not joined together with suchness; and even later when there is no thought construction it is not not joined. You should construe “not mingling and not not mingling” like this as well.

div.head: Explanation of Chapters 46 to 50

q.p: “In their intrinsic nature they are isolated from the elimination of greed,” ’bum ta 330b5 ’dod chags rnam par bstal bas dben pa’i rang bzhin du ’gyur ro; khri brgyad, kha 162a2 ’dod chags bsal bas; nyi khri kha 318a6, le’u brgyad ma nga 256a7 rnam par bsal bas; Jäschke, s.v. stsol ba, points out that bstal ba is “sometimes incorr. for bsal-ba (sel-ba).” PSP 4: 106, ŚsPN3 4616r6 rāga­vinaya­vivikta­svabhāvās; LSPW p. 356 “isolated from (the need for the) disciplining of greed.”
q.orig: eliminated greed and are in their intrinsic nature isolated from it
have a nature that is isolated, owing to their elimination of desire

div.p: and so on. There is no elimination of greed and so on because they are isolated in their intrinsic nature, hence

q.p: “the tokens of greed”
q.orig: token of greed
the indications of desire

div.p: and so on, the tokens of a course of conduct that is greedy and so on, the causes of greed and so on, the objective supports of greed and so on, and greed and the absence of greed and so on—all these dharmas have come about from mind, so it says

q.p:
“that armor is not spliced with form.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: that armor of bodhisattva great beings is not spliced with form
this armor of bodhisattva great beings is not associated with physical forms

div.p: This is teaching that because those dharmas, “form” and so on,

q.p: “absolutely do not exist,”
q.orig: absolutely nonexistent

div.p: they have not been buckled with this armor, having apprehended the causal signs of those phenomena. This is the armor of signlessness.

q.p:
“Lord, bodhisattva great beings have not buckled on armor for the sake of only a partial number of beings.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Lord it is thus: bodhisattva great beings have not buckled on armor for the sake of only a partial number of beings.
Blessed Lord, it is because bodhisattva great beings have not donned this armor for the sake of a small or limited number of beings

div.p: There is no partial number at all they have decided on, thinking, “We will place beings up to this number in nirvāṇa.”

div.head: Cultivation and disintegration

q.p: “It is not something that somebody has to meditate on,”
q.orig: It should not be cultivated by anyone

div.p: because there is no agent.

q.p: “It is not something that has to be meditated on somewhere,”
q.orig: There is nothing that should be cultivated

div.p: because an attribute that has to be cultivated is nowhere to be seen.

q.p: “It is not something that has to be meditated on somehow,”
q.orig: there is nothing in which it should be cultivated

div.p: because an attention that has to be meditated on is also not to be seen. This is

q.p: “the disintegration of meditation”
q.orig: a breaking down of cultivation

div.p:
means it causes the nonexistence of meditation. Cf.
on bhāvanā and vibhāvanā.

q.p:
“Subhūti, you should look closely at a bodhisattva great being in this deep perfection of wisdom irreversible from progress toward awakening.” “Irreversible from progress toward awakening” renders phyir mi ldog pa. khri brgyad, : “Subhūti, you should look closely at a bodhisattva great being irreversible from this deep perfection of wisdom.” Cp. nyi khri
, Twenty-Five Thousand translation: “bodhisattva great beings who are irreversible should investigate this profound perfection of wisdom to determine, Subhūti, if bodhisattva great beings are without attachment to this profound perfection of wisdom.”
q.orig: Subhūti, you should look closely at a bodhisattva great being irreversible from this deep perfection of wisdom
bodhisattva great beings who are irreversible should investigate this profound perfection of wisdom to determine

div.p: You should look closely at irreversible great bodhisattvas—because of this perfection of wisdom are they irreversible, or not?

q.p: “Is the bodhisattva great being not attached to this deep perfection of wisdom?”
q.orig: if bodhisattva great beings are without attachment to this profound perfection of wisdom

div.p: then teaches the causal signs to be looked at closely. It says “to this deep perfection of wisdom,” up to

q.p: “the perfection of giving,”
q.orig: perfection of giving
the perfection of generosity

div.p: up to all

q.p: “the emptinesses,”
q.orig: the emptiness of internal phenomena, the emptiness of external phenomena, the emptiness of external and internal phenomena, and [all the other aspects of emptiness], up to and including the emptiness of the essential nature of nonentities

div.p: finishing with

q.p: “the eighteen distinct attributes of a buddha,”
q.orig: the eighteen distinct qualities of the buddhas

div.p: up to

q.p: “the knowledge of all aspects.”
q.orig: all-aspect omniscience

div.p: So, “you should look closely” whether “the bodhisattva great beings” are “irreversible”—are not attached to those and do they not stand on those.
Because of their disposition, about

q.p: “what others have said”
q.orig: the words spoken by others

div.p: some do not perceive an essential point, some do not believe it, and some do not get attached. They do not get angry and remain in equanimity. Some, because of their disposition, are

q.p: “not separated from”
q.orig: are not diverging from

div.p: the six perfections.
Some, when they have heard this deep doctrine,

q.p: “do not tremble,”
q.orig: not tremble
not afraid

div.p: and so on;

q.p: “delight in”

div.p: it more and more; and listen,

q.p: “take it up, and bear it in mind.”
q.orig: take it up, bear it in mind
they take up, uphold

div.p: You should know that when they have those attributes they are irreversible from progress toward awakening.

q.p: “Should think carefully about this deep perfection of wisdom” Golden 307a2, nyi khri ; khri brgyad (kha 165b1) rnam par spyad is a different spelling of rnam par dpyad. —
q.orig: should appraise this profound perfection of wisdom

div.p: “think carefully” with special insight during clear realization—

q.p: “with a mindstream inclined to emptiness, tending to emptiness, and heading to emptiness.”
q.orig: with mindstreams inclined to emptiness, tending to emptiness, and heading to emptiness
minds intent on emptiness

div.p: Those three statements are governed by small, middling, and big. It means they should think carefully, having come to a clear realization, through the true dharmic nature of

q.p: “emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the unproduced, the unceasing, the absence of defilement, the absence of purification,”
q.orig: signlessness, with mindstreams inclined to wishlessness, inclined to space, and similarly, connect this with with mindstreams inclined to the unproduced, the unceasing, the absence of defilement and the absence of purification,
signlessness and wishlessness…with their minds intent on space, with their minds intent on nonarising and nonceasing, with their minds intent on nonaffliction and nonpurification,

div.p: and so on.

div.head: Suchness and its indivisibility
div.p: Having said that,

q.p: The elder Subhūti inquired, “Lord, do they also think about form?”
q.orig: Lord, do bodhisattva great beings also think carefully about form?
Blessed Lord, do those bodhisattva great beings appraise physical forms

div.p: and so on. Golden 307a6, nyi khri ; khri brgyad (kha 166a1) rnam par dpyod. “Lord, they thus think about this deep perfection of wisdom with a mind-stream inclined to emptiness. Should they similarly think about dharmas—form, feeling, perception, and so on—as well, or should they not?” Then,

q.p: the Lord said, “Subhūti, bodhisattva great beings do not think about form,”
q.orig: “Subhūti,” replied the Lord, “bodhisattva great beings do not think carefully about form.
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “bodhisattva great beings do not appraise physical forms

div.p: and so on, teaches that at the time of clear realization, dharmas—form and so on—do not appear because they are nonexistent things. Therefore, full awakening is not through the dharmas

q.p: “form, feeling,”
q.orig: physical forms. Nor is it attained by means of feelings

div.p: and so on, up to, finally,

q.p: “the knowledge of all aspects,”
q.orig: the knowledge of all aspects[2]
all-aspect omniscience

div.p: but is the clear realization of their suchness. That suchness, furthermore, is not broken apart. The suchness of all dharmas, form and so on, and the suchness of the knowledge of all aspects Golden 307b3; D rnam pa thams cad mkhyen pa nyid kyang gcig go, “and the knowledge of all aspects are one,” is a mistake. are one. It means that they “do not think about” the dharmas “form” and so on because the suchness is the same.

q.p: “Nobody has made the knowledge of all aspects, nobody has made it change. It has not come from anywhere, and is not going anywhere,”
q.orig: nobody has made the knowledge of all aspects, and nobody has made it change. It has not come from anywhere, is not going anywhere,
this all-aspect omniscience [and so forth] has not been created, destroyed, or brought into being by anyone. It has not come from anywhere and it will not go anywhere

div.p: and so on, teaches that if the knowledge of all aspects were to be something that is made; or that changes; or that comes, goes, or remains; or is in one place but not another; or has a

q.p: “number,”

div.p: and so on, it would be a falsely imagined mental image, and then it might fully awaken to dharmas, form and so on. But because it is separated from that mental image, is qualified by space, it cannot therefore fully awaken to form and so on.
Then, having heard this deep doctrine,

q.p: “the gods,”

div.p: with

q.p: “Lord… this deep perfection of wisdom,”
q.orig: Lord, the tathāgatas…this deep perfection of wisdom
Blessed Lord, how do the tathāgatas, arhats, completely awakened buddhas teach, on the basis of this profound perfection of wisdom

div.p:
and so on, khri brgyad
ff. offer praise and say suchness is the true reality in which things are not different.

q.p:
“Here where the habitual idea of two does not exist is the deep state of dharmas.” khri brgyad
, PSP 4: 117 dvayasamudācāro.
q.orig: This is the profundity of all phenomena, in which the habitual ideas of duality do not at all exist

div.p: Because all dharmas have suchness as their nature, and suchness is the same, it is customary to call it one; it is not customary to call it two.

q.p: “Because space is deep,”
q.orig: owing to the profundity of space

div.p: and so on, is just what has been explained before.

q.p: “This doctrine is not taught so form will be taken up or will not be taken up.”
q.orig: this doctrine is not taught so form will be taken up or will not be taken up.
Blessed Lord, this doctrine has not been revealed so that physical forms might be grasped or so that they might not be grasped

div.p: Seizing on a causal sign—this is form—it is “taken up.” Over-negating in all respects—form does not exist—it is “not taken up.”

q.p: “This doctrine is not obstructed by form,”
q.orig: This doctrine is not obstructed by form
it is unobstructed with regard to physical forms

div.p:
and so on. khri brgyad
ff. It is not obstructed because it frames Emend rnam par byed to rnam par ’byed, “explain”? a state in harmony with all dharmas, which is to say, it is not obstructed by any dharma, form and so on, because the two extremes of over-reification and over-negation are absent. Thus, because imagined form does not exist, the extreme of over-reification is absent, and because the true dharmic nature of form does exist, over-negation is absent, hence it is

q.p: “in harmony with form.”

div.p: Similarly, for them all,

q.p: “the suchness of form has not come and has not gone, and, similarly, the suchness of Subhūti has not come and has not gone,”

div.p:
and so on, Golden 308a6 and D have, “Construe them all in the same way. That suchness of form has not come and has not gone. Similarly…” The citation here differs considerably from other versions and suggests our author was looking at a scripture even longer than ’bum. Cf. khri brgyad
; ’bum tha 29b4–5; nyi khri ; khri pa
–. teaches that the suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of Subhūti are the same. It says “has not come and has not gone” to establish that Subhūti

q.p: “takes after the Lord.”
q.orig: imitates the Blessed One

div.p: He has not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere either.

q.p:
“Just that suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of all dharmas, and that suchness of all dharmas is the suchness of Subhūti.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: The real nature of the Tathāgata…is also the real nature of all phenomena. The real nature of all phenomena is also the real nature of the Tathāgata

div.p: This means they are one because suchness is the same.

q.p: “The suchness of the Tathāgata is established”

div.p: teaches that they are also one because of being marked by the establishment of dharmas.

q.p: “Is unchanging and undifferentiated”—
q.orig: is unchanging and nonconceptual

div.p: this “unchanging” teaches that it is a thoroughly established phenomenon because it is the thoroughly established phenomenon that does not alter. This “undifferentiated” teaches that it is a thoroughly established phenomenon because it is the thoroughly established phenomenon without error.

q.p: “Is not obstructed by anything”—
q.orig: is unobstructed in all respects

div.p: it extends over all dharmas, which is to say, it does not exist anywhere at all. Therefore, it says

q.p:
“there is nothing of which that suchness is not the suchness.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: There is nothing at all of which it is not the real nature

div.p: This means that it is also the suchness of all dharmas.

q.p: “And it is never not suchness”—
q.orig: there is nothing at all of which it is not the real nature[2]

div.p: it is also suchness at all times. It

q.p: “is not two”

div.p: because it is the same basic nature,

q.p: “and cannot be divided into two”
q.orig: and cannot be divided into two[2]
and cannot be divided into two

div.p: because you cannot divide it into two types.

q.p: “Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is not broken apart, is not different, and cannot be apprehended, so too the suchness of all dharmas is not broken apart, is not different, and cannot be apprehended. Similarly, the suchness of the elder Subhūti is not broken apart, is not different, and cannot be apprehended either.”
q.orig: Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is not broken apart…be apprehended. Similarly, the suchness of the elder Subhūti is not broken apart, is not different, and cannot be apprehended either.

Just as the real nature of the Tathāgata is undifferentiated, indivisible, nondistinguishable, and nonapprehensible, in the same way the real nature of the elder Subhūti is also undifferentiated, indivisible, nondistinguishable, and nonapprehensible

div.p: This is teaching that the suchness of all dharmas, like the suchness of the Tathāgata, in its nature cannot be apprehended so is not different. And the suchness of the elder Subhūti, like the suchness of all dharmas, also in its nature cannot be apprehended, so it is not different either. K, N omit this paragraph.

It means that just as the suchness of the Tathāgata cannot be broken apart because it is not two, is not different because it cannot be divided into two, and cannot be apprehended because in its nature it cannot be apprehended and hence is the same, and just as the suchness of all dharmas cannot be broken apart, is not different, and in its nature cannot be apprehended, so too the suchness of Subhūti cannot be broken apart and is not different either, because in its nature it too cannot be apprehended.

q.p:
“The suchness of the Tathāgata is not other than the suchness of all phenomena, and what is not other than the suchness of all phenomena is never not suchness. It is always suchness. The suchness of the elder Subhūti is like that. Therefore, since it is not something else, even though the elder Subhūti takes after the Tathāgata he does not take after him in anything.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: The suchness of the Tathāgata is not other than the suchness of all phenomena, and what is not other than the suchness of all phenomena is never…It is always suchness. The suchness of the elder Subhūti is like that. Therefore, since it is not something else, even though the elder Subhūti takes after the Tathāgata he does not take after him in anything.

Just as the real nature of the Tathāgata is not distinct from the real nature of all phenomena, and is always the real nature, never not the real nature, in the same way the elder Subhūti, not being different, imitates the Tathāgata and yet he does not imitate anything at all

div.p: This is teaching that just like the suchness of the Tathāgata, the suchness of all dharmas is also not broken apart because in its nature it cannot be apprehended. And just like the suchness of all dharmas, so too the suchness of the elder Subhūti is also not broken apart because, in its nature, it cannot be apprehended. The suchness of the Tathāgata is not other than the suchness of all phenomena, and what is not other than the suchness of all phenomena is never not suchness, because the suchness of all phenomena is there at all times. The suchness of the Tathāgata is not other than that, so it is there at all times. Similarly, the suchness of the elder Subhūti is not other than the suchness of all dharmas so it is there at all times. Therefore, since it is there at all times, he takes after the suchness of the Tathāgata.

Because he is not marked by birth, it also says “he does not take after him in anything.” khri brgyad
: “Therefore, since [the suchness] is not something else, even though the elder Subhūti takes after the Tathāgata he does not take after him in anything.”

q.p: “Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is not past, is not future, and is not present,”

div.p: and so on, teaches that just as the Tathāgata with a falsely imagined nature is incorporated in the three time periods, but suchness is not included within time, so too all dharmas with a falsely imagined nature are incorporated in the three time periods but their suchness is not included within time. In the same way the suchness of the elder Subhūti is not included within time either.

q.p: “Therefore, [he]… ‘takes after the Tathāgata.’ ”
q.orig: Therefore, it is said the elder Subhūti ‘takes after the Tathāgata.’

q.p:
“Gods, here you should know the suchness of the Tathāgata that is the same, through the suchness of the past that is the same.” khri brgyad
; cf. nyi khri , ’bum tha 30b.
q.orig: the real nature of the Tathāgata is sameness, owing to the sameness of the real nature of the past

div.p: This is teaching: Thus, because the past suchness of all past phenomena has the same intrinsic nature it is the same, and therefore all tathāgatas are the same as well. They too have the same nature as that suchness, so they are also the same. Because of just this—the suchness of all the tathāgatas being the same—the suchness of past phenomena is therefore also the same. And why? Because the suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of all phenomena are the same. Through the sameness of the suchness of all phenomena you should know the sameness of the suchness of the Tathāgata. Through the sameness of the suchness of the Tathāgata you should know the sameness of all past phenomena. Construe the others in the same way as well.

q.p: “On account of the sameness of the dharma of form,” The “dharma of form” is the ultimate attribute of form. Our author’s version of the Sūtra differs.

div.p: and so on, teaches just that suchness of all phenomena in detail.

q.p:
“Gods, thanks to this perfect suchness the Tathāgata… gets to be called Tathāgata.” khri brgyad
. Cf. ’bum tha 40a6–7, nyi khri , both of which omit yang dag pa (bhūta) (“perfect,” “true”).
q.orig: is the real nature of Subhūti and of the Tathāgata, through which bodhisattva great beings, after attaining consummate buddhahood with regard to the real nature, acquire the title tathāgata

div.p: As it has been said, See to from the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā). where this same passage was cited in Harrison’s translation: “ ‘Realized one,’ Subhūti, is a term for perfect reality.”

q.p: “ ‘Tathāgata,’ Subhūti, is a word for true suchness.”

div.head: Shaking of the universe

q.p:
“Shook in six ways” khri brgyad
.—

div.p: the six are

q.p: “quaked… shook… stirred… resounded… roared… and was disturbed.”
q.orig: It shook, shuddered, and juddered. It rocked, reeled, and tottered. It quivered, careened, and convulsed. It trembled, throbbed, and quaked. It rumbled, roared, and thundered. It faltered, lurched, and staggered

div.p:
From them, when each has been subdivided into three based on small, middling, and big, there are the eighteen great omens and, based on the six directions rising up and sinking down, there are twelve to do with the directions. I have already discussed them in the Introduction chapter.
– .

There that “shaking” and so on comes about from two causes. When powerful gods hear the good doctrine, because of the force of the pleasure and delight that arises they dance around and excite each other; and, because of the force of the true dharmic nature, Here dharmatā means both “the actual way things are” and the doctrine as a teaching articulating the way things actually are. even the stable world, in order to demonstrate the greatness of the doctrine, becomes a demonstration, as it were, of obedience to the true dharmic nature the tathāgatas of the past have explained.

There shaking is a great quaking in one region; Cf. Śrījagattalanivāsin’s Āmnayānusāriṇī, man ngag rjes ’brang Degé Tengyur (shes phyin, ba), 212a2–5; Ratnākaraśānti’s Sarotamā (Jaini pp. 204–5). stirring is stirring in its entirety like a leafy tree; quaking is revolving like a fire brand swirling around; resounding is the noise of a long and drawn-out sound; disturbing is upsetting; and a roar is a piercing sound. Alternatively, the earth shakes; all the trees stir; all mountains quake; the big drum of the gods and so on resounds; the ocean and so on is disturbed; and peals of thunder roar. Again, when they first occur, they appear soft and not forceful; after that they are more forceful than that; and finally they are much more forceful even than that, hence subdivided into three they become eighteen.

When the directions are raised up and so on simultaneously, they become greatly disturbed, as though the boundaries have burst Emend mugs to mu gas; mugs would mean “fogged up.” and been destroyed. Hence, they rise up and sink down in a sequence. There when the ground, trees, and mountains and so on in the eastern direction are greatly disturbed it looks like the eastern direction is raised up. When it looks like the eastern direction is raised up, even though the western direction remains in its natural state it looks like it has sunk down. When the ground, trees, and mountains and so on in the western direction are greatly disturbed it looks like the western direction is raised up. When it looks like the western direction is raised up, even though the eastern direction remains in its natural state it looks like it has sunk down. Connect them all like that.

div.head: Synonyms of suchness

q.p:
“Does not take after form, does not take after anything other than form” khri brgyad
rjes su skyes (“take after”) renders anujan, literally “born after.”—
q.orig: does not take after…form[2]
does not imitate physical forms. He does not imitate anything other than physical forms

div.p: since a form aggregate that might come into being is nonexistent, the elder is also nonexistent, so it is not feasible that he takes after form or takes after anything else at all other than form. And it is not feasible that he takes after

q.p: “the suchness of form,”
q.orig: the suchness of…form[3]
the real nature of physical forms

div.p: or takes after anything at all

q.p: “other than the suchness of form,”
q.orig: other than the suchness of…form[4]
other than the real nature of physical forms

div.p: because suchness is unconnected with being born as well.

q.p: “Lord, suchness, unmistaken suchness, unaltered suchness are deep,”
q.orig: Lord, “Suchness, unmistaken suchness, unaltered suchness, the true nature of dharmas, the dharma-constituent, the establishment of dharmas, the certification of dharmas, the very limit of reality, and the inconceivable element are deep.

Blessed Lord, this real nature of all phenomena, the unmistaken real nature, the one and only real nature, the reality, the realm of phenomena, the abiding nature of reality, the maturity of all phenomena, and the very limit of reality are profound

div.p: and so on. Cf. –. To be a tathāgata is suchness. To be unmistaken is unmistaken suchness. To be unaltered is unaltered suchness. It says “suchness, unmistaken suchness, and unaltered suchness” because the thoroughly established phenomenon marked by the inexpressibility of dharmas, the ultimate element, is at all times suchness, is not a mistake, and does not alter. The mark of the thoroughly established phenomenon is threefold: it is a thoroughly established phenomenon that is indestructible, it is a thoroughly established phenomenon without error, and it is a thoroughly established phenomenon that does not alter. It is suchness because it is a thoroughly established phenomenon that is indestructible; it is unmistaken suchness because it is a thoroughly established phenomenon without error; and it is unaltered suchness because it is a thoroughly established phenomenon that does not alter.
The three terms—

q.p: “true nature of dharmas, dharma-constituent, and establishment of dharmas”—
q.orig: the true nature of dharmas, the dharma-constituent, the establishment of dharmas
the reality, the realm of phenomena, the abiding nature of reality

div.p: teach three marks: the mark of the dharma, the mark of the origin, and the mark of what is established.

The state of the dharma The word dharma here means the ultimate attribute of any dharmin (“attribute-possessor”), its emptiness. is the attribute that is the true nature. It is in a form different from all falsely imagined and conceptualized attributes, so that which is established as the state of the dharma, dissimilar to them, and inexpressible, is expressed by the name “true nature of dharmas” because it is established.

“Dharma-constituent” is said to mark the origin. The “dharmas” are the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, the distinct attributes of a buddha, and so on. The term element means cause, so, because it is the origin of the buddhadharmas, it is the “dharma-constituent,” which is to say, the “dharma body.” The meaning is the “dharma body” dharmakāya=dharmatākāya, “the body of the true natures of the attributes [of a buddha].” The word dharma here means “attribute” or “good quality.” The “constituent” is a cause in the sense that the elements that constitute a body are the cause of it.

“Establishment of dharmas” is said to mark what is established. As it is said, “Whether the tathāgatas arise or whether the tathāgatas do not arise, the true nature of dharmas and establishment of dharmas are indeed established.” This, in slightly differing forms, is a recurring statement, as at PSP 2-3: 184 utpādād vā tathāgatānām anutpādād vā tathāgatānāṃ sthitaivaiṣā dharmāṇāṃ dharmatā dharmadhātur dharmasthititā dharmaniyāmatā. Because it is the inexpressible ultimate, the dharma that is thoroughly established, constantly there during the prior period when it is together with stains and also during the later period when there are no stains, it is the establishment of dharmas.
The three terms—

q.p: “the certification of dharmas, the very limit of reality, and the inconceivable element”—
q.orig: the maturity of all phenomena, and the very limit of reality

div.p: are speaking about what is marked by restriction. nges pa renders niyata (“secure,” “definite,” and here “restriction”), and by extension niyāmatā/nyāmatā, Tib skyon med pa nyid, “flawlessness.” When skyon med pa is together with byang chub sems dpa’ (bodhisattvanyāma), skyon med pa (niyāma/nyāma) is rendered “secure state (of bodhisattvas)”; when together with dharmas (dharma(tā)niyāmatā/nyāmatā), skyon med pa nyid is rendered “certification (of dharmas),” (LSPW “established order of dharmas”). The picture is further complicated by deriving nyāmatā (skyon med pa nyid, “flawlessness”) from ni plus āma (“uncookedness,” “rawness”), rendered skyon (“flaw”) and āmana, (sred pa, “craving,” “affection”).

Among these, in “the certification of dharmas” the dharmas are the perfect state dharmas, the reverse of the mistaken dharmas. The certification of them Literally, “the flawlessness in respect to them.” is the state in which they are secure, the state restricted to those alone. Through that state they awaken to suchness at the very first with knowledge at the Joyful level and are certified to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, not otherwise. Therefore, it is called the “certification of dharmas” because it is the cause restricting dharmas (the perfections and so on making up a buddha) to the perfect state, because it said, “Those who have entered into the flawlessness that is a perfect state…” khri brgyad
, explained earlier (Bṭ3 ). Note that here zhugs (from avakram), “entered into,” could have a negative sense: “step down from”; cf. ’bum nga 284b1, le’u brgyad ma nga 9a6, and nyi khri
: “Those who have stepped down from the flawlessness that is a perfect state [are incapable of producing the thought of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening].”

Alternatively, the “flaw” is craving for the dharmas. The nonexistence of the flaw is the flawlessness as explained before.
–. The flawlessness in respect to dharmas is the “certification of dharmas.” The “certification of dharmas” (dharma flawlessness) is the dharma, by awakening to which flawed dharmas are cut off.

As for “the very limit of reality,” because it is the “limit” (what stands at the limit) of “reality” (in the sense of true reality), it means the true reality that has been absolutely determined to be at the limit of reality.

“The inconceivable element” is an inconceivable entity. It is not within the range of what can be inferred by any ordinary speculative thought, so the absolutely determined ultimate known by self-reflexive analytic knowledge is called the “inconceivable element.” Alternatively, it is the element of what is inconceivable, because it is the cause of the amazing, marvelous, inconceivable attributes, which is to say, through the power of the body of the attributes of the buddhas and bodhisattvas the amazing miracles appear in the world.

q.p: “In them you cannot apprehend form, you cannot apprehend the suchness of form.”
q.orig: In them you cannot apprehend…form[2]
In it physical forms are not apprehended, and the real nature of physical forms is not apprehended

div.p: Phenomena, form and so on, do not exist, so you cannot apprehend them. As for suchness, during the period when apprehended and apprehender are in the same state, you cannot apprehend it because that which might be grasped and a grasper do not exist. Alternatively, that is said “Both” are the “form” and “the suchness of form” in the passage just cited. because form and suchness K, N; D “because ‘suchness of form’ is the term used.” are the terms used just during the periods together with stains and when there are no stains.
An exegesis of the clear realization of the dharmas is not given because it is easy to explain.

q.p: Sixty bodhisattvas lacking in what is necessary stopped taking hold of anything and their minds were freed from contamination.
q.orig: The minds of sixty bodhisattvas having a debased Dharma were liberated from contaminants, without further grasping

div.p: Why are those bodhisattvas lacking in what is necessary? It is because, separated from the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, those bodhisattvas practiced a practice of six perfections that can be apprehended and therefore

q.p: “did not enter into secure state,”
q.orig: did not enter into the secure state
they have not entered into the maturity

div.p: and so they did not make unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening their achievement. Hence, they will actualize the very limit of reality and become worthy ones. Those who do just that meditation on

q.p:
“emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness… separated from skillful means… become śrāvakas,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, but are still separated from the perfection of wisdom and have not yet been favored with skill in means, [merely] actualize the very limit of reality and become śrāvakas

div.p: while those who are not so separated reach unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

He asks “why?” and is taught with the illustration of “a bird,” and there is an explanation of skillful means. It is easy to understand. khri brgyad
–.

div.head: Is it hard or not hard to become awakened?
div.p: Then, in regard to the statement,

q.p:
“Lord,” said the elder Śāriputra, “the way I understand the meaning of what you, Lord, have said,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: “Lord,” said Śāriputra, “the way I understand the meaning of what you, Lord, have said
Blessed Lord, as I understand the meaning of the words spoken by the Blessed One

div.p: it is teaching that on account of their particular lineage This is the family of bodhisattvas spoken of in the previous paragraph: “Śāriputra, here you should know that when bodhisattva great beings, starting from the production of the first thought, are inseparable from the thought of the knowledge of all aspects…” they have wisdom and skillful means, their nonapprehending awareness arises from that, and with those everything is achieved.

q.p: “Starting from the production of the first thought”
q.orig: starting from the time when they first begin to set their mind on enlightenment

div.p: means starting from the first level.

q.p:
“Gods! Even though I have fully awakened to all dharmas in all their aspects, still I did not apprehend any dharma that might fully awaken, or through which I might fully awaken, or any dharma I might awaken to.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Gods! Even though I have fully awakened to all dharmas in all their aspects, still I did not apprehend any dharma that might fully awaken, or through which I might fully awaken, or any dharma I might awaken to.

Divine princes, I have indeed attained consummate buddhahood with respect to all phenomena and in all ways. Ultimately, however, there is nothing at all that is apprehended with respect to which I would attain manifest perfect buddhahood, or by which I would attain manifest perfect buddhahood, or on the basis of which I should attain consummate buddhahood

div.p: This means he fully knows all the dharmas that have been brought together in a conventional state of consciousness—the knowledge of a knower of all aspects—but when they are investigated with the knowledge of the ultimate, like seeing things in a dream, he does not see any dharma that knows or that might be known.

q.p: “And why? Gods, it is because all dharmas are absolutely pure.”
q.orig: why, divine princes, it is because all phenomena are absolutely pure

div.p: Here the “pure” is just the nonexistent thing, in the sense of absolutely nonexistent.

q.p: “Lord… full awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening is not hard.” nyi khri ; khri brgyad (kha 175b2) sla in place of mi dka’.
q.orig: Lord, have said, the way it occurs to me, is that the full awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening must be easy.
it is not difficult

div.p: All dharmas are nonexistent, that is, are nonexistent things, so it is not hard to realize that a nonexistent thing is a nonexistent thing. It is hard to correctly realize the defining marks of phenomena that exist. When something is nonexistent, knowing and establishing that it is simply a nonexistent thing is not hard, even though it would be were dharmas to have such an existence and were you to have to accomplish the practice of the perfections and so on to increase the bright dharmas and stop the dark dharmas. But because those dharmas do not exist, therefore even the accomplishment of them is not hard. So, he says “full awakening… is not hard.”
The elder Śāriputra’s intention in saying full awakening

q.p: “must be hard” Golden 314b2.
q.orig: it is difficult

div.p: is this: Having understood that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena that are nonexistent things is a nonexistent thing, like space, then, if it were enough to remain silent in that case it would not be hard. But having thus come to understand that ultimately even full awakening to all dharmas does not exist, and yet, after that still making an effort at the practices of the perfections and working at becoming fully awakened to all dharmas—that sort of thing is hard. That is what he intends.

q.p: “If bodhisattva great beings do not believe that dharmas are like space, but still,”
q.orig: If, even in the case of bodhisattva great beings who do not accept that all phenomena resemble space

div.p:
and so on, teaches khri brgyad
. that if they were not to “believe all dharmas,” because they are nonexistent, “are like space, but still” they could reach awakening, in that case it would be easy,

q.p: “it would not be hard.”
q.orig: it is easy
it were not difficult

div.p: And if that were the case, even in the world, bodhisattva great beings who have not eliminated the notion that something is being apprehended, who are practicing the six perfections, would not turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening and would not fall to the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha level. This is teaching that in fact those who practice while apprehending things like that will not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and therefore that full awakening to just those dharmas by seeing that just those dharmas are absolutely nonexistent things is hard.
Having said this, the elder Subhūti, impatient with his statement that bodhisattva great beings turn back from perfect, complete awakening, says,
