div.p: and so on, teaches that bodhisattvas do not apprehend any dharmas, form and so on. As they progress more and more, they apprehend less and less and thereby enter into an unfindable reality.

q.p: “Lord, if [they]… do not apprehend form,”
q.orig: Lord, if bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom do not apprehend form
Blessed Lord, when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom in that manner, if they do not apprehend even physical forms

div.p: and so on, is asking: how, if they have entered into an unfindable reality, will they accomplish practices that apprehend a basis—the completion of the perfections, entry into the secure state of a bodhisattva, purification of a buddhafield, bringing beings to maturity, awakening, turning the wheel of the Dharma, the work of a buddha, and freeing all beings?

q.p: “Subhūti, bodhisattva great beings do not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of form,”
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “bodhisattva great beings do not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of physical forms

div.p: and so on, teaches that bodhisattvas do not practice the dharmas, form and so on, but rather practice for the state in which all dharmas are unfindable. Golden 355b4. The earlier explanation was teaching that they were findable conventionally as designations, not ultimately.
I have explained the meaning of

q.p: “unmade, unchanging”
q.orig: all dharmas are unmade, all dharmas are unchanging
it is because all phenomena are uncreated and unconditioned

div.p:
before.
, explaining khri brgyad
.

q.p: “How is there an arrangement of three vehicles?”
q.orig: how then will these three vehicles‍—the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the Great Vehicle‍—be established

div.p: means that if all dharmas are unmade and unchanging there will be no division into three vehicles.

q.p: “Subhūti, no arrangement at all can be apprehended in dharmas that are unmade and unchanging”
q.orig: Subhūti, no arrangement at all can be apprehended in dharmas that are unmade and unchanging.
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “no establishment of phenomena that are uncreated and unconditioned is at all apprehensible

div.p: intends that the falsely imagined arrangement of vehicles does not ultimately exist. Here the questions and answers are easy to understand so they have not been explained in detail.

q.p:
“As an ordinary convention, but not ultimately, I keep these beings… away from seizing on the unreal.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Subhūti, in mundane, conventional terms, though not ultimately, I do indeed extricate those beings who perceive nonentities as entities from grasping inauthentic states

div.p: It is saying that ultimately any beings included in the three groups are unfindable. They are simply designated conventionally with those names, simply as an ordinary convention, not ultimately, to stop them seizing on unreal dharmas as real.

q.p: “But Lord, the tathāgatas stood in the ultimate and fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.”
q.orig: Did the Blessed One then attain consummate buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete enlightenment after entering into ultimate reality

div.p: He responds in the negative to this question with

q.p: “no, Subhūti,”
q.orig: No,” replied the Blessed One

div.p: because ultimately there is no standing and there is no full awakening.

q.p:
“Well then, the tathāgatas stood in a succession of miraculous powers and fully awakened” I have added some words from khri brgyad
to make the citation readable in English.
q.orig: Well then, Lord, the tathāgatas stood in a succession of miraculous powers and fully awakened
In that case, did the Blessed One attain consummate buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete enlightenment after entering into mistaken [ways]

div.p: means if not ultimately, well then, as magical creations? Again, the answer he gives is because they absolutely do not exist. A realization inexpressible in its nature and in the form of self-reflexive analytic knowledge of all dharmas is complete awakening. He intends this: “And so why do you still inquire if they stand in the ultimate, or if they stand in a succession of miraculous powers?” With

q.p: “but do not stand in the compounded element or the uncompounded element,”
q.orig: but they do not attain consummate buddhahood while established in any conditioned elements or unconditioned elements

div.p: and so on, it teaches that even

q.p: “awakening”

div.p: is not anywhere at all. It explains that with the analogy of a tathāgata’s magical creation.

As for, khri brgyad
.

q.p: “Subhūti, there is no distinction… between a tathāgata and a tathāgata’s magical creation,”
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “no distinction or difference at all is apprehended between the tathāgatas and their emanations

div.p: and

q.p: “the magical creation does the work,”
q.orig: the magical creation does whatever the work a tathāgata does.
emanations also perform those activities that the tathāgatas perform

div.p: the Lord Buddha was passing into complete nirvāṇa and at that time he did not see a bodhisattva like our lord Maitreya suitable for a prophecy, to whom he could say, “After I have passed away, do the work of a buddha and work for the welfare of beings.” He therefore emanated a magically created perfect form comparable to his own body and said to it, “You must do the work of a buddha.” He then passed into nirvāṇa. When he had done so the Tathāgata’s magical creation did the work of the Buddha in all world systems and benefited beings. When that magical creation saw a bodhisattva suitable for a prophesy, he entrusted beings into that bodhisattva’s hands and demonstrated complete nirvāṇa. Between that magical creation and a tathāgata there is no difference at all.
It says

q.p:
“the true nature of dharmas on account of which the magical creation…” khri brgyad
: “Subhūti, the true nature of dharmas on account of which the tathāgata has become worthy of the offerings of the world with its gods and humans is just that true nature of dharmas on account of which the magical creation has become worthy of the offerings of the world with its gods and humans.”
q.orig: that true nature of dharmas on account of which the magical creation
that emanation

div.p: because they are both the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature. Both come about just in order to benefit beings, and both do their The tathāgatas. work.

q.p:
“But has the Lord not complicated the true dharmic nature of all dharmas” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: has the reality of all phenomena not been purposefully disturbed by the Blessed One

div.p: by explaining nonexistent dharmas as being existent?

q.p: “Subhūti, I have taught… dharmas with words and signs.”
q.orig: I have simply taught the true dharmic nature of dharmas and explained dharmas with words and signs
I have revealed the reality of all phenomena and proclaimed [the nature of] all phenomena through names and signs

div.p: He accepts the ideas of simple folk as ordinary convention. He has explained like that; otherwise, it would not be easy.

q.p:
“There is no settling down to do with names and signs.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: without fixation on names and signs

div.p: He uses conventional designations that are in accord with ordinary people because they are incapable of understanding in other ways. It is difficult for them. There is no settling down on them, however, so there is no fault. This is teaching that were they to settle down, thinking “this is true,” then there would be a fault.

q.p: “Subhūti, were a name to settle down on a name, or were a sign to settle down on a sign”—
q.orig: were fixated on names or fixated on signs

div.p: if names settled down on names or if causal signs settled down on causal signs, then

q.p: “emptiness would settle down on emptiness,”
q.orig: emptiness would also be fixated on emptiness

div.p: and similarly,

q.p: “signlessness”

div.p: and so on would settle down. Thus, it is saying that emptiness and so on do not settle down because they are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature. Similarly, buddhas and śrāvakas do not settle down.

q.p: “Subhūti, all dharmas are thus simply mere names.”
q.orig: these phenomena…are merely words

div.p: Thus, while all dharmas are simply mere names and signs, those in the world do not know them as such. Therefore, bodhisattvas practice so that they will come to that realization. Thus, all dharmas are simply mere names and signs and they reach the knowledge of all aspects by realizing them. This is teaching that were any dharma to be an existent thing then there would be no complete awakening.

div.head: The three knowledges

q.p:
“Subhūti, all-knowledge belongs to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, the knowledge of path aspects… to bodhisattva great beings, and the knowledge of all aspects… to tathāgatas, worthy ones, perfectly complete buddhas.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Subhūti, all-knowledge belongs to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; the knowledge of path aspects, Subhūti, to bodhisattva great beings; and the knowledge of all aspects, Subhūti, to the tathāgatas, worthy ones, perfectly complete buddhas.

Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “that which is called the knowledge of all the dharmas pertains to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Knowledge of the path pertains to bodhisattva great beings. All-aspect omniscience pertains to the tathāgatas, arhats, completely awakened buddhas

div.p: Among these, “all-knowledge”: Beginning as the three forms of the knowledge of all those who know that “all compounded phenomena are impermanent; all contaminated phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are without a self,” all-knowledge is the definitive knowledge of all dharmas based on dharma and subsequent realization knowledge. Abhidharmakośa 6.26 ff. (Pruden, vol. 3, p. 945). That knowledge, furthermore, is not knowledge of all dharmas in all aspects. The knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called all-knowledge because by way of the three marks The three marks in this context are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, being the present, past, and future form of things. and four truths they are not perplexed about all dharmas.

“The knowledge of path aspects”: Here, from the first production of the thought of awakening on the devoted course of conduct level up to the Dharmameghā level, the knowledge operating as insight by penetrating into suchness in the omnipresent sense, the tip sense, and so on, These are the first two of ten antidotes that counteract obstacles to the ten bodhisattva levels given in the Madhyānta­vibhāga 2.14–16 cited earlier ( ). The remaining ones are the outflow’s tip sense, ungraspable sense, undifferentiated continuums sense, being-neither-defiled-nor-pure sense, nondiverse sense, (and the four sovereignties:) sovereignty over nonconceptuality and purification of the buddhafield, sovereignty over knowledge, and sovereignty over action. which acts to cause the transformation of the basis, operates for the happiness and benefit of beings, and causes bodhisattvas to reach the great city of the knowledge of all aspects is called the knowledge of path aspects.

“The knowledge of all aspects” is the knowledge of buddhas as far-reaching as the space element, for the welfare of beings without interruption, that realizes the body of dharmas—a resultant knowledge of the abandonment of residual impression connections called the knowledge of all aspects because it is the result of having comprehended all dharmas in all aspects.

q.p:
“Subhūti, that one aspect on account of which… [it] is called ‘knowledge of all aspects’ is thus the calm aspect.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Subhūti, that one aspect on account of which the ‘knowledge of all aspects’ spoken of again and again is called ‘knowledge of all aspects’ is thus the calm aspect.
As far as the expression ‘all-aspect omniscience…because of the aspect of peace

div.p: That aspect the tathāgatas comprehend, the subsiding of all the aspects of the conceptualizations separated entirely from the world as beings and from the container world, when the morality encompassing the three realms has stopped the net of conceptual thought—that which is the extremely calm aspect that constitutes the spontaneous body of dharmas that is the absolutely pure dharma-constituent accessed as a sameness—is the aspect of all dharmas, hence “all aspects.” The knowledge entity of the sort that has accessed such an aspect is called the knowledge of all aspects.

q.p:
“An abandonment of all residual impression connections” khri brgyad
.—
q.orig: abandoned all reincarnation through the continuity of propensities

div.p: from among the residual impressions left by action and conceptual affliction, here cutting the continuum of the uninterrupted arising, one to the next, of cause and effect is called the abandonment of all residual impression connections.

q.p: “Before reaching the knowledge of all aspects is there an uncompounded abandonment of afflictions?”
q.orig: abandoned afflicted mental states without attaining the unconditioned state

div.p: [The Lord] says [there is] because it is in the form of a cessation. He says, nevertheless, the cessation is simply just an abandonment, so

q.p:
“they still do odd things with their bodies and voices. nyi khri , khri brgyad
omit “voices.” These are not even bad in ordinary persons,”
q.orig: they still do odd things with their bodies. These are not even bad in ordinary persons,

do have physical and verbal aspects of desire, hatred, and delusion. The reincarnation through the propensities of these [afflicted mental states] is harmful to all simple, ordinary persons in common, but not to them

div.p: like gazing in a mirror, hopping while walking, and Pilindavatsa’s use of a word for a low caste woman. This is referring to accounts of a handsome worthy one gazing at himself in a mirror because of the force of habit, Maudgalyāyana’s hopping while walking because of the force of habit from his physical movements as a monkey in earlier lives, and Pilindavatsa’s use of a word for a low caste woman when addressing his apology to the goddess Gaṅgā, because of the force of habit from the language he used as an upper caste person in earlier lives. Mppś English (vol. 1, p. 114). Bailey (p. 199) says Pilindavatsa used the derogatory name for the goddess Gaṅgā when the river had swept away a monastery on its banks. These are not bad, whether for an ordinary person or a noble person.

q.p:
“Do bodhisattvas actualize the very limit of reality having stood on a path… or having stood on what is not a bad path?” This is Subhūti’s one hundred and twenty-sixth question ( ). At khri brgyad
–; PSP 5: 124–26; GilgitC 147–48; ’bum da 173b–174b; nyi khri –; and le’u brgyad ma ca 144a7–145a it comes earlier in the explanation of the differences between the three knowledges.
q.orig: do bodhisattva great beings actualize the very limit of reality having stood on the path?
should bodhisattva great beings, having been established on the path, then actualize the very limit of reality

div.p: and so on. The Lord again says about the possibilities that “they cannot stand on the path because it is the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature.”

q.p:
“Lord, if the path is not an existent thing and nirvāṇa is not an existent thing, why is it taught that ‘this is a stream enterer; this is a once-returner,’ ” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Lord, if the path is not an existent thing and nirvāṇa is not an existent thing, why is it taught that ‘this is a stream enterer; this is a once-returner

Blessed Lord, if the path is indeed nonexistent, and nirvāṇa is also nonexistent, in that case, why is it explained that this one is entering the stream to nirvāṇa, this one is destined for only one more rebirth

div.p: and so on, intends that you can suppose about the explanations of noble persons and of buddhas that they are explanations based on the path, or explanations because of having reached nirvāṇa, but if there are neither, how is there going to be a presentation of noble persons?

q.p: “Subhūti… all of these are categories of the uncompounded.” Harrison (p. 145, n. 44) says that by rendering asaṃskṛta­prabhāvitā “distinguished by the power they derive from the unconditioned” he has “tried to represent more than one of its possible meanings.”
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “all these‍—who are said to enter the stream to nirvāṇa, to be destined for only one more rebirth, to be no longer subject to rebirth, and to be arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva great beings, or tathāgatas, arhats, completely awakened buddhas‍—are indeed distinguished on the basis of the unconditioned

div.p: He again says that even though both a path and nirvāṇa are nonexistent they are categories of the suchness that is the basic nature of the uncompounded.

q.p: “Lord, does something uncompounded make the categories ‘this is a stream enterer’,”
q.orig: Lord, does something uncompounded make the categories ‘this is a stream enterer,
Blessed Lord, is it the unconditioned [reality] that makes distinctions to the effect that this one is entering the stream to nirvāṇa

div.p: and so on, is asking—intending the “categories of the uncompounded”—whether the uncompounded makes, or produces, those categories of persons.

q.p:
“Subhūti, the uncompounded does not make categories,” The order of this and the next three citations does not exactly follow the order in khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “the unconditioned [reality] does not at all make these distinctions

div.p: and so on, teaches that even though the uncompounded is not the producer, still, because of the special feature of entering into suchness through the power of the transformation of the basis, and the special feature of the abandonment of latent affliction, this or that sort of person comes about.

q.p: “Lord, how will there be a later limit of saṃsāra?”
q.orig: Lord, how will a later limit be designated

div.p:
Earlier,
–. in the explanation of the emptiness of no beginning and no end, it said “there is no saṃsāra,” about the unfindable beginning, middle, and end of saṃsāra. Now it asks this, intending that if the worthy ones are categories of the uncompounded there will be an end to saṃsāra.

q.p: “Having taken ordinary convention as the authority, they are simply spoken about, even though ultimately there cannot be categories.”
q.orig: having taken ordinary convention as the authority, they are simply spoken about, even though ultimately there cannot be categories
although one may speak of them, taking words as one’s standard. Ultimately these distinctions cannot be made

div.p: This is teaching that the suchness of ordinary persons and worthy ones is there at all times so there is no later limit, but still, having taken the cutting of the continuum of those falsely imagined dharmas called “the five aggregates” as its point of departure, it explains like that according to ordinary convention. Therefore, it says

q.p: “those for whom an end is demarcated.”
“Lord, if in all dharmas empty of their own marks a prior limit is not apprehended, what need is there to say more about a later limit?”
q.orig: Lord, if in all phenomena empty of their own marks a prior limit is not apprehended, what need is there to say more about a later limit?
all phenomena are empty of their own defining characteristics, past limits are not apprehended, so how could future limits be apprehended

div.p: This is saying the falsely imagined phenomena, the five aggregate “dharmas, are empty of their own marks” because they are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature and hence are like an illusion. So, given that there is no “prior limit” of them perceived as being produced, “what need is there to say more about a later limit” when they are perceived as stopping?

q.p: “Exactly so, Subhūti, exactly so!”

div.p: He rejoices in his statement because all dharmas are not produced and do not stop.

div.head: The meaning of pāramitā

q.p:
“Subhūti… this perfection of wisdom is, of all dharmas, perfect; therefore, it is called perfection of wisdom.” khri brgyad
. “Perfection” renders paramita; “perfect” (more literally, “ultimate superiority”) renders paramapārami. Cf. GilgitC 151 parama­pāramiprāptaiṣā subhūte prajñāpāramitā sarvadharmāṇām; ’bum da 176a6, nyi khri ga 132b5, le’u brgyad ma ca 147a1 shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa ’di ni pha rol du phyin pa’i dam pa thob pa; ŚsPN4 9966r9 paramapāramitās teṣām subhūte prajñāpāramitā sarvadharmāṇām; PSP 5: 127 parama­pāramitaiṣā subhūte sarvadharmāṇām agamanārthena prajñāpāramitety ucyate.
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “this perfection of wisdom…perfection of all phenomena, and that is why one speaks of the ‘perfection of wisdom

div.p: There are four alternative meanings of pāramitā.

Among them, first, The point here is that pāramitā, for an Indian writer, is first understood as derived from parama (“ultimate,” “supreme”), in a secondary form pārama (“ultimacy,” “supremacy”) in the feminine gender (pārami). The -tā ending works as a suffix turning the word (in this case somewhat redundantly) into an abstract noun. For their own reasons, while aware of this more obvious derivation, translators into Tibetan rendered pāramitā as pha rol tu phyin pa, following a creative explanation (nirukti) deriving the word from pāram (neuter gender) (“the other side”), a word related to para (“better,” “beyond,” “other,” etc.) and i (“to go”) with the same -tā ending as a suffix, turning the word into an abstract noun. I have not translated the Tibetan words literally here because it would not convey what the author intended. Readers should also be aware that creative explanations are also derived from pāraya, from pṛ, “to cause to pass”; and from pṝ, “to cause to fill.” I do not think the Sūtra or our author has these roots in mind here, but I am not certain. similar in meaning to the word parama (ultimate), there is the word parami. An abstract noun “superiority” (pārami) is derived from that. It says “superiority” because it is in the form of the limit of all dharmas and all dharmas culminate in it. The received tradition says, “Also when a suffix that makes an abstract noun [like -tā] is at the end it expresses just the thing itself, as, for example, saying of running water, ‘the water element’s fluidity.’ ” I have not identified the work on grammar our author is citing here. “A suffix that makes an abstract noun” renders bhāvapratyaya. “Water-element fluidity” (abdhātu­dravatva) is in reference to the defining characteristic of the water element. “Received tradition” renders Tib lung (āgama). Hence it says, “Subhūti, this is the ultimate (parama) superiority (pārami-tā) of all dharmas.” It means that it is extremely superior, it is the final superiority of all dharmas.
Alternatively, pāram (farther shore) means limit and ita means gone. Hence pāramitā, “gone to the other side.” Therefore, it says

q.p: “with this… all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva great beings, and tathāgatas, worthy ones, perfectly complete buddhas have reached the other side.”
q.orig: it is through this perfection of wisdom that śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattva great beings, and the tathāgatas, arhats, completely awakened buddhas all have arrived at the transcendence

div.p: It is called perfection because it causes them to go to the farther shore.

Alternatively, construe the word parama (perfect) with paramārtha (the ultimate). Because it arises from the ultimate it is an understanding of the ultimate (pāramitā); it comes about with the ultimate as its objective support. The wisdom that has arisen having taken as its objective support the basic nature marked by nonabiding nirvāṇa, which is the ultimate sameness of all dharmas, is the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, it says,

q.p: “Also, Subhūti, with this perfection of wisdom the tathāgata has fully awakened to the fact that all dharmas are not ultimately different; therefore, it is called perfection of wisdom.”
q.orig: Moreover, Subhūti, it is through this perfection of wisdom that the supreme principle … that, too, is why one speaks of the ‘perfection of wisdom

div.p: The wisdom has the ultimate as its objective support so the tathāgatas have fully awakened to the ultimate.

Alternatively, construe the word pāra (farthest limit) with suchness, because it is the farthest limit of everything. The wisdom that has gone into the farthest limit, has reached suchness, is said to be perfection (pāramitā). Therefore, it says,

q.p:
“gone into this perfection of wisdom is suchness, and gone into it also is unmistaken suchness.” Cf. khri brgyad
. “Gone into” (chud) renders antargata, explaining pāram ita.
q.orig: gone into it is the very limit of reality, and gone into it is the true nature of dharmas
the very limit of reality is also included, … and the realm of phenomena is also included

div.p: Because gone into it are suchness and so on, it is said that it has extended over suchness and so on.

q.p: “Neither conjoined with nor disjoined from,”
q.orig: not conjoined with anything at all, nor is it disjoined

div.p: and so on—up to here, the explanation has been of just the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom.

q.p: “This perfection of wisdom causes the practice of all dharmas, this perfection of wisdom bestows all confidences”
q.orig: this perfection of wisdom causes the practice of all dharmas, bestows all confidences
this perfection of wisdom gives rise to the entirety of inspired speech and the entirety of illumination with respect to all phenomena

div.p: means the practice of all dharmas causing the production of all knowledges. The “knowledges” here are the knowledges of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas.

q.p:
“Because all those who do the stopping, those who will stop, and the way the stopping happens cannot be apprehended in the perfection of wisdom.” Golden 362a3–5, citing khri brgyad
, with slight differences. D (F.257.b2–4) has the three forms of the homophone spyod (“a practitioner” and so on) both in the citation from the Sūtra and in the gloss.
q.orig: because all those who do the stopping, those who will stop, and the stopping—none of those can be apprehended in the perfection of wisdom.
because all these are not apprehensible in this perfection of wisdom

div.p: This means a stopper, something that needs to be stopped, and the stopping to be done cannot be apprehended in this perfection of wisdom, so they “Māra and the Māra class of gods” and so on. cannot stop bodhisattvas practicing it.

q.p:
“Furthermore, Subhūti, bodhisattva great beings should practice the reality of the perfection of wisdom—namely, they should practice the reality of impermanence, the reality of suffering, and the reality of selfless.” khri brgyad
. “Reality” and “good” both render the same word don (artha).
q.orig: Furthermore, Subhūti, bodhisattva great beings should practice the reality of the perfection of wisdom—namely, they should practice the reality of impermanence, they should practice the reality of suffering, they should practice the reality of selfless

Moreover, Subhūti, by engaging with the meaning of this profound perfection of wisdom, bodhisattva great beings should engage with the meaning of impermanence, they should engage with the meaning of suffering, they should engage with the meaning of nonself

div.p:
Having taught the condition shared in common by everything with these three, the realities of these eleven nyi khri
. khri brgyad
adds “the meaning of knowledge of things as they really are” for a total of twelve. knowledges, from

q.p: “the good of the knowledge of suffering, the good of the knowledge of origination,”
q.orig: the meaning of the knowledge of suffering. They should engage with the meaning of the knowledge of the origin

div.p: up to

q.p: “the good of the knowledge of mastery, and the good of the knowledge in accord with sound,”
q.orig: the good of the knowledge of mastery, the good of the knowledge in accord with sound,
the meaning of the knowledge that is masterful…the meaning of the knowledge that is semantic

div.p: are the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom, so they teach the good of the perfection of wisdom.

q.p: “According to the reality and the mode”—
q.orig: in that manner

div.p: “the reality” is those realities of impermanence and so on; “the mode” is the intrinsic nature of the perfection of wisdom dealt with below. K, N, Golden 362b2; D adds “that has been taught before.”

q.p: “When… practicing this deep perfection of wisdom’s reality… they should not practice with the idea ‘greed is good for me’ or ‘is bad for me,’ ”
q.orig: practicing this deep perfection of wisdom’s reality should practice like this—namely, they should not practice with the idea ‘greed is good for me’ or ‘is bad for me’
who practice this profound perfection of wisdom should engage in the following manner: They should not engage with the notion that desire is meaningful to them, or that it is meaningless

div.p: and so on, is teaching that they should eliminate the conceptualization of good or bad as different, because in suchness the concern with such things does not exist.

q.p: “They should not practice with the idea ‘form is good for me’ or ‘form is bad for me.’ ”
q.orig: They should not practice with the idea ‘form is good for me’ or ‘form is bad for me’
They should not engage with the notion that physical forms are meaningful to them. They should not engage with the notion that physical forms are meaningless to them

div.p: Viewing form falsely considered as a fact is “bad”; viewing form as unfindable is “good.”

q.p:
“Whether the tathāgatas arise or whether the tathāgatas do not arise” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: whether the tathāgatas have been born or whether the tathāgatas have not been born

div.p: is teaching that

q.p: “the perfection of wisdom does not do anything good or bad to anything,”
q.orig: the perfection of wisdom does not do good or bad to anything.
the perfection of wisdom does not render anything at all meaningful, and it does not render anything at all meaningless

div.p: because

q.p: “the establishment of dharmas,”
q.orig: the abiding nature of phenomena

div.p: just the intrinsic nature, thus

q.p: “remains”
q.orig: remain
are established

div.p: as it is.

q.p: “The perfection of wisdom does not cause any compounded or uncompounded dharma at all”
q.orig: the perfection of wisdom has no effect on conditioned phenomena or on unconditioned reality

div.p: is teaching that because, having looked, the perfection of wisdom does not see any compounded or uncompounded dharma, it does not cause any dharma. So how will the perfection of wisdom cause anything good or bad? This translation is based on Golden 363a1 na in place of D no, and D don dam in place of Golden ston tam.

q.p: “But Lord, the uncompounded is good for all noble… is it not?”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, in that case is the unconditioned [reality] not meaningful for the buddhas and all noble śrāvakas of the buddhas

div.p: It says this intending: does this perfection of wisdom not cause attainment of uncompounded nirvāṇa? It

q.p: “is not there to be good or bad for anything”
q.orig: is not established for their benefit or harm

div.p: means the perfection of wisdom, as a cause, is not in any way good or bad for nirvāṇa. It also teaches that through the simile of

q.p: “the suchness of space.”
q.orig: the real nature of space

q.p: “Lord, having trained in the uncompounded perfection of wisdom, do bodhisattva great beings not reach the knowledge of all aspects?”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, do bodhisattva great beings, having trained in the unconditioned perfection of wisdom, not attain all-aspect omniscience

div.p: He asks this intending: does this perfection of wisdom not produce the knowledge of all aspects?
Having said that, the Lord rejoices in his statement because, when practicing, that is conventionally so. He then negates it, with

q.p: “but not in a dualistic way.”
q.orig: but not in a dualizing manner

div.p: This means the perfection of wisdom and the knowledge of all aspects are one, they are not different and are not two, therefore there is nothing that assists and nothing that is assisted.
What is intended by

q.p: “Lord, does a nondual dharma reach a nondual dharma?”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, is it that something nondual attains something nondual

div.p: It is well known that bodhisattvas reach the knowledge of all aspects with the perfection of wisdom as the cause. In regard to that, he is asking about two possibilities—whether these bodhisattvas without an intrinsic nature reach a perfection of wisdom with a nondual intrinsic nature, “Nondual intrinsic nature” means an intrinsic nature that precludes two different things; “dual intrinsic nature” means an intrinsic nature that allows two different things. or whether bodhisattvas with a dual intrinsic nature reach a perfection of wisdom with a nondual intrinsic nature.
The Lord does not assent because it is not suitable to be expressed as either. He says,

q.p: “Because neither a dual dharma nor a nondual dharma can be apprehended, the knowledge of all aspects is thus reached by way of not apprehending anything at all.”
q.orig: because neither a dual dharma nor a nondual dharma can be apprehended, the knowledge of all aspects is thus reached by way of not apprehending anything at all.

dualistic phenomena or nondual phenomena are indeed not apprehended,” replied the Blessed One. “If you ask why … it is because the nonapprehensible is attained. It will neither be attained through apprehending nor will it be attained through nonapprehension

div.p: Just as all these dharmas cannot be apprehended as being constituted as dual or constituted as being nondual, similarly the knowledge of all aspects is reached by way of dharmas that cannot be apprehended as dual and dharmas that cannot be apprehended as nondual. Other than that, it does not happen at all.

div.head: Explanation of Chapters 64 to 72
div.p: Having heard about such a deep state, he says,

q.p: “Deep, Lord, is the perfection of wisdom,”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, the perfection of wisdom is profound!

div.p:
and so on. khri brgyad
. Connect this with this simile as well: understand, as an illustration, that just as a person who wants roots, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruit does not, in the beginning, apprehend them, similarly a bodhisattva does not apprehend all dharmas. And just as the person gets and makes use of the roots, bark, and so on later when the trunk has grown, similarly all beings are given use of the benefits and happiness when the many accumulations of merit and knowledge have increased and they have gained the knowledge of all aspects.

q.p: “Subhūti, it is because that suchness, on account of which tathāgatas are labeled, is just the suchness… on account of which the suchness of all beings and the suchness of the tathāgatas is labeled.”
q.orig: Subhūti, it is because that suchness…and is just the suchness on account of which the suchness of all beings and the suchness of the tathāgatas is labeled.

Subhūti, the real nature through which the tathāgatas are conceived…the real nature through which all-aspect omniscience is conceived; and the real nature through which conditioned elements, unconditioned elements, [and so forth] are conceived are all simply of that one nature

div.p: The “tathāgatas” are so called because of having gone into reality. The tathāgatas are those who have gone (gata) to suchness (tathatā) (understand “go” as in a phrase like “go to pieces” not in a phrase like “go to another country”); de bzhin nyid (tathatā) (“the state of being the way things are”). Bodhisattvas, too, go into reality, therefore they should indeed be called tathāgatas.
In the second subsection of the passage,

q.p: “standing in this suchness, bodhisattva great beings,”
q.orig: training in this real nature will bring those bodhisattva great beings

div.p: because of comprehending and realizing suchness,

q.p:
“are called tathāgatas.” ’bum da 187b1–2, nyi khri
, le’u brgyad ma ca 151b2–3. The tathāgatas here are “realized ones” (the root gam, “go,” is understood in its secondary meaning of “understand”). khri brgyad
: “Standing in this suchness, bodhisattva great beings gain the knowledge of all aspects, therefore it is called suchness.”
q.orig: be known as tathāgatas
should be known to resemble the Tathāgata himself

div.p: This reality is also called

q.p: “the perfection of wisdom.”

div.p:
After this, the increase in benefits and merits from practicing suchness and the perfection of wisdom is easy to understand. khri brgyad
–.

q.p:
“Candidates for bodhisattva” byang chub sems dpa’ zhugs par gyur pa. I have not emended this reading because there is a very old idea that “a bodhisattva” is a single buddha, like Śākyamuni, in his life before awakening, but unless it is emended to byang chub zhugs par gyur pa it contextually does not make sense. The mistake, if it is one, goes back a long way, leading to the need for our author’s gloss here. PSP 5: 135, and GilgitC 161 sacet subhūte ye trisāhasra­mahā­sāhasre lokadhātau sattvās te sarve bodhi­sattva­pratipannakā bhaveyus, teṣāṃ yat puṇyaṃ tat tathāgata­syārhataḥ samyaksaṃbuddhasya śatatamīm api kalān nopaiti. Conze translates the mistake (LSPW p. 481: “if they had all entered on a Bodhisattva’s special way of salvation, then their merit would be infinitesimal compared with that of a Bodhisattva great being”) and says in note 10, “I do not understand this sentence.” The correct reading is ’bum da 191b6, nyi khri
, khri brgyad
: “Subhūti, even if all the beings included in the great billion world systems were to have entered into the secure state of a bodhisattva their merit would not approach even, up to a hundred thousand one hundred millionth part of the merit of bodhisattva great beings who are candidates for awakening.” A “candidate for awakening” is in the last birth before awakening.
q.orig: candidates for awakening
set out for enlightenment

div.p: are those standing on the path to perfect, complete awakening.

q.p:
“Subhūti… the knowledge of all aspects is a nonexistent thing that is without a defining mark,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: “Subhūti,” he replied, “the knowledge of all aspects is a nonexistent thing that is without a defining mark,
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “that which is called all-aspect omniscience is without entity; it is without defining characteristics

q.p: “without a causal sign”
q.orig: signless

div.p: because it is separated from all words and signifiers;

q.p: “without effort”
q.orig: effortless

div.p: because it is spontaneous;

q.p: “unproduced”
q.orig: nonarising

div.p: because it is uncompounded;

q.p: “and not appearing”
q.orig: nonarising

div.p: because it is marked as not remaining.

q.p: “Subhūti, the objective support of the knowledge of all aspects is a nonexistent thing”
q.orig: Subhūti, all-aspect omniscience is without apprehending

div.p: means “it operates having taken a nonexistent thing as the point of departure”; it is not the objective support condition.

q.p: “The dominant factor is mindfulness.”
q.orig: Mindfulness is its predominant condition

div.p: It says that based on its being its earlier cause. It is not there at that time.

q.p:
“Subhūti, something that has arisen from a union has no intrinsic nature…” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Subhūti,” he replied, “something that has arisen from a union has no intrinsic nature
there is no conditioned essential nature

div.p: Form, feeling, and so on, which are imaginary in their intrinsic nature, are said to be “arisen from a union” because they have arisen dependent on conditions. Such an intrinsic nature is a nominal one because it is necessarily dependent.

q.p: “And anything arisen from a union with no intrinsic nature is a nonexistent thing.”
q.orig: That in which there is no conditioned essential nature is a nonentity

div.p: A dharma that is contingent on something else—that is not an “intrinsic nature”—is called a “nonexistent thing.” It is not nonexistent because it is absolutely nonexistent like a rabbit’s horns and so on; it is because it is the nonexistent thing that is the reverse of a phenomenon that is an existent thing.

q.p:
“Are the intrinsic nature of a nonexistent thing” Cf. khri brgyad
: “Subhūti, in this way all phenomena are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature.” Our author is breaking the compound abhāvasvabhāva (rendered “the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature”) to mean “the intrinsic nature of a nonexistent thing.”—
q.orig: all phenomena are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature
all phenomena have the essential nature of nonentity

div.p: falsely imagined dharmas, form and so on, are called “nonexistent things.” The reversed intrinsic nature they have is also called “the intrinsic nature of a nonexistent thing.”
After that it teaches that the perfection of wisdom is the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature and is skillful means.
There,

q.p:
“Lord, are phenomena separated from the phenomena themselves?” khri brgyad
. This is Subhūti’s one hundred and forty-third question.
q.orig: Blessed Lord, in that case are all phenomena themselves devoid of all phenomena

div.p: means that if all phenomena are separated from all phenomena, in that case something known and something that knows would not exist, and it would not be suitable to say, “It is known.”

q.p: “It is not appropriate that an existent thing knows an existent thing.”
q.orig: it is not appropriate that an existent phenomenon[2]…knows an existent phenomenon[2]
Nor can phenomena that are entities cognize phenomena that are entities

div.p: It is not appropriate that a falsely imagined phenomenon knows a falsely imagined phenomenon, like an illusory elephant a footprint of an illusory elephant.

q.p:
“It is not appropriate that a nonexistent thing knows a nonexistent thing,” Cf. khri brgyad
, nyi khri .
q.orig: it is not appropriate that a nonexistent phenomenon knows a nonexistent phenomenon
phenomena that are nonentities cannot cognize phenomena that are nonentities

div.p: like space;

q.p: “it is not appropriate that an existent thing knows a nonexistent thing,”
q.orig: it is not appropriate that an existent phenomenon knows a nonexistent phenomenon
Nor can phenomena that are entities cognize phenomena that are nonentities

div.p: like an illusory person space; and

q.p: “it is not appropriate that a nonexistent thing knows an existent thing,”
q.orig: It is not appropriate that a nonexistent phenomenon knows an existent phenomenon
Nor can phenomena that are nonentities cognize phenomena that are entities

div.p: like space an illusory person. This is the perfection of wisdom of existent things and nonexistent things.

q.p: “Lord, is ordinary convention one thing and the ultimate another?”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, are mundane relative [appearances] one thing and ultimate [truth] another

div.p: An ordinary convention is marked as a nonexistent thing, so the question is about the ultimate.

q.p: “Just that suchness of ordinary convention is the suchness of the ultimate”
q.orig: Just that suchness of ordinary convention is the suchness of the ultimate.
The real nature of mundane relative [appearances] is the real nature of ultimate [truth]

div.p: means that the suchness of “ordinary convention”—of all dharmas, form and so on—is itself just the suchness of the ultimate.

q.p:
“Subhūti, true reality is called buddha” khri brgyad
. The word bhūtārtha (“true reality”) sounds like the word buddha. This is the response to Subhūti’s one hundred and forty-sixth question.
q.orig: Subhūti, true reality is called buddha.
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “it is genuine reality that is called buddha

div.p: says what the intrinsic nature marking an awakened being is. It means true reality, suchness, the dharma body, is called buddha.

q.p: “Also, they are those who have fully awakened to the true Dharma, Based on our author’s own comment below I have emended D yang dag pa’i don to yang dang pa’i chos (khri brgyad , ga 21a3). therefore they are called buddha,”
q.orig: Also, Subhūti, there are those who have fully awakened to the true Dharma, therefore they are called buddha.
Moreover, Subhūti, it is because they have attained that genuine reality that is consummate buddhahood that buddhas are so called

div.p: and so on, provides three creative explanations. With the knowledge of a worthy one’s path, the lords awaken to the true Dharma—the state of nirvāṇa; then, with the knowledge of a knower of all aspects they have a penetrating realization of true reality as a reality that is empty, calm, and so on; and with the subsequent attainment of the knowledge of those who know all, they subsequently realize the characteristic marks of all. Thus, it says, because

q.p: “there are those who have fully awakened to the true Dharma… have a penetrating realization of true reality, … [and] have fully awakened to all dharmas as they really are, therefore they are called buddha.”
q.orig: there are those who have fully awakened to the true Dharma, therefore they are called buddha. Also, Subhūti, there are those who have a penetrating realization of true reality, therefore they are called buddha. Also, Subhūti, there are those who have fully awakened to all dharmas as they really are, therefore they are called buddha.

because they have attained that genuine reality that is consummate buddhahood that buddhas are so called. Buddhas are so called because they have realized genuine reality. Moreover, Subhūti, buddhas are so called because they have definitively attained consummate buddhahood with respect to all phenomena

q.p: “Lord, what is the word awakening for?”
q.orig: Lord, what is the word awakening for[1]
what does the term enlightenment designate

div.p: Awakening is also taught threefold: intrinsic nature, characteristic mark, and creative explanation. The intrinsic nature is twofold: the thoroughly established intrinsic nature and the falsely imagined intrinsic nature. In regard to the thoroughly established intrinsic nature, it says,

q.p: “Subhūti, awakening is a word for emptiness.”
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “enlightenment designates emptiness

div.p: In regard to the falsely imagined intrinsic nature, it says,

q.p: “Also, Subhūti, awakening is a word for mere designation.”
q.orig: Moreover, Subhūti, enlightenment is so called because this ‘enlightenment’ is a mere name or sign

div.p: As for the characteristic mark, it says

q.p: “true reality means awakening.” Cf. khri brgyad (ga 21a6) byang chub kyi don ni yang dag pa’i don no, “awakening means true reality.” The compounds bodhyartha and bhūtārtha have a similar sound. PSP 5: 140 and GilgitC 169 have abheda (“the undivided reality”) in place of bhūta, as at ’bum da 213b5 and nyi khri (ga 145b4) dbyer med pa.
q.orig: awakening[3] means true reality
genuine reality is the meaning of enlightenment

div.p: The characteristic mark of the ultimate is true reality, called the reality of the ultimate.
As for the creative explanation, it is threefold:

q.p: “that awakening is a realization that all dharmas are a mere designation and causal sign,”
q.orig: enlightenment is so called because it is the realization that all phenomena are merely names or signs

div.p: and so on. There, the creative explanation of it as the realization of the marks of falsely imagined phenomena is: “it is a realization that all dharmas are a mere designation and causal sign.” It says about the dharma body’s way of being marked by the transformation of the basis on account of the realization of dependent phenomena,

q.p: “that… is the awakening of the lord buddhas, therefore it is called awakening.”
q.orig: that awakening is the awakening of the lord buddhas, therefore it is called awakening[10]
enlightenment is so called because it is the enlightenment of the lord buddhas

div.p: As for the realization of the mark of the thoroughly established phenomenon, it says

q.p: “the lord buddhas have fully awakened to it, therefore it is called awakening.”
q.orig: enlightenment is so called because it is the consummate buddhahood that the lord buddhas have attained

div.p: In regard to the awakening of those practicing the perfection of wisdom, it says it

q.p: “is not to accumulate or to diminish… any dharma.”
q.orig: do not practice to accumulate or to diminish, to decrease or to increase, to produce or to stop, or to defile or purify any dharma
nothing at all accumulates or declines, nothing decreases or increases, nothing arises or ceases, and nothing is defiled or purified

div.p: Where it says

q.p: “it is not available in the manner of an objective support that has to be accumulated,”
q.orig: is not available in the manner of an objective support that has to be accumulated
nothing is established by way of apprehending, so that nothing at all will accumulate

div.p: wholesome roots from giving and so on;

q.p: “or that has to be diminished,”
q.orig: or diminished
or decline

div.p: miserliness, immorality and so on;

q.p: “or that has to be decreased,”
q.orig: has to be decreased
decrease

div.p: the dark side;

q.p: “or that has to be increased,”
q.orig: or increased
or increase

div.p: the bright side;

q.p: “or that has to be produced,”
q.orig: has to be produced
arise

div.p: the unproduced buddhadharmas;

q.p: “or that has to be stopped,”
q.orig: or stopped
or cease

div.p: defilements that have been produced;

q.p: “or that has to be defiled,”
q.orig: or has to be defiled
or be defiled

div.p: during the period with stains;

q.p: “or that has to be purified,”
q.orig: or purified
or purified[2]

div.p: during the period without stains, it says that because awakening is in its basic nature the elimination of all objective supports.

q.p:
“Practice the perfection of giving in a dualistic way” khri brgyad
. This citation is part of an introduction to the following section that explains skillful means as not apprehending anything.
q.orig: if it is not with duality that they practice the perfection of generosity

div.p: means with apprehended and apprehender as existent things. As it will say immediately after this below,

q.p:
“even bodhisattva great beings who have attended on the lord buddhas, have planted wholesome roots, and have been looked after by spiritual friends will not be able to gain the knowledge of all aspects,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: even those who have revered the lord buddhas, have perfected the roots of virtuous action, and have attended upon spiritual mentors cannot now attain all-aspect omniscience

div.p: because, on account of the power of apprehending things, they do not have skillful means.

q.p:
“How will… [they] fully grasp the perfection of giving?” khri brgyad
This is Subhūti’s one hundred and forty-ninth question.
q.orig: how will bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom fully grasp the perfection of giving
how will they acquire the perfection of generosity

div.p: He asks this with the thought that “giving gifts, having taken awakening as the object, is labeled the perfection of giving.”

q.p: “[They] do not practice the perfection of giving in a dualistic way”
q.orig: it is not with duality that bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of generosity

div.p: means they do not practice with the idea, “I will do this for awakening,” conceptualizing the two—an apprehended and an apprehender—as existent things.

q.p: “Lord, if they do not practice the perfection of giving in a dualistic way”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, if it is not with duality that they practice the perfection of generosity

div.p: is asking: if they are not making a dedication to awakening in a dualistic way, how will the wholesome roots grow and flourish?

q.p: “Subhūti, those who practice dualistically do not Emend rnam par ’phel bar ’gyur to rnam par’phel bar mi ’gyur (khri brgyad , ga 22b2). Golden folio 367 is missing. grow and flourish on wholesome roots”
q.orig: those who practice in a dualistic manner do not grow the roots of virtuous action

div.p: teaches that just practicing without dualism causes the wholesome roots to grow and flourish, not dualistic practice. This is the practice of the perfection of wisdom without dualism.
Then the practice of the six perfections endowed with skillful means, the practice of the dharmas on the side of awakening, the practice of the buddhadharmas, and the praise of the bodhisattvas who

q.p:
“do not move from their intrinsic nature” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: do not stir from the essential nature

div.p:
are easy to understand from the scripture itself. khri brgyad
–.
As for the four possibilities in

q.p:
“can a nonexistent thing fully awaken to a nonexistent thing,” nyi khri
, khri brgyad
– present the alternatives in a different order. Alternatively, “nothing that makes them known.”
q.orig: can nonentities attain consummate buddhahood through nonentities

div.p: and so on, it is not suitable to connect full awakening with those sorts of four possibilities so a scriptural authority for them does not exist.

q.p:
“Seeing sameness like this, not like an existent thing and not like a nonexistent thing either, is clear realization.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Seeing sameness, not like an existent thing and not like a nonexistent thing either, is clear realization
Clear realization is such that there are neither entities nor nonentities

div.p: A falsely imagined phenomenon, like something conjured up by magic, is not in the form of an existent thing nor in a totally nonexistent form like a rabbit’s horns. That sameness that is not an existent thing and not a nonexistent thing is seeing, “is clear realization” of the sameness of an existent thing and nonexistent thing—

q.p:
“the perfection of wisdom without thought construction.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: should practice the perfection of wisdom that is without conceptual elaboration

q.p: “To illustrate, Subhūti, worthy ones… having trained on all the paths”—
q.orig: Just as an arhat of the eighth level, having trained in all attributes

div.p: having trained on the paths of stream enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and worthy one—

q.p: “do indeed enter into the flawlessness that is a perfect state,”
q.orig: enters into the authentic maturity

div.p: do enter into a worthy one’s state of flawlessness. For the moment, they

q.p: “will not reach the result of worthy one in a single instant of the path”
q.orig: will not reach the result of a worthy one in a single instant of the path
never attains the fruit of arhatship

div.p: means for as long as they have not finally produced the moment of the path of freedom.

q.p: “Through the wisdom of the unique single instant”—
q.orig: through the wisdom of a single instant

div.p: through the instant of

q.p: “the vajropama meditative stabilization.”
q.orig: vajra-like meditative stability

q.p:
“Having beheld all eight levels, pass beyond them with knowledge and seeing,” Cf. khri brgyad
.
q.orig: they transcend eight levels through their cognition and insight

div.p: just as explained earlier in the section teaching knowledge of mastery. Cf. –; also –, .

q.p:
“On that bodhisattva great beings should accomplish vocalizations, conventional terms, and sounds,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: bodhisattva great beings should communicate in and acquire all the languages and symbols

div.p: similar to the vocalizations of the various beings.

q.p:
“Do not bring about and do not take away any dharma at all” khri brgyad
. This is Subhūti’s one hundred and sixty-second question, “Lord, if those dharmas—the dharmas on the side of awakening and the awakening—are not conjoined and not disjoined… how, Lord, will the dharmas on the side of awakening be those that bring about awakening?” —
q.orig: cannot nurture or starve anything at all

div.p: he asks: those dharmas on the side of awakening with no characteristic mark, the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature, do not bring about awakening, do they? And the Lord raises his voice in praise, with

q.p: “exactly so, Subhūti, exactly so!”
q.orig: Subhūti, it is so! It is so

div.p:
Nothing at all brings about anything at all, because dharmas are marked by remaining the same. Still, even though that is the case, it formulates this Here “this” stands for the passage (khri brgyad
–) explaining that the dharmas on the side of awakening and so on are the perfection of wisdom. conventionally, as a method so that simple folk will comprehend, because having understood in this gradual sequence and practiced like that, they become awakened.

q.p:
“Noble Dharma and Vinaya” Cf. khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Dharma and the Vinaya

div.p: teaches that in its intrinsic nature it tames attachment and so on, and, when it has been achieved, is marked by remaining tamed. Tib ’dul ba, “tamed, taming.” Alternatively, based on Skt vi-nī (“separate”), “in its nature it is separate from attachment and so on, and, when practiced, is marked by remaining separated.” This

q.p: “noble Dharma and Vinaya”
q.orig: Dharma and Vinaya

div.p: is the

q.p:
“perfection of wisdom.” Cf. khri brgyad
, nyi khri , ’bum da 261b3.

“The disintegration of meditation on all dharmas is meditation” khri brgyad
. Cf. Bṭ3 ; also .
q.orig: The cultivation of the breaking down of all phenomena constitutes the cultivation

div.p: means meditating on “all dharmas,” form and so on, as nonexistent things.

q.p:
“[They] do not meditate on ‘form is an existent thing’ ” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom do not meditate on…is an existent thing
they do not cultivate the notion that physical forms are entities

div.p: means they do not meditate on “form is an existent thing in its intrinsic nature.”

q.p:
“Someone attached to the two extremes, thinking ‘this is me,’ in reference to an existent thing” khri brgyad
.—
q.orig: Those who in this manner become attached to the two extremes will not be liberated

div.p: this means someone attached to the two extremes of permanence and annihilation with the notion of an existent thing: “This is me, which is to say, I exist separately,” “I am form,” “I am feeling,” and so on.

q.p:
“Subhūti, the perception of form is a duality.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “the perception of physical forms is dualistic

div.p: There is no doubt that where there is the perception “it is form,” the false imagining that it is there or it is not there, or that it is an existent thing or a nonexistent thing, arises. Alternatively, it says “duality” because of a grasped and grasper in the form of existent things.

q.p: “To the extent there is an existent thing, to that extent there are volitional factors.”
q.orig: To the extent that there are entities, there is cyclic existence

div.p: The conceptualization of an existent thing gives rise to volitional factors that are good, bad, and so on. To “thoroughly reject an existent thing” is not to thoroughly reject the maturation. If this is a citation from our author’s version of the Sūtra I have not been able to locate it in the versions I have consulted. “A maturation” (rnam par smin pa) renders vipāka, specifically the new form of life from conception to death as a result of earlier karma. In this context I take it to mean a life taken for the sake of others.

q.p:
“[They] gain control over all dharmas,” nyi khri
.
q.orig: sovereignty over all phenomena

div.p: over perfect, complete awakening;

q.p:
“[they] gain control over the range of all phenomena,” khri brgyad
. This is Subhūti’s one hundred and seventy-fourth question, “Lord, if all phenomena are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature, how did the Tathāgata fully awaken to all the phenomena that are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature, and, having fully awakened to them, gain control over the range of all phenomena?”
q.orig: gain control over the range of all phenomena?
acquire sovereignty over their perceptual range, which is sovereignty over all phenomena

div.p: the clairvoyances and the ten controls. These are listed below ( –); also Edg, s.v. vaśitā 2, citing the Mvy, gives the ten controls (dbang, vaśita) (Edg calls them “masteries”) as control over life (āyus), thought (citta), human requirements (pariṣkāra), dharma, miraculous power (ṛddhi), birth (janma/utpatti), belief (adhimukti), prayer (praṇidhāna), action (karma), and knowledge (jñāna).

q.p: “Here, earlier when I was practicing the bodhisattva’s practice of the six perfections,”
q.orig: I was formerly engaged in the conduct of a bodhisattva, practicing the six perfections

div.p: and so on, is teaching the following:

q.p: “When I was the one practicing the six perfections and entering into absorption in the clairvoyances and so on, having eliminated perceptions with any objective support, I produced and practiced a naturally purified perception without relishing the experience of the causal signs. Having fully awakened by just paying attention to space, and, following that, having fully awakened to the four noble truths with subsequent attainment knowledge, I actualized the qualities of a buddha. By paying attention to the conventional I prophesied beings in the three groups.”

div.p: This means he was therefore faultless because he practiced in a state where nothing is apprehended and became awakened in a state where nothing is apprehended.
With,

q.p: “Lord, how has a tathāgata, worthy one, perfectly complete buddha,”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, how did the tathāgata, arhat, completely awakened Buddha

div.p:
and so on, khri brgyad
. This is Subhūti’s one hundred and seventy-fifth question. the elder is asking: if concentrations, clairvoyances, and beings are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature, how have you produced them, and prophesied those beings? Then the Lord, with

q.p: “Subhūti, were an intrinsic nature of sense objects or of wrong unwholesome dharmas,”
q.orig: if desires and negative, nonvirtuous attributes had an entity

div.p: and so on, teaches that because they are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature everything is established, not otherwise. So, it is because sense objects and wrong unwholesome dharmas are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature that they have been prophesied and the concentrations produced. They

q.p:
“are not existent things, or nonexistent things, or intrinsically existent things, or dependently existent things” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: are without entity, without essential nature, and without extraneous entity

div.p: is teaching that they are not constituted as falsely imagined existent things, are not totally nonexistent things like a rabbit’s horns, also are not something constituted as its own existent thing, and are also not something constituted as a dependent existent thing.

q.p: “How… will there be serial action, serial training, and serial practice?”
q.orig: how, even while all phenomena are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature, will there be serial action, serial training, and serial practice—the serial action, serial training, and serial practice
although all phenomena have the essential nature of nonentity, why is it, Blessed Lord, that bodhisattva great beings undertake the serial practice, serial training, and serial progression

div.p: The intention is that just as apprehending and not apprehending a magically produced illusory elephant and so on happens suddenly, so too the bodhisattvas’ realization that does not apprehend anything happens suddenly; it does not happen gradually.
With

q.p: “Subhūti, here bodhisattva great beings from the very outset have heard from the lord buddhas… that an intrinsic nature… is nonexistent,”
q.orig: here bodhisattva great beings from the very outset have heard from the lord buddhas, from the bodhisattvas attending on many buddhas, and from the worthy ones, non-returners, once-returners, and the stream enterers that an intrinsic nature of the lord buddhas is nonexistent

bodhisattva great beings[1]…hear in the beginning from the lord buddhas, bodhisattva great beings, arhats who revere many buddhas, those who are no longer subject to rebirth, those who are destined for only one more rebirth, and those entering the stream to nirvāṇa that the lord buddhas have the essential nature of nonentity

div.p: and so on, the Lord explains that bodhisattvas are not vigorously attempting the series of practices for their own benefit; rather, they are gradually making the vigorous attempt so that all beings will come to a gradual understanding, because they are incapable of a sudden understanding.

q.p: “Starting from the first production of the thought,”
q.orig: commencing from the time when they first begin to set their mind

div.p: and so on, teaches the order of the unfolding series.

q.p: “Having [transcended the śrāvaka level and pratyekabuddha level], they enter,”
q.orig: Having transcended the śrāvaka level and pratyekabuddha level, they enter
transcend the levels of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and then enter

div.p:
after they have produced the thought. khri brgyad
and khri brgyad
. Generally speaking, “the first production of the thought” marks the beginning of a bodhisattva’s path, or else it marks the path when the bodhisattva first awakens (the so-called “path of seeing”). Here our author is talking about bodhisattvas when they have become irreversible from progress toward full awakening. Alternatively, these two are statements in general, and are not meant as citations from the Sūtra.

q.p:
“Do you think you can apprehend a ‘there-is’ or a ‘there-is-not’ in all the phenomena that are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature” khri brgyad
–. This is the question in response to Subhūti’s one hundred and seventy-seventh rhetorical question, “Lord, if all phenomena are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature, well then, there is no form, up to there is no consciousness; there are no aggregates, there are no constituents, and there are no sense fields; there are no applications of mindfulness, and similarly, up to there is no knowledge of all aspects; there is no Buddha, there is no Dharma, and there is no Saṅgha; there is no path, there is no result, there is no defilement, there is no purification, there is no attainment, and there is no clear realization; and similarly, up to there are no phenomena, any of them?”
q.orig: do you think you can apprehend a ‘there-is’ or a ‘there-is-not’ in all phenomena that are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature?
do you think that it is apprehensible whether all phenomena have or do not have an essential nature of nonentity

div.p:
and that are the intrinsic nature of six perfections? Cf. khri brgyad
– for the addition of this gloss to “all phenomena” in this context. If taken Our author is explaining the two parts, abhāva and svabhāva in the Skt compound “nonexistence of an intrinsic nature” (abhāvasvabhāva, dngos po med pa’i ngo bo nyid). See
– and notes, and
– and notes. Our author is saying that if you take the entire compound as meaning “nonexistent” then you annihilate phenomena completely. If you take it as a dvandva meaning phenomena are nonexistent things and are intrinsic natures, then the former would be nonexistent and the latter existent (at the extremes of “there-is-not” and “there-is”); therefore, the compound means phenomena are not at the two extremes. as nonexistence, it becomes an annihilation. Those who say they are not existent things, and they are intrinsic natures, say there are not existent things and say there are intrinsic natures, so it is teaching that it is not suitable to take them at the extremes of “there-is” and “there-is-not.”

q.p:
“Just the absence of an apprehended object is attainment, just the attainment of the absence of an apprehended object is clear realization.” khri brgyad
. This is the response to Subhūti’s one hundred and seventy-ninth question.
q.orig: just the absence of an apprehended object is attainment, the attainment of just the absence of an apprehended object is clear realization
nonapprehension is attainment, that nonapprehension is clear realization

div.p: If it had said “attainment is without an apprehended object, and clear realization does not apprehend an object,” there would be something to be attained and a clear realization to be had, so there would be the absence of an apprehended object and hence the colossal blunder of apprehending something. This is the reading in K, N, and Golden 369b5. D differs. It says, “If it had said ‘attainment is without an apprehended object, and clear realization does not apprehend an object’ there would be something to be attained and a clear realization to be had, so there is an apprehended object. Therefore it teaches that just the apprehended object is spoken of as ‘attainment… clear realization,’ and ‘unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.’ ” Therefore it teaches that just the absence of an apprehended object is spoken of as “attainment… clear realization,” and

q.p: “unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.”
q.orig: unsurpassed, complete enlightenment

q.p:
“How will there be the clairvoyances arisen from maturation?” nyi khri
; khri brgyad
has five clairvoyances.
q.orig: How will there be the five clairvoyances arisen from maturation
How could there possibly be extrasensory powers that derive from maturation

div.p: The clairvoyances arisen from maturation and the perfections arisen from maturation are located from the eighth level on up.

All of the explanation of serial practice is easy to understand. khri brgyad
–.
In regard to the question,

q.p:
“Lord, when bodhisattva great beings are practicing the perfection of wisdom, how do they complete the six perfections in a single thought?” khri brgyad (ga 47b4–5) with yongs su ’dzin pa, “incorporate,” in place of “complete.” At
Subhūti’s one hundred and eighty-third question is the same as at nyi khri . Twenty-Five Thousand renders yongs su ’dzin pa “acquire.”
q.orig: Lord, when bodhisattva great beings are practicing the perfection of wisdom, how do they incorporate the six perfections in a single thought
Blessed Lord, when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, how do they acquire the six perfections through a single setting of their minds on enlightenment

div.p: and so on, it says

q.p: “when they give gifts it is informed by the perfection of wisdom,”
q.orig: whatever gift they give, their giving is informed by nothing other than the perfection of wisdom
whatever gifts bodhisattva great beings may dispense, these are not acquired by anything other than the perfection of wisdom

div.p: explaining that because they are informed by the perfection of wisdom all beings also become one.

q.p:
“Nothing other than” khri brgyad
: “they are informed by nothing other than the perfection of wisdom.”
q.orig: not acquired by anything other than

div.p: means simply just the one.

Then again, in response to the second question, khri brgyad
: “Lord, how, informed by the perfection of wisdom, does a bodhisattva great being incorporate the six perfections in a single thought?” it explains that it is a single thought because it is not a dualistic thought. The cultivation of all dharmas, the six perfections and so on, while

q.p: “not having a dualistic notion”
q.orig: they do not have a dualistic notion
without dualistic perception

div.p: is easy to understand.

q.p:
“When they give gifts with a thought free from causal signs, without outflows, the perfection of maturation is completed.” Cf. khri brgyad
ff., ’bum da 349b1–5 ff., nyi khri ff., and le’u brgyad ma ca 204b4 ff. This may be a summary of the section rather than an actual citation from a version of the Sūtra no longer available to us.
q.orig: They give the gift with a thought free from causal signs, with a thought without outflows
they dispense generosity with a mind that is free from concepts concerning all phenomena that are signless

div.p: It teaches that, because from the eighth level on up afflictions do not arise and it is a maturation.

q.p:
“This gift you have given is worthless” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: This sort of gift you have given is worthless
such gifts of yours, which are useless and ephemeral

div.p: is said by the Māra class of gods.

Then the completion of the six perfections and the maturation of the clairvoyances can be grasped from the text itself. It is also very easy to understand the exposition of the perfections arisen from maturation from the teaching about the knowledge of the mark of all dharmas. khri brgyad
– is the perfections arisen from maturation; – is the teaching about the knowledge of the mark of all dharmas, answering the question of how dharmas that have no mark can be different.

div.head: Explanation of Chapter 73
div.p: Then the question,

q.p: “Lord, how, when all dharmas are like a dream, have nonexistence for their intrinsic nature, and are empty of their own marks,”
q.orig: Lord, how, when all dharmas are like a dream, have no basis, are the nonexistence of an intrinsic nature, and are empty of their own marks
Blessed Lord, since all phenomena are dreamlike nonentities, with the essential nature of nonentity and empty of intrinsic defining characteristics

div.p: Among the extraordinary gifts of Dharma, most have already been explained. I will explain the ones I have not explained before. Among them is,

q.p:
“What is conflict-free meditative stabilization?” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: what is seclusion devoid of afflicted mental states

div.p: Having become absorbed in a meditative stabilization sustained by the power of the thought “may afflictions not arise in others on account of me,” through the force of the earlier prayer that is a vow that does not provide an opportunity for afflictions to arise in the mindstreams of others, is called “conflict-free absorption.”

q.p: “There, what is knowledge from prayer?”
q.orig: What is knowledge from prayer?
what is knowledge based on aspiration

div.p: Immediately after a prayer has been made to know some phenomenon included in knowable things—anything at all from the phenomena of the three time periods and three realms included in the ordinary and extraordinary—that knowledge through which it comes to be known is called “knowledge from prayer.”

q.p: “There, what are the four total purities?” PSP 6-8: 59, AAVN 102b2–3 (Sparham 2006–11, vol. 4, p. 79).
q.orig: What are the four total purities
what are the four utter purities

div.p: The absolute separation from the “basis”—all the final bases of suffering with which all beings are afflicted—and the independence to appropriate, remain in, and die in whatever body one wants is the

q.p: “thoroughly purified basis.”
q.orig: the utter purity of the physical body

div.p: Control gained over what are counted as magical productions and transformations, and over objective supports, is the

q.p: “thoroughly purified objective support.”
q.orig: the utter purity of objective referents

div.p: The increase of the wholesome in the mind to the fullest extent because of separation from the final basis of mental suffering is the

q.p: “thoroughly purified mind.”
q.orig: the utter purity of mind

div.p: Control over the absence of obstructions to the knowledge of all knowable things because of separation from the final basis of suffering that is on the side of ignorance is

q.p: “thoroughly purified knowledge.”
q.orig: the utter purity of wisdom

div.p: There what are the ten controls?

q.p: “Control over lifespan”
q.orig: Control[2] over lifespan
control over the lifespan

div.p: is remaining for as long as they want;

q.p: “control over mind”
q.orig: control[3] over mind
control over mind

q.p: “control over necessities”
q.orig: control[4] over necessities
control over resources

div.p: is being endowed at will with all necessities, food and so on, immediately after just having the idea of them;

q.p: “control over action”
q.orig: control[5] over action
control over actions

div.p: is the transformation at will of all actions that evolve into birth;

q.p: “control over birth”
q.orig: control[6] over birth
control over birth

div.p: is the birth at will in all birthplaces, in whichever birth they desire;

q.p: “control over belief”
q.orig: control[7] over belief
control over resolve

div.p: is the accomplishing of real things, whatever they are just as they have believed them to be;

q.p: “control over prayer”
q.orig: control[8] over prayer
control over aspiration

div.p: is this—all their prayers being answered at will;

q.p: “control over magical powers”
q.orig: control[9] over magical powers
control over miraculous abilities

div.p: is the accomplishing of all necessary magical powers at will;

q.p: “control over knowledge”
q.orig: control[10] over knowledge
control over wisdom

div.p: is the speedy knowledge of what they want to know—those very deep things to be known; and

q.p: “control over the doctrine”
q.orig: control[11] over the Dharma
control over phenomena

div.p: is the skill at gaining, at will, collections of speech sounds, collections of words, and collections of phrases, and making a perfect presentation of all the doctrine.

q.p:
“What are the three things the tathāgatas do not have to guard against?” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: what constitute the three unguarded states of the tathāgatas

div.p: The three things they do not have to guard against are easy to understand from the scripture itself.

q.p: “[The] three applications of mindfulness”
q.orig: three applications of mindfulness
what are the three consolidations of the tathāgatas’ attitude

div.p: are easy to understand as the absence of attachment and anger.

q.p: “A natural state not robbed of mindfulness”—
q.orig: natural state not robbed of mindfulness

div.p: in whatever way and at whatever time the tathāgatas work for the welfare of beings, when it is accomplished, at that time it is called the “natural state not robbed of mindfulness.”

div.head: Major marks and minor signs of a buddha

q.p:
“What are the thirty-two major marks of a great person?” khri brgyad
has “tathāgata” in place of “great being;” nyi khri has both “tathāgata” and “great being.”
q.orig: what are a tathāgata’s thirty-two major marks?
what are the thirty-two major marks of a great person

div.p: These are presented to engender faith in persons who take the body as the measure of greatness. There, bodhisattva great beings and buddhas are called

q.p: “great person”

div.p: because of their great humanity on account of great lineage, belief, prayer, vigorous attempt, setting out, practice that accomplishes the final result, wisdom and skillful means, and so on. Because they are great persons, these make that clear so they are the “major marks of a great person.”

Qualm: Well then, the number “thirty-two” is meaningless because there is no difference between the major or minor parts of their body when appearing as a great person, so it is not appropriate to think “there are this many.”
That is true, but still, the specific number is tailored to the type of experience that follows from studying and being mindful so here too the explanation is with just that number.
The explanation of these major marks, furthermore, is in four parts: overview, explanation, cause, and result.
The first is the brief teaching; then, the commentary on the major marks is the explanation, the description of earlier karma the cause, and what they presage is the result.

q.p: “They have wheel marks on the surfaces of their hands and feet.”
q.orig: They (1) have wheel marks on the surfaces of their hands and feet
They have hands and feet that are marked with the motif of the wheel
