div.p: Ordinarily a wheel is of two kinds: a wheel that is a weapon and the locomotion wheel, such as a wagon wheel and so on. They occur on both their hands and also their feet. The earlier karma for them is twofold: one, included in the perfection of morality, is listed as having

q.p: “welcomed and accompanied gurus.”
q.orig: welcomed and accompanied gurus
received and accompanied spiritual teachers

div.p: This results in the appearance of locomotion wheels on the soles of their feet. The one included in the perfection of giving is having

q.p: “listened to the doctrine, strung garlands, visited temples and caityas, and given the gift of servants.” Cf. khri brgyad (ga 78b1). g.yog ’khor (“being in the circle of servants”) for parivāra conveys more clearly the intended meaning.
q.orig: listened to the doctrine, offered flower garlands, visited temples, reliquaries, and so on, and have made the gift of being in the circle of servants.
listening to the Dharma, and paid their respects to temples, stūpas

div.p: This results in their appearance on the palms of both hands.

q.p: “Wheels with a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs”—
q.orig: wheel with a thousand spokes…a hub, and a circumference

div.p: when these three are not complete it signifies that, having become wheel-turning emperors, they will go forth to homelessness. At that time, they will not become completely awakened, like, for example, King Śaṅka. MW, s.v. śaṅka, also gives the name śaṅkana. When they have become complete in every respect they will become completely awakened, therefore it says

q.p: “complete in every respect.”
q.orig: complete in all respects

div.p: Qualm: Among these, the various other signs taught in other sūtras—the śrīvatsa, svastika, vardhamāna, In general, these are all symbols of royalty, but exactly what the symbols are is contested, or at least they change over time and in different geographical locations or religious traditions. “Lakṣmī’s calf,” the śrīvatsa (dpal be’u), is perhaps the endless knot; the svastika (bkra shis ), “may it be well,” is of course not the Nazi version of the symbol but the one placed flat. Mvy sdong ris [’khyil ba] (= g.yung drung ’khyil ba?) renders vardhamāna. I have understood it provisionally to be the same as the nandyāvarta symbol, probably a w-shaped symbol, cf. Bhattacarya 2000 and Johnston 1932 who say A.K. Coomaraswamy says vardhamāna is “a lidded jar… to hold powder”; Johnston himself says “its primary sense is the name of a particular lucky pattern.” Johnston thinks the vardhamāna pattern is what Coomaraswamy says is an early śrīvasta pattern. full pot, joined fish, victory banner, conch shell, throne, white parasol, fly whisk, and so on—have not been taught, have they?
That is true, but still, when it explains the main one—being endowed with the major wheel sign—it indicates those as well.

Some say all the major marks that do not appear on the two feet of a tathāgata are not absent because they are included as the necessary insignia of a universal emperor. Hence, it says “complete in every respect.” The reading is uncertain. K, N mtshan gyi ’khor bsgyur de dag nyid. D mtshan gyis ’khor lo de dag nyid. If the reading is mtshan gyis ’khor de dag nyid, it means, “Because the accompanying ones are included with the major sign.”

q.p: “It is a sign presaging an extremely large circle of servants.”
q.orig: It is a sign presaging an extremely large circle of servants.
This is a prior indication that they will have an extremely large assembly

div.p: This is shared by wheel-turning emperors and buddhas. Because it has a hub Emend ste to lte. and spokes, and is held by a rim, it is similar to “an extremely large circle of servants.”

q.p: “Feet that are well placed”—
q.orig: feet that are well positioned

div.p: lord buddhas are not like others for whom the ground is uneven, the soles of whose feet are not flat, or who plant the point of the foot or a side of the foot or the heel on the ground when walking, or who bound along taking breaks in the middle. This is a conjectural translation. Cf. Mvy skabs phyin pa as a translation of mṛṣṭa, “touched.” The idea is perhaps that a buddha glides along just above the surface while lesser beings have to “touch down,” as it were. The whole sole of their foot is flat, lands on the ground when walking, touches the ground evenly, so it is said they have “feet that are well placed.” The entire face of the earth is even and has no change in elevation, no pebbles, boulders, water, mud, thorns, pits and so on, and as rulers over many hundreds and thousands of world systems even the distant is close by. Teaching the earlier karma it says

q.p: “their commitment is firm.”
q.orig: they have been steadfast in their commitments

div.p: It says this because in regard to all undertakings, on account of the force of the sustaining power of truth, renunciation, peace, and wisdom, nobody can make them break it.

q.p: “It is a sign presaging that they cannot be swayed.”
q.orig: It is a[2]…presaging that they cannot be swayed.
This is a prior indication that they will be unswerving and extremely steadfast

div.p: They all—Māra, opponents, tīrthikas and so on—cannot sway them.

q.p: “Hands and feet with connecting webbing” jālaka (“connecting webbing”).—
q.orig: hands and feet that are webbed

div.p: from the first finger joint there is no gap in between the fingers on hands with totally stunning “connecting webbing,” but still they are suited for slipping on jewelry such as a ring and so on. This suggests something like a force-field, so stuff cannot fall through, even though it does not constitute a block. The idea is that nobody falls through the safety net. Cf. Abhayākaragupta’s Muni­matālaṃkāra (thub pa’i dgons rgyan Degé Tengyur [dbu ma, ’a], 286a4–5) sor mo’i tshigs dang po nas brtsams pa’i sor mo’i bar la seng seng po med na yang sor gdub la sogs pa’i rgyan gzhug tu rung ba’i sor mo can no. And the earlier karma is because of

q.p: “their assiduous practice of the four ways of gathering a retinue.”
q.orig: they have become familiar with the four attractive qualities

div.p: It is explained that both their hands have “connecting webbing,” because of the force of gathering a retinue

q.p: “by giving”
q.orig: generosity

div.p: and so on; and both their feet have “connecting webbing” because of the force of the other three ways—

q.p: “consistency between words and deeds,”
q.orig: harmony

div.p: and so on.

Alternatively, they are understood to have come about from two hands gathering a retinue. The beings who have been gathered into the retinue have touched the feet. The appearance of the fingers and toes is with no gaps.
They are like “the four ways of gathering a retinue” because they gather and have become soft.

q.p: “The speedy gathering of a retinue”—
q.orig: they will swiftly gather [disciples]

div.p: this means the eight retinues The eight retinues (four human and four divine) “known in the Pāli suttas as the aṭṭha parisā” (Bucknell 20) are kṣatriya (army), brāhmaṇa (priest), gṛhapati (business), śramaṇa (mendicant), Cāturmahārājakāyika gods, Trayastriṃśa gods, Māras, and Brahmās. quickly gather for the explanation of the Dharma.

Someone else explains “hands and feet with connecting webbing” differently. Setting aside the two thumbs on the hands of the lord buddhas, the tips of all the fingers are aligned, that is, the fingers are marked by each being connected with each part, standing aligned like a lattice work window or the tops of columns, so, on all the toes and fingers all the marks of each joint line appear aligned so they appear like a lattice; thus they have “hands and feet with connecting webbing.” Banerjea (1930), citing Rhys Davids (1910, p. 14, n. 5) “there is no ‘webbing’ between fingers and toes, but that these are set in right lines, like the meshes of a net,” gives the Pāli commentary: jalahatthapado ti na cammena patibaddha angulantaro. Ediso hi phanahatthako purisadosena upahato pabbajjam pi na labhati. Mahapurisassa pana catasso hatthanguliyo panca pi padanguliyo ekappamana honti, tasam pana ekappamanatta jalalakkhanam annamannam pativijjhitva titthanti, ath’assa hatthapada sukusalena vaddhakina yojitajalavata-panasadisa honti, tena vuttam jalahatthapado ti. He says the hands are certainly not shaped like the hood of a cobra because a person with such hands would not even be accepted into the order. The four fingers and five toes are aligned. They are like a lattice-work window put together (yojitajalavatapanasadisa) by a skilled carpenter.

It is said, “When unimportant beings touch the two feet of a tathāgata there is an extremely pleasant feeling, and after death they are born in the ranks of the gods. Such is the power of feet with that major sign—connecting webbing.”

q.p: “Delicate and soft feet and hands”—
q.orig: hands and feet that are tender and soft

div.p: because “delicate” means pliable, and “soft” Mvy says gzhon sha chags renders taruṇa. I am unsure what word our author is glossing. means having a perfect hue.

q.p: “Stands out prominently in seven ways,”
q.orig: seven prominent parts

div.p: because they—

q.p: “the backs of their hands and upper parts of their feet, shoulders, neck, and head”—
q.orig: the arms, legs, shoulders, and nape are amply formed

div.p: are parts that have filled out. The earlier karma is the

q.p: “perfectly prepared hard and soft food and drink.”
q.orig: they have granted the enjoyment of delicious food, delicacies, and drink

div.p: From having given what has been perfectly prepared, their hands and feet have become “delicate and soft”; from having given many things to eat, “the parts stand out prominently in seven ways.” Alternatively, they went on their feet and gave with their two hands. Alternatively, their two hands and feet have become like that because, having given with their two hands, beings have served at their feet. “The parts stand out prominently in seven ways” because they are similar to the seven mental constituents The khams bdun are probably, of the eighteen constituents (dhātu, khams), the six consciousnesses (from eye consciousness constituent to thinking-mind consciousness constituent) and the thinking-mind constituent. that have been satisfied.
How do you know that one karma gives rise to two major signs?
The explanation is that even though it is taken as being one karma, it accomplishes two or even three major signs on account of its being done and accumulated to an extreme degree.

q.p: “They have long toes and fingers.”

div.p: What goes wrong in fingers that are too long, too short, too fat, too thin, and crooked, and so on, has been eliminated. There is nothing wrong with them, and they are in correct proportion relative to the palms of the hands, are of proper length, and are gradually filled out and have slender tips. They are called “long fingers.”
They have

q.p: “stretched-out heels”
q.orig: broad heels

div.p: because they have heels free from what goes wrong in heels. They are of proper length and in correct proportion relative to the feet. There, having taken the entire sole of the foot as having four parts, when three parts are the foot and one part is the heel, it is “of proper length.” Rhys Davids (1910, p. 14, n. 3) “If the foot of a ‘Great Man’ be measured in four parts, two are taken up by the sole and toes, one is under the leg, and one is the heel projecting rearward.”
They have

q.p: “a big… body”
q.orig: a big and straight body
a body that is tall and upright

div.p: because they have a perfect build and are tall in height;

q.p: “and a straight body,”
q.orig: and straight body
and upright

div.p: because unlike those of other persons they do not bend.

q.p: “[It] is not crooked”
q.orig: are not crooked

div.p: anywhere from the shoulders, waist, or knees. D adds “[to] the front and back and any side.”

In this “long toes and fingers and stretched-out heels,” the locutions “long” and “stretched-out” are words for proportionate and fitting; This translation is based on tshig mdzod chen mo, s.v. rkyen ’bab, explained as skabs dang ’tsham par ’byung ba. they are not words for very long and very stretched out.
Also, in regard to the explanation of the earlier karma,

q.p: “because they have freed convicts condemned to death, have sustained life by giving food and drink and so on, and assiduously practiced abstaining from killing”—
q.orig: because they have released [living creatures] from bondage, acted in the service of living things, and renounced the killing of living creatures

div.p: having freed those who are going to be killed from having a short life, those humans remain in their ordinary life, they do not suddenly come to live a longer life; and similarly, giving them all that is required for sustaining themselves, they make it so that they do not have a shortened life, but do not suddenly make them have a longer life. Similarly, also, with the toes and fingers and heels here, the “long” is a nontruncated state; it is not additional length.

q.p:
“At seven hasta
they are elevated in height.”
q.orig: exceeding seven cubits in height

div.p: They are elevated in height relative to an ordinary body. Take this as the measure of an ordinary body. You cannot with certainty take the measure of the body of the Lord because, having looked for the top of the head, it cannot be seen. Because of

q.p: “abstaining from killing”
q.orig: renounced the killing of living creatures

div.p: their physical karma is not twisted, similar to “a straight body.”

q.p: “Lower legs from the feet up that are not knobby”—
q.orig: They have legs that are ample

div.p: prominent bones of the knee joints and ankle joints are said to be “knobby.” In others those two bones are big, so the feet and calves are not attractive. Movement is not easy because they are not flexible, so the movement is unattractive. The calves of the Lord are attractive because the joints do not show; they are flexible, so the movement is attractive.

Others say, “The ankle bones of ordinary humans are toward the back of the foot, so their feet look like they have been nailed on. They are not flexible so they cannot be turned freely, In place of ci bder *yathāsūkham (the translation “freely” is from Valby, s.v. ci bder), K, N have ci bden, “whatever is true.” therefore when they move, the soles of the feet do not show.”

The ankle bones of great persons are higher up on the foot. This is a conjectural translation of zhabs kyi gong bas mtho ba. If gong ba means gong bu, read “higher up relative to the mass of the foot.” Also, only the lower parts of their bodies move, the upper parts do not appear to move. Their feet can be turned easily. When you look from the front, back, right, and left, the soles of the feet appear and the movement is attractive.

q.p: “Body hair that points upward”—
q.orig: body hairs that curl upward

div.p: when the hairs on the bodies of great persons grow in the follicles, they grow pointing upward toward the top, like looking upward at a beautiful face.
Again, just as the earlier karma,

q.p: “the wholesome dharmas they have undertaken,”
q.orig: they have undertaken wholesome dharmas
they have adopted virtuous attributes

div.p: grow higher and higher, the parts of the legs are higher, and the body hair faces upward. The similarity is in the appearance of height.

q.p: “Calves like the aiṇeya antelope”—
q.orig: calves resembling those of Śarabha Aiṇeya

div.p: those who have calves that are like those of the black antelope are said to have “calves like the aiṇeya antelope.” The calves of ordinary humans have flesh that hangs down tshig mdzod chen mo says rlo ba is an archaism for ’phyang ba, “hang down.” in one part, or they wobble or are too thick or too long or too short. Those of great persons have flesh that is compact, and they taper, are evenly shaped, very spherical, and well built, occupying only the space of eighteen aṅgula. MW, s.v. vitasti, says 12 aṅgulas equal about nine inches.
Again, the earlier karma is

q.p: “having shown respect, they have made vocations and branches of knowledge available”
q.orig: having shown respect, they have made crafts and branches of knowledge available
they have acted in the service of classical learning and the arts

div.p: so those trainees have increased and flourished, and by having made necessary goods available they have become strong. The calves are similar to that because the muscles have developed and have become like the calves of the black antelope.

q.p: “It is a sign presaging a speedy grasp of things.”
q.orig: It is a[4]…presaging a speedy grasp of things
This is a prior indication that they will swiftly acquire [such works]

div.p: Those great persons quickly grasp all the buddhas have said, and the tathāgatas also grasp in a single instant the stream of questions of all beings.

q.p: “Tubular and long arms”—
q.orig: arms that reach down the thighs when standing upright

div.p: “tubular” because they are big, thick arms; “long” because they reach down to their knees. They are long. Again, the earlier karma is similar because they extended their arms out a long way giving gifts to others, and because the doctrine they give is vast.

q.p: “[Their] private parts are hidden in a sheath.”
q.orig: They are endowed with a contracted male organ

div.p: The “private part” is a secret that is a private part, hence “private part.” About that private part hidden in a sheath, not present before the eyes, it says the “private part is hidden in a sheath.” It means the private part portion is hidden in the sheath and not present before the eyes, like a golden colored lotus flower hidden in the sheath of the surrounding calyx. Again, the earlier karma is

q.p: “[they] reconciled friends and relatives and did not separate”
q.orig: they did not separate from each other those friends…reconciled those who had fallen out
they have exhorted associates, friends, allies who do not live apart

div.p: them and so on. A sheath and a private part are similar in that way. They are similar because on account of something that can be hidden the secret portion was not obvious.

q.p: “A color like gold”—
q.orig: a golden complexion

div.p: this teaches that their body is dense, glossy, and has a very clear color.

q.p: “Extremely fine skin”—
q.orig: skin of extremely delicate complexion

div.p: this teaches that inner and outer

q.p: “dirt particles”
q.orig: no dust

div.p: and stains and so on do not

q.p: “stick to it.”
q.orig: sticking to it
adheres to their body

div.p: Here, washing hands and feet and needing to be washed and so on is done by way of conventional designation so those who look after them will get merit, and to fit in at the appropriate times. Rhys Davids: “Hence the Buddhas only wash as an example to their followers.”

q.p: “Each strand of body hair grows curling to the right”—
q.orig: hair that grows distinctly, curling to the right

div.p: “each strand of body hair” because from their body hair follicle grows just a single strand of body hair; “curling to the right” because they are circular, like an ornamental coiling snake ring, or the circle of a coiling snake, both of which coil to the right.

q.p: “An ūrṇā marks their face.”
q.orig: Their face is adorned with a hair ringlet [between the eyebrows]

div.p: When there is a pliable, soft body hair, white in color and glossy, in the spot between the eyebrows, a full hasta or a pair of hasta or three hasta and so on in length when it is stretched out, that, when let go again, D slar btang na is supported by Abhayākaragupta’s Muni­matālaṃkāra (thub pa’i dgongs rgyan, Degé Tengyur [dbu ma, ’a], 286b3). coils to the right with the tip on the upper part, just the measure of an Indian gooseberry fruit, skyu ru ra (ābalaka), emblic myrobalan. like an egg-shaped drop of silver, beautifying whatever face it is on, it is said that “an ūrṇā marks their face.” The earlier karma is that

q.p: “they have avoided society, and accorded an appropriate status to parents and so on, served them, given them gifts, not displeased them,” K, N gus par ma byas pa; khri brgyad (ga 79a3) mgu bar byas pa.
q.orig: avoided society, and because, having accorded an appropriate status to their spiritual superiors—their preceptors, teachers, parents, brothers and sisters, and so on—they have served them, given them gifts, and pleased them
they have abandoned social diversions, and served, revered, and obeyed their superiors, including preceptors, masters, parents, and siblings, in the appropriate manner

div.p: and so on. That is for both these major marks. On account of that, those strands grow curling to the right and the ūrṇā is long and has an excellent shape.

q.p: “[Their] upper body is like a lion’s.”
q.orig: Their torso resembles that of a lion

div.p: Their upper body is like a lion’s upper body so they have an “upper body like a lion’s.” It says this because their chest is broad and big in size—perfectly broad and big because it is filled out. K, N shas rgyas pas yangs shing; D sha rgyas pas spangs; Abhayākaragupta’s Muni­matālaṃkāra (thub pa’i dgongs rgyan, Degé Tengyur [dbu ma, ’a], 286b5) rgyas pa yangs pa sha rgyas pa’i brang can nyid kyi phyir dang.

q.p: “[Their] shoulders are well rounded without an indentation at the throat.”
q.orig: their shoulders are well rounded
They are endowed with amply curved and elegant shoulders

div.p: Put the word “well” together with “rounded.” The “rounded” teaches that the Adam’s apple does not show. This means it is spherical and compact like the neck of a golden pot. This explanation certainly makes excellent sense, but it is not found elsewhere. PSP 6-8: 62 kāñcana­paṭṭasuvimṛṣṭo. MW, s.v paṭṭa, “a slab”; khri brgyad (ga 78a2) gser gyi glegs ma, “a highly polished golden door panel.”
Again, the earlier karma is

q.p: “[they] did not speak unkindly,”
q.orig: speak kind words
they neither speak unpleasant words

div.p: similar in style to a lion, the cause of a beautiful throat;

q.p: “did not belittle others,”
q.orig: do not belittle others
nor do they scold anyone

div.p: the cause of the chest being broad like a lion’s; and being

q.p: “eloquent and not jarring, and their speech is the same as the roar of a lion,”
q.orig: but maintain harmony, speaking pleasant words with eloquence

div.p: the cause of a beautiful neck.

q.p: “The part between the collarbones is filled in”—
q.orig: They are endowed with extremely broad collarbones

div.p: the part between the collarbones is expanded and broad.

q.p: “They know tastes as tasty.”
q.orig: They are endowed with a superior organ of taste

div.p: Those who know the tastes of the six tastes These are sweet, salty, sour (like a lemon), bitter like the bitter gourd (Hindi karela), astringent (like an unripe banana), and pungent (like chili). are said to “know tastes as tasty.” In this context, take to “know” as to like, as in “treats like a mother, treats like a father” and so on. Because they enjoy and are satisfied by the tastes, it is said they “know the tastes.” The gullets of great persons have seven thousand receptive tastebuds giving rise to the experience. If they eat even as little as a single tiny sesame seed, it spreads throughout the entire body. Szántō (18.iv.2017), ms. 5r5–5v1: mahā­puruṣāṇāṃ hi sapta rasāharaṇī sahasrāṇi grīvāyām ūrdhvamukhāni pravarttante sarve pi rasā mukhai prakṣiptā amṛtarasatulyā bhavati. When all tastes are introduced to the mouth they become like the taste of nectar. That is the karma of the major mark. How it is similar to the earlier karma is easy to understand. Here karman means the way the habit formed by doing an earlier action again and again. It translates out as an experience experienced at the highest stage of physical development. The pūrvakarma (“earlier karma”) is forming the habit by doing the action again and again earlier.

q.p: “A build like an Indian fig tree”—
q.orig: a build like an Indian fig tree
endowed with a girth like the banyan tree

div.p: some say nya gro means beneath. Take this as the lower part of the body. Take the ro dha as the upper part of the body. Their build is the same. So, when the upper part and the lower part of their body, starting from the waist, are equal in size it is said that they have “a build like an Indian fig tree.” This derives the nya gro in nyagrodha (“an Indian fig tree”) from ny-añc, “bend down,” in the sense of beneath something, here the lower part of the body; and the ro dha from ruh (“grow up”), here the upper part of the body. The parimaṇḍala (“a build,” an encompassing measurement) means that they are equal in size. Abhayākaragupta’s Muni­matālaṃkāra (thub pa’i dgongs rgyan, Degé Tengyur [dbu ma, ’a], 287a1) n+yag ni dma’ ba ste sku smad do, ro dha ni sku stod do is better. Thus, nya gro intends just the ny-ag from ny-añc (“to bend down”); ro dha is like a past passive participle from ruh (“to grow up”). It is referencing the fact that the Indian fig tree (a banyan tree) sends out secondary roots from its branches that then take root and grow.

Others say take the nya gro to be from the top of the head down to the feet; take the ro dha as the width; and take the build as the two outstretched arms. So there, when the height and width of their body is the same length of their two outstretched arms, it is said that they have “a build like an Indian fig tree.”
Some say the trunk and branches of an Indian fig tree are equal in height and width. All the bodies of great persons are like that, the same in being the size of two extended arms.

q.p: “[They] have an uṣṇīṣa on the top of their head”—
q.orig: They are endowed with the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head

div.p: take this as a head like a bound turban. dbu ze’u ka bcings pa. This is a conjectural translation of ze’u ka as “turban.” ze is a word for rngog ma (a “mane”) and a ze’u ka is perhaps a diminutive. Jäschke, s.v. ze, cites ze ka from Czoma di Korosi’s Dictionary as meaning a “hump.” Rhys Davids (1910, p. 16, n. 4): “This expression, says the Cy., refers to the fullness either of the forehead or of the cranium. In either case the rounded highly-developed appearance is meant, giving to the unadorned head the decorative dignified effect of a crested turban, and the smooth symmetry of a water-bubble.” Edg, s.v. uṣṇīṣa, “having a head the size and shape of which makes it seem turbanned.” It is explained that the heads of others are not fully developed, are elongated or squashed and are not symmetrical. The heads of great persons are arranged evenly like a turban, spherical, completed, well shaped, and well developed.

Others say this major sign is to teach that the forehead is fully developed in size. The flesh in between and above the right ear and the left ear of the foreheads of great persons is well shaped; the size of the forehead is fully completed and beautiful like a royal golden turban that has been bound on.
Again, the earlier karma is that they were

q.p: “first”—
q.orig: first[1]

div.p: they were chief

q.p: “at doing”
q.orig: doing

div.p: all wholesome actions, making

q.p: “parks, assembly halls,”
q.orig: platforms, and temples

div.p: places to quench thirst and so on—therefore

q.p: “they have a build like a fig tree,”
q.orig: they have[18]…like an Indian fig tree
They are endowed with a girth like the banyan tree

div.p: and

q.p: “an uṣṇīṣa on the top of their head,”
q.orig: the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head

div.p: because, having become chief in the assembly, they raised their head uncowed and fearlessly encouraged others to engage in these actions. Hence,

q.p: “these are signs that presage holding the highest office.”
q.orig: these are signs that presage holding the highest office
These are prior indications that they will acquire great dominion

q.p: “A long thin tongue”:
q.orig: an extremely long [and slender] tongue

div.p: “long”—big or lengthy; “thin”—pliable.

q.p: “The voice of Brahmā”—
q.orig: a voice like Brahmā
the divine voice of Brahmā

div.p: because it is a voice like Brahmā, or the finest voice.

q.p: “The call of the kalaviṅka bird”—
q.orig: the kalaviṅka bird

div.p: like the sound of the Indian cuckoo.

q.p: “They have lion-like jaws”
q.orig: lion-like jaws
They are endowed with lion-like jaws

div.p: because they are similar in part to the moon on the twelfth day before it is full, and the edges of the jaws are muscled and excellently rounded. K, N omit sha mkhregs shing, “muscled.”

q.p: “Very white teeth,”
q.orig: extremely white teeth

div.p: because they shine;

q.p: “extremely white,”

div.p: even more than the planet Venus.

q.p: “Even teeth,”
q.orig: even teeth

div.p: because they

q.p: “are not too long or too short,”
q.orig: neither too high nor too low

div.p: or uneven.

q.p: “Teeth without gaps”—
q.orig: close-fitting teeth

div.p: because there are

q.p: “no spaces between their teeth,”
q.orig: without gaps between them

div.p: and so on, they are good looking.

q.p: “Forty teeth,”
q.orig: forty even teeth

div.p: because while other humans have thirty-two or thirty-eight teeth, on the contrary their teeth number forty and are complete.

q.p: “Dark blue eyes”—
q.orig: dark pupils

div.p: the globe in the middle of the round of their eyes is moist and black. The two edges of the black globe are white. When the two eyelashes are still, they remain moist and dark blue. The two corners are a little bit redder. In between the eyelashes and eye is like a golden color. Thus, even though they do have the five clarities of sense faculties, still, because the circle of the eye is the foremost, it says “dark blue eyes.” Abhayākaragupta’s Muni­matālaṃkāra (thub pa’i dgongs rgyan, Degé Tengyur [dbu ma, ’a], 287a5–6).

q.p: “[Their] eyelashes are like those of a cow,”
q.orig: eyelashes like a cow’s
They have eyelashes like those of a cow

div.p: because, like a calf that right from birth has a youth’s eyelashes, the color of

q.p: “the upper and lower eyelashes”
q.orig: the upper and lower lashes

div.p: is extremely glossy, and they are

q.p: “not entangled, so… [their] eyelashes are like those of a cow.”
q.orig: not entangled, so…eyelashes are like those of a cow
They have eyelashes like those of a cow in that the upper and lower lashes are well positioned and untangled

q.p:
“Eighty minor signs” khri brgyad
ff.—
q.orig: eighty minor marks

div.p: they are called “minor signs” This is explaining “minor sign” by breaking up the parts of anuvyañjana into anu (“subsequent”) plus vi and añj (“to beautify”) or añc (“to make clear”) vi añc (“to expand on”). Muni­matālaṃkāra (thub pa’i dgongs rgyan, Degé Tengyur [dbu ma, ’a], 287a6–7) mtshan ’di rnams rjes su gsal par byed pa’am mtshan dang rjes su mthun par gsal bar byed pa’am/ skyes bu chen por rab tu gsal bar byed ces pa’am/ rjes su mthun par mdzes par byed ces pa dpe byad bzang po brgyad cu rnams te. because they subsequently expand on the major marks or are subsequently divided in conformity with the major marks, that is, they indicate that they are great persons or make them handsome in conformity with the major marks.

q.p: “Lord buddhas have nails with a color like copper”
q.orig: they have nails with a color like copper
lord buddhas are endowed with copper-colored nails

div.p: is an explanation of a minor sign. They

q.p: “are isolated from all conditioned things” ’bum na 52a5, nyi khri (ga 237a3), le’u brgyad ma ca 244a2. khri brgyad (ga 79b7) ma chags pa’i thugs mnga’ bas, “have minds free from attachment to all conditioned things.”
q.orig: have minds free from attachment to all compounded phenomena
are detached from any conditioning

div.p: is its corresponding cause. Connect them all like that.

q.p:
“Bodhisattva great beings gather beings with those six perfections, by kind words.” khri brgyad
. See also ..
q.orig: Bodhisattva great beings gather being with those six perfections, by kind words
all these six perfections—that bodhisattva great beings attract beings through their pleasant speech

div.p:
Having brought them into the fold with kind words, they gather them into a retinue with the six perfections, so “kind words” is in the list. “Kind words” is the second of the four ways of gathering an assembly—giving gifts, kind words, beneficial actions, and consistency between words and deeds. This harkens back to the statement at
: “Subhūti, here, looking down with my buddha eye on as many world systems as there are sand particles in the Gaṅgā River in the eastern direction I have seen bodhisattva great beings gathering humans with the four ways of gathering a retinue. What are the four? The ways of gathering are by giving gifts, kind words, beneficial actions, and consistency between words and deeds.” The first, “giving gifts,” comprises all the practices (dharmas) down to the minor signs ending at .

q.p:
“They have gathered beings… with those same six perfections by… beneficial actions.” Cf. khri brgyad
, nyi khri .
q.orig: They have gathered beings…with those same six perfections…beneficial actions
bodhisattva great beings attract beings through their purposeful activity by means of these six perfections

div.p: The aspiration to do something of benefit goes ahead of the six perfections that gather them into a retinue. Connect the later ones like that as well. Cf. nyi khri . “With those same six perfections, by consistency between words and deeds, they gather beings into a retinue.” Here it says “later ones” (plural) because “with those same six perfections” goes with “skill in letters” (dhāraṇī) as well.

q.orig: Become skilled at one syllable
become skilled in the formation of a single syllable

div.p:
Through the sequence of dhāraṇī letters as gateways—“the letter a is the door to all dharmas because they are unproduced from the very beginning,” and so on At khri brgyad
the 42 letters (“the arapacana syllabary”) are each given a meaning. —they should, through one letter, become skilled at the accomplishment of the signlessness meditative stabilization.

q.p: “Know K, N, Golden 378b6. through one syllable that all have a decline.”
q.orig: Know through one syllable that all have a decline
realize all the natural expressions [of speech] that are refined through a single syllable

div.p: To have a decline is to decline. ldan pa renders -gata, cf. Whitney’s Sanskrit Grammar 1273c, p. 435. This means compounded phenomena have a complete change.

q.p:
“Meditate on forty-five syllables being included in one syllable.” khri brgyad
. However, PSP 6-8: 68, ŚsPN4/2 0087r1, Gilgit 625.5 dvācatvāriṃśad; ’bum na 56a1, nyi khri , le’u brgyad ma ca 247a4 bzhi bcu rtsa gnyis, have the “forty-two” letters in the arapacana alphabet.
q.orig: cultivate the gathering of anything up to and including forty-two syllables in a single syllable

div.p: Meditate on the meditative stabilizations of all the syllables being included in the a that accomplishes the nonproduction meditative stabilization.

q.p: “Meditate on one syllable being included in forty-five syllables.”
q.orig: cultivate the gathering of a single syllable in the forty-two syllables

div.p: Meditate on the meditative stabilizations of the forty-five syllables being in just the a.

q.p:
“All dharmas, Subhūti, being the appearance of that for which there are no letters, are magical creations.” khri brgyad
(reading chos de, “that Dharma” or “that doctrine,” in place of “all dharmas”). Cp. ŚsPN4/2 87r4, Gilgit 625.8 na cākśarākāra­nirmuktaḥ subhūte sarvadharmaḥ; ’bum na 56a6, nyi khri ga 241a, le’u brgyad ma ca 248b1 chos ston kyang / chos de yi ge’i rnam pa dang bral ba yang ma yin te; LSPW pp. 536–37: “And yet that Dharma is not quite free from the mode of letters!”; khri pa (nga 333b5) yi ge dang yi ge med pa la ma g/rtogs pa’i chos gang yang med do, Ten Thousand translation: “There is no doctrine at all that is not included in the syllables and the absence of syllables.”
q.orig: That Dharma, Subhūti, being the appearance of that for which there are no letters, is a magical creation.
And yet, Subhūti, that Dharma is not quite divorced from the form of the syllables

div.p: This means they are generated as an appearance of the inexpressible dharma-constituent.
With

q.p: “how do bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom arisen from maturation,”
q.orig: how do bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom

div.p:
and so on, khri brgyad
ff. This is Subhūti’s one hundred and ninety-ninth question, “Lord, if, because of the emptinesses of what transcends limits and no beginning and no end, a being absolutely cannot be apprehended, a dharma also cannot be apprehended, and a dharma’s intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended, well then, Lord, how do bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom arisen from maturation… teach the Dharma to beings?” he is asking: If

q.p: “a being… and a dharma… cannot be apprehended,”
q.orig: a being absolutely cannot be apprehended, a dharma also cannot be apprehended
beings, too, are absolutely nonapprehensible, nor indeed is the Dharma apprehensible

div.p: which is to say, do not appear when they practice what has arisen from maturation because what has arisen from maturation is an absence of conceptual thinking, how could they give an explanation of the Dharma? How, given that they would be connecting them with dharmas on the side of awakening that do not exist, would they not

q.p: “be connecting them with error?”

div.p: Having asked that,

q.p: the Lord said, “Exactly so, Subhūti, exactly so!”
q.orig: the Lord said to him, “Exactly so, Subhūti, exactly so!
Subhūti, it is so! It is so,” replied the Blessed One

div.p: and so on, delighting in those words.

q.p: “Having thus seen that all those dharmas are empty, teach the doctrine to beings,”
q.orig: having seen all phenomena as emptiness, they teach the Dharma to beings

div.p:
and so on, khri brgyad
. teaches that although it is true that Subhūti, beings, and dharmas are empty, still beings do not know them as emptiness. Hence the Lord teaches the doctrine in order that they will know, and when he teaches the doctrine, he teaches the doctrine so that one way or the other it does not disagree with that emptiness.

q.p: “They see that all dharmas are without obscurations”
q.orig: they know all phenomena to be without obscuration

div.p: means they see them separated from falsely imagined obscurations, as absolutely pure.

The similarity based on the analogy of a tathāgata’s magical creation has been dealt with already.
.

q.p:
“By way of their not being bound and not being freed” khri brgyad
.—
q.orig: in a manner that is neither bound nor liberated

div.p: during the period when the true dharmic nature of form has stains it is a falsely imagined thing isolated from an intrinsic nature, so it is “not bound”; and even during the period when it is stainless there is no purification plucked out of thin air, so it is “not freed.”

q.p: “Form’s state of not being bound and not being freed is not form.”
q.orig: form[2]’s state of not being bound and not being freed is not form[3]
Nor does the nonbondage and nonliberation of physical forms constitute physical forms

div.p: The “state of not being bound and not being freed” is the thoroughly established state. This means it is not the intrinsic nature of a falsely imagined form. Alternatively, taking the construction as a bahuvrīhi, “it does not have the form that is a falsely imagined thing as its intrinsic nature.” Brunnhölzl (2011, pp. 42–43) renders this: “ ‘the lack of bondage and the lack of liberation’ refer to the state of the perfect [nature], which is not the nature of imaginary form.”

q.p: “Are absolutely pure”—

div.p: “in their basic nature” is intended.

q.p: “Something nonexistent is not located in something nonexistent,”
q.orig: Nonentities do not dwell in nonentity

div.p: because it does not rest on it, just as, to illustrate, space is not located in space.

q.p: “Something’s own existence is not located in something nonexistent,”
q.orig: something’s own existence is not located in something nonexistent[2]
Intrinsic entities do not dwell in intrinsic entities

div.p: because it does not exist, just as, to illustrate, sharpness is not located in a rabbit’s horns and so on.

q.p:
“And something else’s existence is not located in something nonexistent or in something’s own existence,” khri brgyad
. PSP 6-8: 70, ŚsPN4/2 93r5, ’bum na 71a2, nyi khri ga 243b4, le’u brgyad ma ca 249b5, khri pa nga 336a1–2 all have a reading similar to LSPW pp. 537–38: “Because one cannot apprehend of them an own-being in which they could be established. For the nonexistent does not stand in the nonexistent, own-being does not stand in own-being, other-being does not stand in other-being.”
q.orig: and something else’s existence is not located in something nonexistent or in something’s own existence
nor do extraneous entities dwell in extraneous entities

div.p:
because both something else’s existence and something’s own existence are nonexistent. Connect the others Here gzhan dag (“others”) means the rest in the list, starting from “form” given at khri brgyad
: “ ‘form is empty,’ up to by way of not apprehending ‘consciousness is empty,’ up to by way of not apprehending ‘compounded and uncompounded dharmas are empty.’ ” like that as well.

q.p:
“The lord buddhas, the bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, worthy ones, and all the noble beings understand khri brgyad
, ’bum na 71a5; PSP 6-8: 70 has anubaddha in place of anubuddha. just that true dharmic nature of dharmas”
q.orig: the lord buddhas, the bodhisattvas, the pratyekabuddhas, the worthy ones, and all the noble beings understand just that true dharmic nature of dharmas
those lord buddhas, those bodhisattva great beings, those pratyekabuddhas, and those śrāvakas, too…all attain realization in pursuit of this reality

div.p: teaches that all have just the one clear dharma realization.

q.p: “Without going beyond that true dharmic nature of dharmas”—
q.orig: do not transcend the reality of all phenomena

div.p: when giving an exposition of the Dharma they do not go beyond that.

q.p: “Subhūti, the dharma-constituent does not go beyond anything, and suchness and the very limit of reality do not go beyond anything either.”
q.orig: the dharma-constituent does not go beyond anything, and suchness and the very limit of reality do not go beyond anything either
Subhūti, it is because the realm of phenomena is not transcended; the real nature and the very limit of reality are not transcended

div.p: Take them specifically with their particulars: the lord buddhas’ “dharma-constituent,” which is to say, dharma body, does not go beyond anything; the bodhisattvas’ “suchness” does not go beyond anything; and the śrāvakas’ and pratyekabuddhas’ “very limit of reality” does not go beyond anything.

q.p: “Because they have no intrinsic nature that goes beyond anything”
q.orig: because they are without any essential nature that might be transcended

div.p: means an intrinsic nature that can be gone beyond does not exist.

q.p: “Lord, if, in the dharma-constituent, there is no going beyond, and in suchness and at the very limit of reality there is no going beyond,”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, if in that manner the realm of phenomena is not transcended, and the real nature and the very limit of reality are also not transcended

div.p: and so on, poses the following question: Form, feeling, and so on are in their intrinsic nature changeable, so it appears they go beyond something. Thus, there is a going beyond something when it comes to form and so on, but there is none when it comes to the dharma-constituent and so on, so, at that time are form and so on and the dharma-constituent and so on different?

q.p: “No, Subhūti,” the Lord replied,
q.orig: No, Subhūti,” he replied
Subhūti, that is not so!” replied the Blessed One

div.p: and so on, teaches that the dharmas—form, feeling, and so on—and the three, the dharma-constituent and so on, are not different. The intention of this is that “ultimate form does not go beyond anything.”
Then the elder Subhūti said,

q.p: “Lord, if form is not one thing and the dharma-constituent is not another,”
q.orig: Lord, if form is not one thing and the dharma-constituent is not another
Blessed Lord, if physical forms are not one thing, and the realm of phenomena another

div.p: and so on—he asks: if there is no difference between form, feeling, and so on, and the dharma-constituent and so on, well then, will there not be

q.p: “a detailed presentation of the results”
q.orig: a detailed presentation of the bad results
the fruits of any attributes

div.p: of wholesome and unwholesome actions because all dharmas will be uncompounded just as the dharma-constituent and so on are? Then the Lord says,

q.p: “Subhūti, … based on conventional truth,”
q.orig: Subhūti[2]… based on conventional truth
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “the systematic presentation of the [various] fruits may be disclosed when relative truth is taken as the standard

div.p: and so on. This is saying that even though all phenomena are uncompounded in their intrinsic nature, nevertheless for

q.p: “simple… folk,”
q.orig: simple, ordinary folk
ordinary people

div.p: who make them into falsely imagined objects, there are falsely imagined wholesome and unwholesome things, and through the force of that there are also bright and bad maturations. The Lord, governed by that, has given an exposition of them by way of their being “conventional truth.” Ultimately all dharmas are the intrinsic nature of suchness, so

q.p: “an exposition of a detailed presentation of”
q.orig: the systematic presentation of

div.p: karma and maturation is impossible because ultimately they

q.p: “are undifferentiated”—
q.orig: cannot be conceived

div.p: those dharmas “are undifferentiated,” are not something that can be expressed, hence they are

q.p: “not something that can be talked about,”
q.orig: cannot be described

div.p: and thus

q.p: “name and form are not produced and do not stop, are not defiled and not purified.”
q.orig: the true existence of name and the true existence of form are nonarising, unceasing, without affliction, and without purification

div.p: From among the formless phenomena and form phenomena, saying “name” and “form” is conventional truth mode. Ultimately that suchness is thoroughly established and hence is undifferentiated. It cannot be expressed, so it is “not something that can be talked about.” It is uncompounded so it is “not produced”; it is not produced so it does “not stop”; it is isolated from an intrinsic nature so it is “not defiled”; and it is pure in its intrinsic nature so it is “not purified.”

q.p: “They are an emptiness of what transcends limits and an emptiness of no beginning and no end.”
q.orig: This is the emptiness of the unlimited and the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end

div.p: Those same phenomena, undifferentiated and so on, are talked about as the two emptinesses.

q.p: Subhūti said, “Lord, if the detailed presentation of results is based on conventional truth,”
q.orig: Subhūti asked him, “Lord, if the detailed presentation of results is based on conventional truth
Blessed Lord, if the systematic presentation of the fruits is dependent on relative truth

div.p: and so on. He is asking: if you are going to make a presentation of results that are unreal why would you not make a presentation of

q.p: “simple, ordinary folk,”
q.orig: ordinary people

div.p: and so on,

q.p: “in the result of stream enterer,”
q.orig: the fruit of entering the stream to nirvāṇa

div.p: and so on?

q.p: Then the Lord said, “Subhūti, were simple, ordinary folk to know the conventional truth or the ultimate truth,”
q.orig: the Lord said to him, “Subhūti, were simple, ordinary folk to know the conventional truth or the ultimate truth,
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “do ordinary people understand relative truth or ultimate truth

div.p: and so on. He is saying that while there is no detailed presentation of results, nevertheless there is a presentation of the falsely imagined result of stream enterer, and so on, because of the comprehension of falsely imagined things. Simple, ordinary folk do not comprehend, therefore they do not cultivate the path. Noble persons do comprehend, therefore just for them there should be a detailed presentation of the path, and what is not the path, and the results.

The elder Subhūti asks, khri brgyad
. This is Subhūti’s two hundred and first question.

q.p: “Lord, when they have become habituated to the path”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, will the fruit then be attained by those who have cultivated the path

div.p: as cause,

q.p: “does the result appear and do they attain the result?”
q.orig: or is the fruit attainable

div.p: If it does, it would happen just as an ultimate.
Then the Lord said,

q.p: “No, Subhūti. The result does not appear, and they do not attain the result from having become habituated to the path.”
q.orig: No, Subhūti!” replied the Blessed One. “The fruit will not be attained by those who have cultivated the path

div.p: He has refuted both the path and result because they are falsely imagined phenomena.

q.p: “Nor, Subhūti, do they attain the result from having not become habituated to the path.”
q.orig: nor indeed is the fruit attainable through the path

div.p: This is explaining that they are falsely imagined phenomena, but not arbitrary.

q.p: “A result to be attained with the path does not exist, it will not be attained with what is not the path, and it does not exist on the path either” ’bum na 86a4–5.
q.orig: They do not attain the result with the path and not with what is not the path, and not without standing on the path
the fruit will not be attained without cultivating the path, but neither is the fruit attainable through the path, and the fruit will not be attained without abiding on the path

div.p: teaches the certification of dharmas.

q.p: “In the dharma-constituent they do not make a presentation of the results by way of apportioning them.” char bcad pa’i tshul gyis, bhāgacchedena. This is the reply to Subhūti’s two hundred and second question that reads “by curbing”; cf. .
q.orig: do not make a presentation of the results in a way that curbs…the dharma-constituent

div.p: This means that in the dharma-constituent, having apportioned them like that, there is ultimately no detailed presentation.
With

q.p: “Lord, if the compounded element and uncompounded element have not been apportioned,”
q.orig: Lord, if the results…have not been presented in detail by curbing the compounded element and the uncompounded element
Blessed Lord, if the fruit is not established by eradicating conditioned or unconditioned elements

div.p: and so on, the elder Subhūti asks why, then, has a detailed presentation been given having specified particular abandonments, paths, and results. Then the Lord said,

q.p:
“Subhūti, … is the result of stream enterer… compounded or… uncompounded?” I have added the last part of khri brgyad
to make the citation readable in English.
q.orig: Subhūti,” asked the Blessed One in return, “are the fruit of entering the stream to nirvāṇa, the fruit of being destined for only one more rebirth, the fruit of no longer being subject to rebirth, arhatship, individual enlightenment, and unsurpassed, complete enlightenment conditioned, or unconditioned

div.p: and so on. Ultimately they have no stages of comprehension and awakening. Thus the “result of stream enterer,” and so on, are uncompounded and in them there is no division into stages. Therefore, given that they are all an awakening to emptiness, none has been apportioned.

div.head: Explanation of Chapters 74 to 82

q.p: “Lord, how have… they realized well what marks dharmas as dharmas” ’bum na 88b4.
q.orig: “Lord, how have bodhisattva great beings realized well what marks dharmas as dharmas?
Blessed Lord, how do bodhisattva great beings realize the defining characteristic of phenomena, of which all phenomena partake

div.p: means how have they, if ultimately there is no realization of what has not been apportioned.

q.p: “Lord, how do they meditate on the path of a magical creation?”

div.p: is asked using the analogy of a magical creation.

q.p: “Subhūti, it is based on meditating on a path,”
q.orig: Subhūti, it is based on meditating on the path

div.p: and so on, says the achievement is just analogous to a magical creation.

q.p: “Lord, how do bodhisattva great beings realize all dharmas that are nonexistent things”

div.p: means how, if they are nonexistent, is there a realization? There is no achievement of the realization of a rabbit’s horns and so on.

q.p: “Is there any existent thing apprehended in a tathāgata’s magical creation, thanks to which it is defiled and is purified?”

div.p: This teaches that for the tathāgatas there is no defilement and there is no purification. There is no realization because the forms of suffering life and liberation are similar; it is nothing at all because it is simply posited as just nonexistent.

q.p:
“Lord, … if the five forms of life in saṃsāra from which beings will be liberated do not exist, how is there going to be a bodhisattva’s personal heroic power?” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Lord, if all are like…if the five forms of life in saṃsāra from which beings will be liberated do not exist, how is there going to be a bodhisattva great being’s personal heroic power?
they are without cyclic existence with its five classes of living beings

div.p: This means that in its basic nature saṃsāra is unreal, so in its intrinsic nature it is liberated.

q.p: Then the Lord said, “What do you think, Subhūti,”
q.orig: What do you think, Subhūti,” asked the Lord
do you think

div.p:
and so on. Bodhisattvas do not see beings or a cycle of existences. Those analogies of a dream and so on teach that they did see earlier, but beings do not know they are nonexistent, so their “personal heroic power” is causing them to understand. This is summarizing khri brgyad
–. “They”—the bodhisattvas—do see “beings to be liberated from hell, or the animal world” and so on as like a dream and an illusion, but the beings do not know “they,” the hells and so on, do not ultimately exist, so “their”—the bodhisattvas’—power is causing “them”—the beings—to understand.

q.p: “Subhūti, if, just on their own, beings knew that all dharmas are like a dream, up to are like a magical creation,”
q.orig: Subhūti, if, just on their own, beings knew that all dharmas are like a dream and are like a magical creation
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “if beings of their own accord had known that all phenomena are like a phantom emanation

div.p:
and so on, khri brgyad
. This is the response to Subhūti’s two hundred and seventh question. teaches just that.

q.p:
“The basic nature of all dharmas is name because they point somewhere.” khri brgyad
. This relates nāman (“name”) with the root nam (“to bow”) and the derivative nimna (“incline to”). The idea is that they get up onto the roof of the ultimate on the ladder of the conventional. The context is as follows: Subhūti asks who exactly are the nonexistent beings that bodhisattvas heroically work to liberate. The Lord says ( ) a “name” and says, “Subhūti, these—namely ‘name’ and ‘causal sign’—are names plucked out of thin air,” and so with all dharmas “they are made-up name designations,” followed by this statement. nyi khri , ’bum na 92b3–4 differ.
q.orig: all names have been designated by words and concepts

div.p: All falsely imagined dharmas with a falsely imagined basic nature are called “name.” Therefore, they point like that to that intellectually active mind of beings, or that basic nature points to that intellectually active mind. This is a conjectural translation. I have not understood this line.
With

q.p: “is signlessness one thing and śrāvaka dharmas another?”
q.orig: do you think that signlessness is one thing and the attributes of the śrāvakas are another

div.p:
and so on, khri brgyad
. This is the response to Subhūti’s two hundred and eleventh question. the Lord explains that if, given that all dharmas are signless, he had presented śrāvaka dharmas and so on as having signs, then there would be a fault, but because they are all signless there is therefore no fault.

q.p:
“Does that not complicate the dharma-constituent?” khri brgyad
. This is Subhūti’s two hundred and thirteenth question, “Lord, if bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom are aware in that way of those dharmas that are different from each other, well then, Lord, does that not complicate the dharma-constituent?”
q.orig: would the realm of phenomena not be disrupted?

div.p: This means it would complicate it, because, when they realize defining marks in dharmas that have no defining marks, they would grasp each differently even though they are in fact suchness.

q.p: “Subhūti, the dharma-constituent would be complicated if there were to be any other dharma not included in the dharma-constituent,”
q.orig: it would be complicated if any other dharma not included in the dharma-constituent were to be apprehended
Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “the realm of phenomena would be disrupted if there were any extraneous phenomena existing apart from it

div.p: and so on. With this the Lord teaches that even though they conceive of dharmas like that, still, later they realize with wisdom that all are not different because of having the dharma-constituent as their intrinsic nature. Therefore, they do not complicate the dharma-constituent.
is the suchness of form.

q.p: “Do they train in form?”

div.p: Subhūti is asking: since all dharmas are exhausted in the dharma-constituent, the dharmas, form and so on, would be absolutely nonexistent, so, when they train in them would it not be similar to an error?

q.p:
“Are aware of all dharmas as they really are, the dharma-constituent,” khri brgyad
. This is part of the long response at khri brgyad
–.
q.orig: they know all phenomena to be the realm of phenomena

div.p: and so on, says: They see the dharmas, form and so on, as just the dharma-constituent, not as something else. They cannot inspire beings to take it up in some other way, so they teach the dharma-constituent with skillful means, having designated form and so on as signlessness.

q.p:
“Subhūti, if the dharma-constituent were not exactly the same later as it was before, and if it were not like that in between as well,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Subhūti, if the realm of phenomena were not in the future exactly the same as it was in the past, and if it were not exactly the same in the interim

div.p: and so on, is teaching: “before,” at the time of a foolish, ordinary person, the dharma-constituent was impure; “in between,” at the time of a bodhisattva, it is pure and impure; and “later,” at the end, it is absolutely pure. So far so good, but you should not understand from this that there are specific features there. In its intrinsic nature it is pure at all times, pure in its absolutely pure nature.

q.p:
“Subhūti, having taken the very limit of reality as the measure” khri brgyad
. If the ultimate nature that is pure from the beginning and nirvāṇa, and the ultimate nature of beings caught in saṃsāra based on falsely imagined things conjured out of thin air, is the same ultimate nature, how can you talk about beings in saṃsāra getting to nirvāṇa?
q.orig: Subhūti, bodhisattva great beings cultivate the perfection of wisdom, having taken the very limit of reality as their standard

div.p: is saying: Bodhisattvas do not practice the perfection of wisdom for the sake of beings, they practice for the sake of the very limit of reality. Thus, having set aside nonexistent beings because they are not existent, they establish them in the very limit of reality that is their intrinsic nature. The very limit of beings is made into the very limit of reality.

q.p: “Lord, if just the very limit of reality is also the limit of beings”
q.orig: Lord, if the very limit of reality is also the limit of beings
Blessed Lord, if the very limit of reality is not one thing and the very limit of beings

div.p: is asking: if a “limit of beings” were not to exist as anything other than the very limit of reality, well then, beings and the very limit of reality would be the same, so what you have said, that they

q.p: “establish beings at the very limit of reality”
q.orig: establish beings in the very limit of reality

div.p: would not be right. If they were to establish just that in that, they would be saying “the very limit of reality enters into the very limit of reality,” and that is not right either.
The Lord says,

q.p: “With skillful means they establish the limit of beings at the very limit of reality without complicating the very limit of reality.”
q.orig: with skillful means establish the limit of beings at the very limit of reality without complicating the very limit of reality
through skill in means they do establish the very limit of beings in the very limit of reality, and they do not disturb the very limit of reality

div.p: An intrinsic nature does not enter into an intrinsic nature. Having eliminated a falsely imagined limit of beings and a falsely imagined real basis of beings with skillful means, they establish them in their intrinsic nature, which is absolutely pure suchness, “establishing them at the very limit of reality.” Therefore, this means that the very limit of reality and the limit of beings are an undivided unity,

q.p: “are not two.”
q.orig: are indivisible

div.p: Then he asks,

q.p:
“What are the skillful means?” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: what is the skill in means

div.p: And

q.p: “Subhūti, here, starting from the first production of the thought, bodhisattva great beings,”
q.orig: Subhūti,” replied the Blessed One, “when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, commencing from their first setting of the mind on enlightenment

div.p: and so on, teaches that having transformed all dharmas into the very limit of reality, the completion of the six perfections is skillful means.

The instruction in the perfections is easy to understand. khri brgyad
–.

q.p: “Lord, if all phenomena are empty of a basic nature, and if in the emptiness of a basic nature a being is not apprehended, nor are a dharma and a path apprehended,”
q.orig: Blessed Lord, if in that manner all phenomena are empty of inherent existence‍—and if in the emptiness of inherent existence beings are not apprehended, nor is anything at all apprehended

div.p:
and so on, khri brgyad
. asks the following: if all phenomena are empty of an intrinsic nature and “a being… a dharma, and a path” do not exist,

q.p: “how will bodhisattva great beings,”
q.orig: how then, Blessed Lord, do bodhisattva great beings

div.p: having brought beings to maturity, having purified a buddhafield, and having cultivated the knowledge of path aspects,

q.p: “stand in the knowledge of all aspects?”
q.orig: embark on all-aspect omniscience

div.p: Then the Lord, with

q.p: “Subhūti, were all phenomena not empty of a basic nature,”
q.orig: Subhūti, if all phenomena were not empty of inherent existence

div.p: and so on, teaches that if dharmas or paths were to exist separately, it would be right to apprehend something, and in that case there would be all living beings and so on, and bodhisattvas would not, therefore, having stood in emptiness, become buddhas, and would not explain all dharmas, form and so on, as emptiness. But there are no such dharmas or paths in the emptiness of a basic nature. Therefore, that emptiness is established. Having stood in emptiness they therefore become buddhas and explain all the emptiness dharmas. Hence it is established that they enter into the knowledge of all aspects thanks to the emptiness of a basic nature.
He continues with

q.p: “Subhūti, if inner emptiness were not empty of a basic nature,”
q.orig: Subhūti, if the emptiness of internal phenomena were not empty of inherent existence

div.p: and so on, teaching that not only the trivial dharmas, form and so on, are empty, but that the sixteen emptinesses, inner emptiness and so on, are empty of a basic nature too. Were inner emptiness and so on not empty of a basic nature, the explanation of all dharmas as emptiness would not be well founded.

div.head: Emptiness of a basic nature

q.p:
“The emptiness of a basic nature would have been destroyed.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: the emptiness of inherent existence would collapse

div.p: If inner emptiness and so on were not also empty of a basic nature, the teaching

q.p: “that ‘all dharmas are empty of a basic nature’ ”
q.orig: that all phenomena are empty of inherent existence

div.p: would get damaged, in the sense of being destroyed. Then

q.p:
“the emptiness of a basic nature does not perish, is not immovable, and is not nonrecurring” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: the emptiness of inherent existence will neither collapse, nor will it endure eternally, nor will it go away in the future

div.p:
teaches the emptiness that is the mark of the establishment of dharmas. This mark of the establishment of dharmas, furthermore, is taught fourfold: khri brgyad
. not perishing and so on; not increasing or decreasing and so on; not being established and not being established after having set out; and not obstructing.

There, the first of those subsections is: it “does not perish” because it is uncompounded; it “is not immovable” because it is constituted as a nonexistent thing; and it “is not nonrecurring” because it is freedom from forms of life. Then it again teaches these same three in detail with

q.p: “it does occupy a location,” D and Golden 385b6 both read yul na ni gnas (alternative translation: “it is there as an object”). If emended to ni mi based on the reading at khri brgyad (ga 104a6), it would mean “it does not occupy a location,” which is certainly easier to understand.
q.orig: it does not occupy a location
it does not dwell in any location

div.p: teaching that it is in an uncompounded state because something compounded occupies a location; it

q.p: “does not stand in a place,”
q.orig: it does not dwell in any direction

div.p: because it is pervaded by a nonexistent thing; and it

q.p: “does not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere,”
q.orig: does not come from anywhere, and does not go anywhere
it does not arise from anywhere, and it does not go anywhere

div.p: because it is freedom from forms of life.

The second subsection on not increasing and so on is as before.
,
,
.

q.p:
“All dharmas are not established” Cf. khri brgyad
: “In regard to all dharmas, there is no establishment and there is no destruction.” Our author’s gloss supports the better reading at khri brgyad K ’jug (“and not established after having set out”). The Tib renderings of Skt sthā (gnas) and prasthā (’jug) should be understood having in mind Tib forms of prior-state and resultant nonvolitional verbs (Tournadre 2010).
q.orig: all dharmas, there is no establishment
All phenomena are not to be engaged

div.p: because they are in their intrinsic nature not established,

q.p: “and not established after having set out”

div.p:
because an escape does not exist. These two teach the investigation of the two—the “established” and the “established after having set out”—in the statement about dharmas other than these two, “established in which bodhisattvas are, after setting out, established in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.” Cf. khri brgyad
(reading K, etc., ’jug in place of D ’jig, “destroyed”). “Having stood there, bodhisattva great beings stand in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, but do not see any dharma established at all after having set out.”

q.p: “They do not see any dharma at all as obstructing”
q.orig: they do not observe anything at all that is obscured thereby

div.p: as an attachment to emptiness.

q.p: “They see all dharmas as not obstructing”
q.orig: they observe…that all phenomena are without obscuration

div.p: means they see all dharmas are empty. Then, they

q.p: “do not apprehend… a self,”
q.orig: self is not apprehensible

div.p: and so on, teaches

q.p: “the emptiness of a basic nature.”
q.orig: emptiness of inherent existence

q.p: “In that”—
q.orig: in the

div.p: in this emptiness of a basic nature. The “emptiness of a basic nature” teaches that persons have no self, and dharmas have no self. The illustration of

q.p: “a tathāgata’s… magically created monk or nun”
q.orig: monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen emanated by the tathāgatas

div.p: establishes those two selflessnesses.

q.p:
“Just that error is itself not error.” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: those erroneous views are not actually erroneous

div.p: Earlier, in the context of the falsely imagined, “just that” foundation “is itself error”; in the context of the thoroughly purified it is “not error.”

q.p: “Because of having thought construction as cause” Cf. khri brgyad (ga 105a4) ma yin pa, “not having thought construction as cause.” —
q.orig: because of having…thought construction as cause
because they have originated [merely] from the causal basis of false imaginations

div.p: it has in mind a falsely imagined result.

q.p: “They, furthermore, are not exactly like the ultimate there”
q.orig: they too do not exist as such from the point of view of ultimate reality

div.p: means

q.p: “the applications of mindfulness,”
q.orig: the four applications of mindfulness

div.p:
and so on, are falsely imagined, they are not the ultimate. That emptiness of a basic nature is also called “perfection.” This is connecting paramārtha (“ultimate”) with pāramitā (“perfection”). Just below (khri brgyad
): “Therefore, bodhisattva great beings, having stood in the perfection that is the emptiness of a basic nature…”

q.p:
“That emptiness of a basic nature, furthermore, is the emptiness of a basic nature at the prior limit,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: This emptiness of inherent existence is indeed the emptiness of inherent existence with respect to the past

div.p: and so on, teaches it is emptiness at all three times.

q.p:
“Thus, it is amazing how they practice all dharmas that are the emptiness of a basic nature without complicating the emptiness of a basic nature.” Cf. ’bum na 146a4, nyi khri , khri brgyad
.
q.orig: it is amazing how bodhisattva great beings practice without complicating the emptiness of a basic nature
it is wonderful that bodhisattva great beings practice everything in that manner through the emptiness of inherent existence, and yet do not disrupt the emptiness of inherent existence

div.p: The idea is that engaging with dharmas that do not exist would complicate emptiness. So, he says

q.p: “form is not one thing and the emptiness of a basic nature another.”
q.orig: form…is not one thing and the emptiness of a basic nature another
[by holding] that physical forms are one distinct thing and the emptiness of inherent existence another

div.p: Thus, it is saying “it is amazing” how when bodhisattvas engage with phenomena, they see that form and so on “is not one thing and the emptiness of a basic nature another,” that just those, form and so on, are the emptiness of a basic nature.

q.p: “Fully awaken to form itself as the knower of all aspects”—
q.orig: fully awaken to…form…as a knower of all aspects

div.p: this means fully awakening to the dharmas, form and so on, at the time of the knowledge of all aspects because there is no difference between them.

q.p:
“On the contrary, the world together with the gods, together with Māra, together with Brahmā” khri brgyad
.—
q.orig: On the contrary, those in the worlds frequented by gods and the worlds frequented by Māra and Brahmā

div.p: “on the contrary,” they do not know that form and so on are only one. It means ordinary beings

q.p: “do not know”
q.orig: deludedly think

div.p: as they really are that form and so on are only one, and

q.p: “on account of not knowing,”

div.p: they

q.p: “settle down on”
q.orig: fixated on

div.p: them and accumulate karma, grasp hold of and

q.p: “appropriate form,”
q.orig: appropriate…form[4]
acquire physical forms

div.p: and so on, that are its maturation. On account of that they come into suffering existence caused by appropriation, and

q.p: “are not liberated from”
q.orig: will not be liberated from

div.p: suffering.

q.p:
“…the emptiness of a basic nature … [they] do not complicate form with ‘it is empty, or it is not empty.’ ” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: the emptiness of a basic nature, bodhisattva great beings do not complicate…form…with ‘it is empty,’ or ‘it is not empty’
the emptiness of inherent existence, do not disrupt physical forms, holding that they are either empty or not empty

div.p: Form does not make emptiness complicated on account of the perception of duality, because there is no duality.

q.p:
“It is because the ‘this is form,’ and ‘this is emptiness’… that might make that sort of complication have no intrinsic existence” khri brgyad
.—
q.orig: Because the ‘this is form,’ and ‘this is emptiness,’ up to ‘this is feeling . . . ,’ ‘perception . . . ,’ ‘volitional factors . . . ,’ and ‘consciousness,’ and ‘this is emptiness’; similarly, connect this with each, up to ‘this is awakening,’ and ‘this is emptiness’ that might make that sort of complication have no intrinsic existence.

all these phenomena are without any inherent existence that might disturb one into thinking, ‘These are physical forms, and this is emptiness. These are feelings, perceptions, formative predispositions, and consciousness, and this is emptiness. These are [the attributes and goals], up to and including unsurpassed, complete enlightenment, and this is emptiness.’

div.p: no intrinsic existence that constitutes an existent thing.

q.p:
“Bodhisattva great beings do not practice awakening and form within having made a division.” Cf. khri brgyad
. This part is an explanation of khri brgyad
–, although our author’s version of the Sūtra differs. He is saying, in essence, that the Sūtra is saying that bodhisattvas treat the constituents of themselves as bodhisattvas, their form aggregate and so on, the same as the constituents of themselves in an awakened state. Both are the same from the perspective of the emptiness of a basic nature that is not different from the different dharmas.
q.orig: a bodhisattva great being’s awakening is not practiced within a division
the enlightenment of the bodhisattvas does not engage in dualistic concepts

q.p: “They do not practice form having made a division in awakening.”
q.orig: A bodhisattva great being’s awakening is not a practice of…form
The enlightenment of the bodhisattvas does not engage in physical forms

div.p: This means they do not engage with form having made a division into the bodhisattva and the awakening in “bodhisattvas practice awakening.”

q.p: “Subhūti, bodhisattva great beings do not think, ‘I am practicing awakening and form.’ ”

div.p: They do not, making a division, engage with form, thinking, “I am practicing awakening.”

q.p:
“A practice of taking anything up” khri brgyad
.—
q.orig: engage in grasping

div.p: engaging with a causal sign.

q.p:
“Stand in the basic nature of form” khri brgyad
.—
q.orig: Stand in the basic nature of…form
established in the essential nature of physical forms

div.p: stand in the emptiness of form.

q.p:
“Moreover, … simply based on… labeled by way of ordinary convention” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: According to the reality that is conceived in mundane, conventional terms, bodhisattva great beings will attain consummate buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete enlightenment

div.p: teaches that ultimately even unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening does not exist.
When they practice just those dharmas it means they practice just those, giving and so on,

q.p:
“without apprehending giving, … a benefactor,” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: without apprehending gifts, donors

div.p: and so on.

q.p:
“Lord, how, when bodhisattva great beings are practicing the perfection of wisdom, do they make an effort at the awakening path?” nyi khri ; cf. khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Lord, how do bodhisattva great beings practicing the perfection of wisdom make an effort at the awakening path?
Blessed Lord, when bodhisattva great beings practice the perfection of wisdom, how do they persevere in the path of enlightenment?

div.p: How, if all the awakening path does not exist, is the idea.

q.p: “[They] do not disengage from form,”
q.orig: do not disengage from…form
nor disassociate from physical forms

div.p: because form and so on do not exist.

q.p:
“How will the perfection of wisdom… be accomplished” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: how do bodhisattva great beings actualize the perfection of wisdom

div.p: given that it does not exist?

The explanations of skillful means and of the perfection of wisdom that cannot be grasped are easy to understand. khri brgyad
–.
The question,

q.p:
“Has there been or will there be a real basis of form in the way a foolish ordinary person has settled down on it?” khri brgyad
.
q.orig: Has there been or will there be a real basis of…form…in the way a foolish ordinary person has settled down on it
has there existed, or will there exist an entity of physical forms such as that on which ordinary people are fixated?

div.p: is a statement about the three times.

q.p:
“If something that really existed was there before” khri brgyad
; cf. nyi khri .—
q.orig: something that really existed before
had existed in the past

div.p: this means that if they were to grasp all those they grasped as there before as not there later,

q.p: “there would be the fault.” “The fault is that a bodhisattva and tathāgata ‘would have been there before and would not be there later.’ There would also be the fault that the five forms of life in the stream of cyclic existence would have been something that really existed before and would be something that really does not exist later,” and so on.
q.orig: there would thus be the fault
there would be a fault

q.p:
“Lord, what is the bodhisattva great beings’ path?” khri brgyad
. This is Subhūti’s two hundred and twenty-fourth question.
q.orig: Blessed Lord, what path of enlightenment do bodhisattva great beings practice

div.p: is a question about the path that comprises bringing beings to maturity and purifying a buddhafield.

Then the explanation of the six perfections, the explanation of the path, the explanation of the training in all dharmas, and the explanation of no location can be grasped from a close reading of the scripture. khri brgyad
– is the explanation of the six perfections; – is the explanation of the path; – is the explanation of the training in all dharmas; and – is the explanation of no location. “Close reading” renders rjes su bsnyags pa (Jäschke says it is a colloquial form of snyeg; Mvy samanubandh), literally “to hasten after.”

q.p:
“Lord, if all dharmas are unproduced, well then, Lord, how will bodhisattva great beings produce a path to awakening?” khri brgyad
. This is Subhūti’s two hundred and twenty-ninth question.
q.orig: Blessed Lord, if all phenomena are nonarising, how will bodhisattva great beings achieve the path of enlightenment?

div.p: This intends that the statement “they should produce the unproduced” is not logical. With,

q.p: “All dharmas have not been produced. How so? All dharmas have not been produced for those who do not occasion anything,” “Do not occasion anything” means that they have not accumulated the karma that would give rise to the production, or they have removed the accompanying conditions that would make the karma ripen.
q.orig: All phenomena are nonarising. If you ask how that is so, all phenomena are nonarising for those who do not effect conditioning.
